heading_path: 1.1 Introduction
text:
### **1.1 Introduction**

The Kingdom of Eswatini under the leadership of the Ministry of Health is committed to improve the quality of health care that positively impacts the health of the population. In view of this, the Government has prioritized the health of women, newborn, children and adolescents. The Kingdom of Eswatini strives to ensure that every pregnant woman and newborn receive quality care throughout pregnancy, childbirth and postnatal period. The adaptation of the WHO ANC recommendations for positive pregnancy experience is one way for the Government of Eswatini to achieve the national Maternal and Neonatal Health (MNH) targets, hence the need for the development of the National ANC guidelines.

According to the SRH annual report, there was an increase in 1<sup>st</sup> ANC coverage from 92% in 2016 to 95% 2017. In SRH Report 2017, 96% pregnant women tested for HIV 35% tested positive and 93% were initiated on lifelong ART for the prevention of mother to child transmission of HIV. This trend improved from 39% in 2015 but was higher compared to women testing positive in 2016 (34%). In 2017, 97% of pregnant women were screened for syphilis and 2 % of these were syphilis positive. The same report showed a gap in the treatment of syphilis with only 84% of the women being treated for syphilis.

heading_path: 1.0 Background > 1.2 Situation Analysis
text:
Pregnancy is a critical period for the mother and unborn baby thus quality care during pregnancy is very essential. The 2016 WHO recommendations on ANC for positive pregnancy experience recommends a shift from 4 focused ANC visits to a minimum of 8 contacts to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women experience of care. The guidelines can be deployed as a platform of national essential health care package and can ensure that the health system is prepared to provide quality ANC services.

In spite of the impressive progress made, there is urgent need for more investment in improvement of the quality of maternal and neonatal health. Of note, is that the majority of the deaths are preventable. The SARA, 2017 notes that availability of ANC services stands at 75 percent whilst the mean readiness score is low at 56 percent. In this regard the SARA recommended in-service trainings of health care workers in the provision of ANC services as well as equipping all health facilities with updated guidelines for providing ANC services .

text:
### **1.3 Rationale for ANC Guidelines**

This guideline is meant to guide and standardize provision of integrated ANC services to pregnant women and adolescents so that they can experience respectful, individualized, person-centred care at every ANC contact. It also facilitates provision of effective clinical practices, relevant and timely information, and psychosocial and emotional support, by practitioners with good interpersonal skills within a well-functioning health system.

heading_path: 1.4 Guiding Principles of Antenatal care service delivery
text:
# 1.4 Guiding Principles of Antenatal care service delivery

This guideline is in line with the Global and National commitments. It operationalizes the SRH policy and embraces its guiding principles and values. The guiding principle and values for the ANC guidelines are as follows:
**I. Non-discrimination (Human rights)**

Within the overall right to health which incorporates the fundamental human right to sexual and reproductive health, all women and girls are entitled to ANC services irrespective of their culture, religion, age, race, disability, HIV status, sexual orientation and economic status.

**II. Client centeredness**

*Each ANC client will receive respectful, individualized, person-centered services that meet their needs, medical condition, cultural and socioeconomic circumstances and facilitated through good rapport and communication between the care provider and the pregnant woman as well as ensuring confidentiality and informed consent.*

**III. Quality Care services**

ANC services that are safe, effective, timely, efficient, equitable and people-centered are delivered to individual adolescent girls and women with a view to produce improved desired health outcomes for both the mother and the baby. The ANC services must be based on scientific knowledge and evidence-based guidelines.

**IV. Integration**

ANC service provision will be integrated to ensure that a wide spectrum of health care services that include HIV, TB, Malaria and other non-communicable diseases are accessible and acceptable to the pregnant woman and at all levels in line with the ANC guidelines.

**V. Community involvement and participation**

## 1.5 Governance, Coordination and Organisation

### 1.5.1 <u>The Policy environment</u>

The National Health Sector Strategic Plan III (2019-2023) focuses on the attainment of universal health coverage. This can be attained when all the people in the Kingdom have access to quality, effective and affordable health care services. The SRH policy further stipulates that quality MNCH Services shall be provided by competent and skilled service providers during ANC within adequately equipped health facilities. The Ministry of Health must therefore ensure that the requisite human resources, infrastructure, equipment and supplies, technical guidance tools are availed for service delivery and that the capacity of service providers is strengthened if they are to deliver high quality services based on the guidelines. As such, with a conducive policy environment, the country is poised for scaled up universal ANC coverage.

### 1.5.2 <u>Governance and Coordination of Health services</u>

The Directorate in the Ministry of Health provides overall leadership and is technically led by the SRH Program Manager working with Program Officers at the national level. The national team works with an Inter - Agency Technical Coordinating Committee (IATCC) for SRH and is responsible for planning, monitoring and, implementation of the activities of the SRH program including ANC. At the decentralized level there is the Regional Health Management Team (RHMT) which has an oversight function of coordination and the implementation of the program at subnational level.

heading_path: 2.0 ANC Contact Schedule
text:
## **2.0 ANC Contact Schedule**

ANC is key in saving lives and for creating the necessary foundations for healthy motherhood .<sup>11</sup> Evidence shows that there is an increase in perinatal mortality related to Focused Antenatal Care (FANC), and women want more contacts with the health worker during pregnancy for a positive pregnancy experience. In addition, increased contacts enhance the likelihood of early detection and management of pregnancy complications hence the rationale for more ANC contacts.

A new model with eight (8) scheduled contacts is adopted to make the maximum impact.

text:
### Eight ANC contacts schedule: 1st contact 8-12 weeks, then 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks

A new model with eight scheduled contacts is adopted (WHO 2016), replacing focused ANC (4 visits), to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women's experience of care.

| Contact | Recommended schedule |
| --- | --- |
| 1st contact | As soon as the woman suspects she is pregnant; during the first trimester (preferably 8–12 weeks) |
| 2nd scheduled contact | 20 weeks |
| 3rd scheduled contact | 26 weeks |
| 4th scheduled contact | 30 weeks |
| 5th scheduled contact | 34 weeks |
| 6th scheduled contact | 36 weeks |
| 7th scheduled contact | 38 weeks |
| 8th scheduled contact | 40 weeks |

Eswatini ANC Guidelines | 2.0 ANC Contact Schedule > 2.2 Essential Package of ANC Interventions (page 14)

Essential package of ANC interventions at each of the 8 contacts: maternal and foetal assessment, counselling topics, point-of-care tests, lab investigations, ultrasound, preventive measures (IFA, calcium, deworming, PrEP), clinical practices, management, and cadres (part 8 of 9).
Contact 8 at 40 weeks: Maternal assessment: Ask how mother is doing, clinical estimation of gestational age, physical examination, SFH/abdominal palpation, TB screening, IPV, ask about foetal movements, rule out PROM, ask about symptoms of labour; Foetal assessment: FHR auscultation, ask about foetal movements; Counselling topics (information, education and counselling): Nutrition; diet; physical activity, rest, HIV test; avoid: caffeine intake, alcohol/tobacco/substance abuse; IPV, danger signs, emergency preparedness, IYCF, breastfeeding, FP/HTSP, EIMC, early stimulation of the baby; counsel on admission if no signs of labour at 41 weeks; Point-of-care tests: Urine dipstick, malaria test; Lab investigations: —; Radiological tests: Ultrasound if indicated; Preventive measures: IFA, calcium, combination prevention (PrEP, condom, VMMC for men); Essential good clinical practices: Weight, BP, MUAC, male involvement, STI screening; Treat / manage: Common physiological disorders; manage complications; refer as per client's needs; Others: Complete ANC card and give to woman; fill ANC register/CMIS.
source_flags: The PDF prints each contact as a rotated landscape table with no text layer; cells were transcribed from the page images.

Several cells are printed twice (contact 3, 4 and 5 preventive measures, clinical practices, management and 'Others'), and on contact 5 text from the maternal-assessment and counselling cells overflows into the preventive-measures and clinical-practices cells. Cleaned up here; the order of the overflow text was inferred.
The 'Cadres' row on p.22 has six columns in the first block and five in the second; mapped to the 11 columns in printed order, so the mapping should be checked.
Calcium and IFA are listed at every contact but doses are not given in this table.

Eswatini ANC Guidelines | 2.0 ANC Contact Schedule > 2.2 Essential Package of ANC Interventions (page 14)

Essential package of ANC interventions at each of the 8 contacts: maternal and foetal assessment, counselling topics, point-of-care tests, lab investigations, ultrasound, preventive measures (IFA, calcium, deworming, PrEP), clinical practices, management, and cadres (part 9 of 9).
Cadres to provide the services: Maternal assessment / Foetal assessment: Midwives, obstetricians, doctors; Counselling topics (information, education and counselling): Midwife, general nurse, nursing assistants, dieticians, nutritionist, health promotion, community health workers, doctors, obstetrician, sonographers; Point-of-care tests: Midwives, general nurses, doctors; Lab investigations: Lab technician; Radiological tests: Radiology, sonographers, obstetricians, midwives; Preventive measures: Nursing assistants; general nurse, midwives; Essential good clinical practices: Midwives (BP), obstetricians (BP), doctors (BP); community health workers (weight, MUAC, height); Treat / manage: Midwives, doctors, obstetricians; Others: Midwives, obstetricians, doctors.
NB: 1. All cadres will be expected to provide IEC; depending on the roster, all midwives will be expected to provide individual counselling. 2. Health promotion will be done for community engagement. 3. Complete the ANC card, enter information into the register and give the card to the pregnant woman. 4. ANC services are offered at clinic, PHU and health centre. 5. Referral for complications to the next level.
IPV – intimate partner violence; HTSP – healthy timing and spacing of pregnancy; IYCF – infant and young child feeding; EIMC – early infant male circumcision; ASB – asymptomatic bacteriuria; IFA – iron and folic acid; SFH – symphysis-fundal height; FHR – foetal heart rate.

heading_path: 3.1 History taking
text:
## 3.1 History taking

At the first contact visit **HISTORY TAKING** must be done. Take a full and relevant history including:
- Demographic profile
- Current and Previous obstetrics history
- Medical (including Mental Health) and surgical history
- Social History (Use of alcohol, tobacco and other substances)
- Family and social circumstances and risk factors (Familial and genetic disorders, allergies)
- Previous antenatal care record should be reviewed to inform the initial assessment

heading_path: 3.2 Maternal assessment
text:
## 3.2 Maternal assessment

Maternal screening forms part of the routine assessment of the pregnant woman where the care provider must do the following:
- Ask about the mother's concerns
- Examination head to toe
- Abdominal palpation
- Screen for Preeclampsia, Anaemia and Asymptomatic Bacteriuria, TB, Malaria, HIV, Syphilis, Hepatitis, gestational diabetes, substance abuse and IPV as appropriate for contact
- Measure gestational age through a Symphysis fundal height (SFH) which is measured using a tape measure. The measurement should correspond to the gestational age of the pregnancy with an allowance of 2cm either ways. Abdominal palpation can also be used to measure fundal height.
- Undertake an ultrasound examination at appropriate (12-24 weeks) gestation as per the guidelines
- Nutritional Assessment: BMI must be established as a baseline assessment for all pregnant women; Weight, height, MUAC should be assessed at each visit
- Blood pressure monitoring at each visit
- Test mid-stream urine for protein.

heading_path: 3.3 Foetal Assessment.
text:
## **3.3 Foetal Assessment.**

* Foetal heart rate (FHR) must be monitored in all pregnant women. A normal FHR is 110 – 160 beats/minute; while an Abnormal FHR <110 b/m and >160 b/m;
* A symphysis fundal height (SFH) is measured in all pregnant women using a tape measure and the measurement should correspond to the gestational age of the pregnancy with an allowance of 2cm either ways.
* Enquire about fetal movement from 20 weeks
* Radiological investigation – **An Ultrasound scan is to be done for every pregnant woman before 24 weeks to identify the following:** gestational age, foetal viability, anomalies (multiple pregnancies, etc.). In case of complications such as antepartum haemorrhage mal-presentations, IUGR, an additional ultrasound may be performed.

heading_path: 3.4 Point of care tests
text:
## **3.4 Point of care tests:**

All point of care tests must be done as stipulated in the contact schedule or in the next contact if it was missed.

### **RPR test for syphilis.**

* Every pregnant woman is tested for syphilis at the first antenatal contact, and retest should be done every 8 weeks. If RPR positive give one (1) dose Benzathine Penicillin 2.4mu IM stat, then weekly x 2 doses. Encourage partner tracing and treatment.
* If hyper-sensitive to benzathine penicillin, refer to STI guidelines for treatment
* Take blood for TPHA in the next contact if RPR positive and treated in the previous contact.

heading_path: 3.4 Point of care tests > Haemoglobin for monitoring anaemia .
text:
### **Haemoglobin for monitoring anaemia .**

* Check for pallor at every contact and check hemoglobin at contact 1,3, and 6.

### **HIV**

* Each pregnant woman must be asked about her HIV status and offered HIV testing services at the first contact if negative or of unknown status (refer to the National Integrated HIV guidelines).
* If the pregnant woman refuses the test or is not willing to disclose the result of previous test or no test results available, assess for signs suggesting severe or advanced HIV infection; Counsel on benefits of testing and knowing their status, safer sex including use of condoms and benefits of involving and testing the Partner.

heading_path: 3.4 Point of care tests
text:
## 3.4 Point of care tests:

### **TB**

* Every pregnant woman should be screened for TB at every contact, if positive, Refer to National TB guidelines.

<hr/>

<sup>12</sup> WHO 2016 ANC recommendations

## **Rapid hepatitis B**

- All pregnant women should be screened for viral Hepatitis B during first antenatal contact
  Rescreening is recommended for negative clients at the same time as rescreening is done for syphilis and HIV (every 8 weeks).
- If positive, counsel and refer to next level of care to start treatment

heading_path: 3.4 Point of care tests > Malaria
text:
## **Malaria**

- Test using RDT and treat if positive. (Refer to national malaria treatment guideline)

## **Urine dip-stick.**

- All pregnant women are to be tested for glycosuria and proteinuria at every scheduled contact using a urine dipstick
- If glycosuria is evident or client has history (self or family) of diabetes mellitus, further blood tests are recommended to exclude gestational diabetes. (see section 6. 7 of this guideline)
- For any other abnormality treat or refer accordingly.

heading_path: 3.5 Laboratory
text:
## **3.5 Laboratory:**

- Test for Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)
  - Collect a midstream urine specimen to check for ASB through a Gram stain or culture at the 1<sup>st</sup> contact visit and repeated at 26 weeks (contact 3).
  - For management of ASB <u>see section 7.2 of this guideline</u>.
- Full blood count (FBC).
  - Conduct FBC testing for diagnosing anaemia and this will guide on the course of action.
  - Normal hemoglobin level should be >11 g/dl
  - If HB is <11 g/dl see section 7.1 for management
  - On each subsequent contact look for conjunctival pallor; palmar pallor. Ifpallor is moderate or severe Check haemoglobin level(see section 7.1 of this guideline)

heading_path: 3.6 Preventive measures
text:
## **3.6 Preventive measures**

All health care providers in health facilities must ensure that all pregnant women get all recommended preventive measures in line with the 8 contact schedule. The interventions include prevention of Tetanus, Nutritional anaemia, HIV, Intestinal worms, malaria in pregnancy. Facility based and community based health workers must emphasize the importance of treatment adherence.

heading_path: 3.0 Providing ANC Services > 3.6 Preventive Measures > Tetanus-Diphtheria (Td) Vaccination
text:
### Td (tetanus-diphtheria) vaccination in pregnancy by prior TTCV doses: unknown/none, 3 or 4 childhood doses, later boosters – doses needed and intervals

If a pregnant woman received:
- No TTCV doses or unknown vaccination status → she will need: (a) 1 Td dose as early as possible; (b) 1 Td dose at least 4 weeks later; (c) 1 Td dose at least 6 months later; (d) 1 Td dose at least 1 year later; (e) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection).
- Only 3 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at the first ANC visit; (b) another Td dose 4 weeks later (to be protected for that pregnancy); (c) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 3 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td or 1 DT dose later → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td dose later → 1 Td dose at that contact (no further doses required).
- 4 TTCV doses and 2 Td boosters → no vaccination; the woman is fully protected.
(TTCV = tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine.)

heading_path: 3.7 Counselling and information provision > 3.7.1 Caffeine intake
text:
### 3.7.1 Caffeine intake

- Women must be informed that a high daily intake (>300mg per day) is probably associated with a higher risk of low birth weight and pregnancy loss.
  Explain that a cup of coffee contains about 60mg of caffeine whilst caffeine containing teas contain 50mg per 250ml cup.
  Explain that caffeine can be found in tea (black tea and green tea) coffee, caffeinated soft drinks, chocolate and some medicines.
- Discourage pregnant women from taking caffeine because of the associated risks.

heading_path: 3.7 Counselling and information provision > 3.7.5 Emergency preparedness and Complication readiness
text:
## 3.7.5 Emergency preparedness and Complication readiness

- Educate the women on danger signs in pregnancy. These include:
  - Vaginal bleeding,
  - Draining liquor,
  - Reduced / loss of fetal movement,
  - Swelling of hands and feet,
  - Severe headache
  - Blurred vision,
  - Fever,
  - Convulsions and unconsciousness
  - Severe abdominal pains.
- **Emphasise and alert the pregnant woman to go to hospital if the above conditions present.**
- Advise the woman on the importance of getting to the hospital without delay and how to prepare for emergency delivery

text:
## 3.7.6 Counsel on Family planning

Counsel the pregnant woman on the following:
- Enquire about the plans to have more children
- Explain the importance of family planning
- Explain about birth spacing and that for the health of the mother and baby, it is recommended to space at least 24 months between births.
- Explain the importance of waiting at least 2 years after caesarean section before conceiving again
- Explain about safer sex , STI prevention including HIV.
- Explain the methods of family planning indicating options for:
  - Immediate use
  - 6 weeks postpartum
  - < 6months postpartum
  - > 6 months postpartum
- Explain about Lactational Amenorrhea (LAM)
- Assist the client to identify when they would like to start using a FP method after delivery

## 3.7.7 Routine and follow-up contacts

Advise that:
- All pregnant women must have eight (8) scheduled antenatal contacts.
- Explain that these contacts are for women without any complications. And that if they have pregnancy complications, they should seek care from a qualified health professional immediately.

- Advise to return if she does not deliver within 1 week after the expected date of delivery.
- Emphasize the importance of seeking medical care for any problems that arise during the pregnancy

heading_path: 3.7 Counselling and information provision > 3.7.9 Baby stimulation
text:
## 3.7.9 Baby stimulation

- Advise the pregnant woman on baby stimulation whilst in utero. The following are suggestions:
  - Make contact with your baby in some way every day in a private, peaceful and quiet place (Be consistent)
  - Get comfortable and relax - “tune out” from the rest of the world and focus only on your baby for at least 15 minutes twice a day or 30 minutes in one go. Soften your tight muscles by being calm and be slow whilst doing abdominal breathing which will settle you and your baby very quickly
  - You can play music, simply talk to your baby or read the baby a story while you massage your belly and make this a habit and continue to do this throughout pregnancy, especially after the sixth month. Do gentle intentional touch with a purpose using small amount of simple baby oil, tissue oil or a cold pressed oil, so as to reduce the friction on the skin, and enable your hands to glide around the abdomen.
  - Encourage the woman to allow the father to experiment with different ways of massaging the mother's belly as his touch will make her feel loved and special and these feelings will pass on to the baby who will feel the same.

## 4.0 **Standard precautions for infection control and prevention**

- Observe these precautions to protect the woman and her baby, and you as the health provider, from infections with bacteria and viruses, including HIV.

## 4.1 **TB IPC**

- Screen all pregnant women for TB
- If they screen positive provide mask and collect sputum and then document on appropriate registers.
- Ensure proper ventilation in screening room
- Health worker must put on a well -fitting respirator

text:
## 4.2 **PPE for health worker**

- Wear sterile gloves when performing vaginal examination/drawing blood
- Wear gowns, safety shoes or shoe covers.
- Sterilize and clean contaminated equipment
- Change linen after each use

## 4.3 **Injection safety**

- Keep a puncture resistant and open enough container nearby.
- Use each needle and syringe only once
- Do not recap, bend or break needles after giving an injection.
- Drop all used (disposable) needles, plastic syringes and blades directly into this container, without recapping, and without passing to another person.
- Send for incineration when the **container is three quarters** full

## 5.0 Nutrition in Pregnancy

Pregnancy and lactation is a time when a woman needs to pay a lot of attention to her diet. During this period, the growing foetus is entirely dependent on the mother for nourishment and growth in the uterus. This is possible only when pregnant mother receives all the nutrients from her diet. Risks of poor nutrition during pregnancy include –among others- low birth weight, higher risk of child being born with deformity, maternal anaemia, maternal obesity or undernourishment with their associated complications.

heading_path: 5.1 Weight gain
text:
## 5.1 Weight gain

Obesity during pregnancy increases the odds of spontaneous and recurrent miscarriages, suboptimal ultrasound screening for foetal anomalies, congenital heart and neural tube defects, wound Infections, anaesthesia complications, depression, breastfeeding problems, and many other adverse outcomes.

Most normal gestational weight gain occurs after 20 weeks of gestation. On an average a pregnant mother needs to gain 10-12 kg weight. However, recommended weight gain depends on the woman's pre-pregnant body mass index (BMI). Women who are underweight at the start of pregnancy (BMI < 18.5 kg/m2) should aim to gain 12.5–18 kg. Women who are normal weight at the start of pregnancy (BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m2) should aim to gain 11.5–16 kg. Overweight women (BMI 25–29.9 kg/m2) should aim to gain 7–11.5 kg. Obese women (BMI > 30 kg/m2) should aim to gain 5–9 kg. Pregnant women are discouraged from engaging in stringent weight reduction diets. Nonetheless, women should be advised on appropriate weight management before pregnancy. If, however they are already obese by the time they get pregnant, nutrition counselling / advice should be provided to ensure optimum weight gain without compromising the maternal and foetal health status.

heading_path: 5.2 Nutrition and Diet
text:
## 5.2 Nutrition and Diet

An optimal diet for a pregnant woman should include the three food groups and ensure that the meals are as varied and as colourful as possible on a daily basis. Examples of foods from the different groups are shown below:
**Protein foods:** flesh foods such as meat, chicken, fish, liver, eggs and milk and milk products, Legumes such as beans, lentils, peas, groundnuts.

**Energy foods:** Staples: grains such as maize, wheat, rice and sorghum; Roots and Tubers such as sweet potatoes, potatoes.

**Fruits and Vegetables:** Vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables such as mango, papaya (paw-paw), oranges, dark-green leafy vegetables (spinach, pumpkin leaves, inkaka, *chuchuza*, *imbuya*, lettuce), carrots, yellow sweet potato, pumpkin, and other fruits and vegetables such as banana, pineapple, watermelon, tomatoes, avocado, and cabbage.

Wash your hands before you begin your food preparation.

- Wash your hands before you begin your food preparation.

text:
## 5.3 Basics on Food Preparation

- Rinse cooking utensils and wipe table tops before use.
- Wash fruits and vegetables under cold running water to remove any lingering dirt and reduce bacteria before cutting them to preserve water soluble vitamins.
- Soak green leafy vegetables before cutting them for about 5 minutes in salty water to destroy snails and rinse under running water.
- When preparing fruits and vegetables, cut away any damaged or bruised areas because those are the areas in which bacteria can thrive.
- Soak lentils and beans before cooking them to remove the phytates and other minerals that prevent absorption of iron.
- Do not thaw and refrigerate meat.
- Wash your hands and utensils after handling raw meat to prevent cross contamination.

heading_path: 5.4 Physical activity
text:
## 5.4 Physical activity

- Being physically active is encouraged during pregnancy.
- Women should aim at maintaining a good level of fitness throughout pregnancy by walking and doing normal household chores such as, cleaning, cooking, and washing.
- Pregnant women are discouraged from overexertion and recommended to reduce their workload. Avoid standing for long periods
- They should have regular resting moments throughout the day.

heading_path: 5.5 Micronutrient supplementation
text:
## 5.5 Micronutrient supplementation

All pregnant women should take daily oral iron and folic supplementation with 30mg to 60 mg of elemental iron and 400 ug (0.4mg) folic acid to prevent anaemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth.

Pregnant women should also receive daily calcium supplements of 1.5gram per day.

Encourage women to increase iron-intake by combining foods that help absorption such as spinach, livers, guavas and oranges with your vegetables.

Use margarine (sparingly) where possible as this is fortified with iron. The expecting mother to be encouraged to eat Folic acid rich foods such as green leafy vegetables, beans, bread and Calcium rich foods such as milk, yoghurt and cheese.

**NB:** The use of multiple micronutrient supplementation including multivitamins, Vitamin D, E, B6, Zinc, omega 3 & 6, etc. is not recommended for routine antenatal care clients.

heading_path: 5.6 Key messages
text:
## 5.6 Key messages

- All pregnant women should be counseled on nutrition and diet at each ANC visit. These messages should be reinforced by the CHWs during home visits.
- Pregnant women should take a diet with diverse food types to improve the quality and micronutrient intake.
- Pregnant women should avoid coffee, caffeinated soft drinks, energy drinks, chocolate, fatty foods, raw or undercooked meats in pregnancy.
- Health workers should dispel misconceptions and myths about certain foods in pregnancy.
- Pregnant women who are obviously malnourished need special attention, counselling and advice from a trained nutritionist.

heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.1 Vaginal Bleeding in Early Pregnancy > 6.1.1 Abortion Definition
text:
## **6.0 Managing complications of pregnancy**

Management of the different complications is as follows:

### **6.1 Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy**

Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy may be associated with abortion; Ectopic pregnancy or Gestational trophoblastic disease (Molar pregnancy).

## 6.1 Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy

#### **6.1.1 Abortion definition**

The National Center for Health Statistics, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the World Health Organization all define *abortion* as expulsion or extraction of pregnancy before 20 weeks’ gestation or with a fetus born weighing 500 g.

text:
### Ectopic pregnancy: symptoms (amenorrhoea, unilateral lower abdominal pain, spotting, shoulder tip pain, collapse), signs, and emergency management (IV lines, urgent referral) Ectopic pregnancy is implantation of the pregnancy outside the uterine cavity. | Symptoms | Signs | Management | | --- | --- | --- | | - Often asymptomatic (unsure of dates)
- Amenorrhoea (usually 6–8 weeks)
- Lower abdominal pain (classically unilateral)
- Vaginal bleeding (usually spotting and brown in colour)
- Diarrhoea and vomiting should not be ignored
- Dizziness and light-headedness
- Shoulder tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation – haemoperitoneum)
- Collapse (if ruptured) | - Often no specific signs
- Uterus usually normal size
- Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness occasionally
- Adnexal mass very rare
- Confusion and restlessness
(Suspect ectopic pregnancy in any woman of reproductive age with a history of amenorrhoea and unilateral lower abdominal pain, tachycardia, dizziness, fainting.) | - Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do pregnancy test and haemoglobin. NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient.
- Insert 2 large-bore IV lines
- Run normal saline or Ringer's lactate
- Refer urgently to hospital
- Ultrasound scan must be done. This is an emergency and must be managed immediately! |

heading_path: 6.3 Antepartum haemorrhage > 6.3.1 Definition
text:
### *6.3.1 Definition*

Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is bleeding from or into the genital tract, occurring from 28 weeks of pregnancy until before delivery of the baby. **NOTE: ANY BLEEDING IN A PREGNANT WOMAN SHOULD BE TAKEN SERIOUSLY.**

APH may be classified as:
* Spotting—staining, streaking, blood spotting on underwear or sanitary pad.
* Minor hemorrhage—blood loss less than 50 ml that has settled.
* Major hemorrhage—blood loss of 50-1000 ml with no signs of clinical shock
* Massive hemorrhage—blood loss greater than 1000 ml and/or signs of clinical shock.

heading_path: 6.3 Antepartum haemorrhage > 6.3.2 Causes of APH
text:
### *6.3.2 Causes of APH:*

***The major causes of APH are *placenta praevia* and *abruptio placentae*. Placental causes:***

Placenta praevia, Abruptio placentae and vasapraevia (rare). **Non-placental causes:** uterine rupture, cervicitis, cervical erosions or polyps, cervical cancer, vulva l varicosities, trauma (post-coital /GBV or other causes) and hemorrhoids .

heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.3 Antepartum Haemorrhage > 6.3.3 Diagnosis of Antepartum Haemorrhage
text:
### Antepartum haemorrhage: abruptio placentae vs placenta praevia vs ruptured uterus – signs and symptoms; general emergency management (ABC, IV lines, no digital vaginal examination, refer) APH is bleeding from or into the genital tract from 28 weeks of pregnancy until before delivery of the baby. Any bleeding in a pregnant woman should be taken seriously. Spotting; minor haemorrhage <50 ml that has settled; major haemorrhage 50–1000 ml with no signs of shock; massive haemorrhage >1000 ml and/or signs of clinical shock. | Probable diagnosis | Signs and symptoms | | --- | --- | | Abruptio placentae | - Vaginal bleeding
- Intermittent or constant abdominal pain
- Shock
- Tender, tense uterus
- Decreased or absent fetal movement
- Fetal distress or absent fetal heart sounds | | Placenta praevia | - Vaginal bleeding (painless, bright red), may be precipitated by intercourse
- Shock
- Relaxed uterus
- Fetal presentation not in the pelvis; malpresentation; lower uterine pole feels empty
- Normal fetal condition | | Ruptured uterus | - Vaginal or intra-abdominal bleeding
- Severe abdominal pain (may decrease after rupture)
- Shock
- Abdominal distension or free fluid
- Abnormal uterine contour
- Tender abdomen
- Easily palpable fetal parts
- Absent fetal movement and fetal heart sounds
- Rapid maternal pulse | **Management (applies to every row):** General management:
Shout for help! (Inyandzaleyo!)
- Follow A, B, C: airway clear, breathing, circulation.
- Assess the haemodynamic status of the patient.
- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do urgent ward Hb.
- NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient; also confusion and restlessness.
- Resuscitate as appropriate: insert 2 large IV lines; correct hypovolaemia using normal saline or Ringer's lactate; strict fluid balance chart, insert Foley's catheter, monitor input and output; if available give oxygen 4–6 L per minute by face mask; blood grouping and cross-match, FBC.
Refer the patient to hospital as soon as possible.
NOTE: DO NOT PERFORM DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PLACENTA PRAEVIA IS RULED OUT.

heading_path: 6.4 Pre-eclampsia > 6.4.1 Definition
text:
### *6.4.1 Definition*

Pre-eclampsia is new onset of hypertension presenting after 20 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria with or without oedema and can present as late as 4-6 weeks postpartum.

Pre-eclampsia is new onset of hypertension presenting after 20 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria with or without oedema and can present as late as 4-6 weeks postpartum.

heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.4 Pre-eclampsia > 6.4.2 Signs and Symptoms
text:
### Pre-eclampsia: mild (BP ≥140/90 twice 4 hours apart) vs severe (BP ≥160/110, proteinuria, headache, blurred vision, epigastric pain, oliguria, thrombocytopenia) – referral and pre-referral magnesium sulphate Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation with significant proteinuria, with or without oedema; it can present as late as 4–6 weeks postpartum. | Category | Signs and symptoms | Management | | --- | --- | --- | | Mild pre-eclampsia | - BP ≥140/90 on ≥2 occasions measured at least 4 hours apart, without evidence of end-organ damage, in women with previously normal BP before 20 weeks' gestation
OR
- An increase in systolic BP by 30 mmHg or diastolic BP by 15 mmHg | Refer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). At the hospital, manage as per guidelines. | | Severe pre-eclampsia: any 1 of the following in the presence of pre-eclampsia | - SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg
- Proteinuria >5 g in a 24-hour urine collection or 3+ on dipstick
- Pulmonary oedema / cyanosis
- Urine output <30 ml/hr (oliguria)
- Persistent headaches
- Blurred vision
- Epigastric pain ± impaired liver function
- Oligohydramnios
- Decreased fetal growth
- Placental abruption
- Thrombocytopenia | Refer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM if at the clinic or PHU. At the hospital, manage as per guidelines. |

heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.5 Eclampsia > 6.5.2 Risk Factors and Symptoms
text:
### Eclampsia: risk factors, symptoms and emergency management of convulsions (left lateral, airway, oxygen, magnesium sulphate, urgent referral) Eclampsia: seizures that cannot be attributed to other causes in a woman with pre-eclampsia. | Risk factors | Symptoms | Management | | --- | --- | --- | | - 1st pregnancy
- Age >40 years
- Overweight (BMI >35 at 1st ANC visit)
- Family history of PIH / pre-eclampsia
- Multiple pregnancy
- Last pregnancy >10 years ago
- Chronic kidney disease
- Diabetes mellitus
- Autoimmune diseases
- Race – black
- Chronic hypertension | - May be asymptomatic
- Headache not relieved by simple analgesia
- Altered mental state
- Blindness
- Shortness of breath
- Blurred vision or flashing
- Epigastric / right upper quadrant abdominal pain
- Rapid swelling of face, hands and feet
- Non-specific complaints of being unwell
- Convulsions | - Urgently refer the patient to the nearest hospital.
- Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM.
- For a patient with convulsions: do not leave the patient alone; shout for assistance, state 'Eclampsia'; turn the patient to the left lateral position; ensure the airway is clear and the patient is breathing; protect the patient from falling/injury; do not place anything in the mouth; oxygen by mask at 4–6 L per minute; when the convulsion ends, start IV; take vital signs.
- At the hospital, stabilise the patient and deliver by the safest, fastest route; manage eclampsia as per guidelines. |

heading_path: 6.0 Managing Complications of Pregnancy > 6.6 Premature Rupture of Membranes
text:
### Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and preterm PROM (PPROM): assessment, clinic management (no digital vaginal exam, refer), hospital management by gestation (steroids betamethasone/dexamethasone, antibiotics erythromycin/amoxicillin, induction) PROM is drainage of amniotic fluid through the cervical canal before the onset of uterine contractions; it may be preterm (before 37 weeks) or at term (after 37 weeks). | Diagnosis | Assessment | General management (clinic, PHU) | Management at health centre / hospital | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) | - Verify the patient's estimated due date; this will be needed for management decisions.
- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure and temperature 4-hourly.
- Do urine dipstick.
- Check fetal heart rate. | - DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.
- Refer to health centre or hospital. | - If term, this may indicate onset of labour.
- Assess for other signs of labour.
- Perform a sterile speculum examination to assess whether the cervix is open.
- Give antibiotics if prolonged rupture of membranes.
- Allow to deliver if in labour. | | Preterm PROM (PPROM) | - Assess as indicated in PROM.
- Ultrasound at least twice a day.
- Consider weekly maternal FBC. | - DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.
- Refer to health centre or hospital. | If rupture is:
- Before 28 weeks: observe vital signs; initiate the process of evacuation by stimulation after counselling the mother and significant others about the risks.
- Before 34 weeks (28–33 weeks): administer steroids – intramuscular betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 24 hours, OR intramuscular dexamethasone.

heading_path: 6.7 Hyperglycaemia
text:
## **6.7 Hyperglycaemia**

Glycosuria in pregnancy may be the first sign of gestational diabetes.

### ***6.7.1 Glycosuria on dipstick testing:***

Glycosuria of 2+ or above may indicate a need for confirmation by random blood sugar. Fasting plasma glucose > 7mmol/l or random plasma glucose > 11.1 mmol/l or Hyperglycaemia first detected at any time during pregnancy should be classified as either:
* Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy
* Gestational Diabetes mellitus

text:
#### ***7.1.1 Definition***

Anaemia is generally defined as haemoglobin level less than 11g/dl or specifically:
* ✓ **HB <11g/dL** in 1<sup>st</sup> trimester
* ✓ **HB <10.5g/dL** in 2<sup>nd</sup> trimester
* ✓ **HB <11g/dL** in 3<sup>rd</sup> trimester

#### ***7.1.2 Symptoms***

The signs and symptoms are often non-specific with tiredness being the most common. Women may also complain of weakness, headaches, palpitations, dizziness and dyspnea.

text:
### Anaemia in pregnancy by haemoglobin: no anaemia (>11 g/dl), moderate (7-11 g/dl: double-dose iron 3 months), severe (<7 g/dl: urgent referral) – clinic vs hospital management

Anaemia: Hb <11 g/dl in the 1st trimester, <10.5 g/dl in the 2nd trimester, <11 g/dl in the 3rd trimester. Symptoms are often non-specific (tiredness, weakness, headaches, palpitations, dizziness, dyspnoea).

| Haemoglobin level | Diagnosis | Clinic / PHU | Health centre and hospital |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| >11 g/dl (no pallor) | No clinical anaemia | Give the usual daily dose of iron and folic acid and counsel on compliance. Provide counselling on nutrition. | Give the usual daily dose of iron and folic acid and counsel on compliance. Provide counselling on nutrition. |
| 7–11 g/dl OR palmar and conjunctival pallor | Moderate anaemia | Give a double dose of daily iron for 3 months and counsel on compliance and nutrition (such as chuchuza, imbuya, spinach etc.); re-assess at the next ANC contact or sooner if danger signs occur. If haemoglobin [<]8 g/dl or symptoms occur (shortness of breath, dizziness), urgently refer to health centre or hospital. | Give a double dose of daily iron for 3 months and counsel on compliance and nutrition; re-assess at the next ANC contact or sooner. If symptoms occur, do further clinical and laboratory assessment and treat accordingly. |
| <7 g/dl and/or severe palmar and conjunctival pallor, OR any pallor with respirations [>]30/minute or breathlessness at rest | Severe anaemia | Refer urgently to health centre or hospital. | Conduct further clinical and laboratory assessment and treat accordingly. Counsel to give birth at a facility with transfusion capacity. |

## *KeyMessage: Antenatal education*

* Explain that urinary tract infections are common in pregnancy; the risk beginning in week 6 and peaking during weeks 22 to 24. If experiencing symptoms (sense of urgency, painful and frequent urination of small volumes - often through straining often with a residual feeling of incomplete emptying), seek medical attention.
* UTIs are not transmissible

heading_path: 7.3 Syphilis
text:
## **7.3 Syphilis**

* At first contact with pregnant woman, conduct a rapid blood test for syphilis(RPR)
* Give benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once weekly for three consecutive weeks .
* Once pregnant women have been diagnosed with syphilis ensure that partner get treated.

**Note: Although erythromycin and azithromycin treat the pregnant women they do not cross the placental barrier completely and as a result the foetus is not treated. It is therefore**

**necessary to treat the new born infant soon after delivery . ( Refer to neonatal clinical care guidelines)Syphilis during pregnancy can lead to severe adverse compli cations to the foetus or newborn.**

text:
## 7.4 **Hepatitis B**

* Test pregnant women for hepatitis B at first contact
* A pregnant woman who test positive for Hepatitis B must be referred to the hospital for further management.

### 8.1 Community awareness and engagement for ANC

Community awareness and community engagement contributes to improved ANC coverage, improved hospital delivery, new-born care preparedness and better neonatal outcome.

As part of this guideline, Community based health care workers are responsible for:
- ✓ Sensitization of women for early booking before three months
- ✓ Give advice and information on nutrition and healthy eating
- ✓ Educate on maternal danger signs and prompt referral
- ✓ Educate on the eight contact with the facility
- ✓ Advice on birth preparedness plan
- ✓ Distribution of IEC material on maternal and nutrition information
- ✓ Reporting on community based HIMS on the selected indicators.

heading_path: 8.1.1 Key messages > 8.1.1.1 Nutrition
text:
### 8.1.1.1 Nutrition

- Eat a variety of foods during pregnancy for example, Food that gives energy (maize meal pap, potatoes, sweet potatoes, rice); body building foods ( chicken, red meat, fish eggs, nuts); foods that protects the body ( fruits, vegetables, beans) and foods that replenish the blood ( liver, spinach, green leafy vegetables, beans).
- Vit A/Iron/calcium rich food are: milk, pawpaw, lettuce, pumpkin, carrots, *imbuya*, *chuchuza*, *inkaka*, *umbidvo wetintsanga*, *ligusha*
- Drink plenty of safe water
- Avoid coffee, energy drink, chocolate, raw and undercooked meat

text:
### 8.1.1.4 Ultrasound

Ultrasound is a useful diagnostic tool during pregnancy. Ultrasound helps to estimate duration/age of the pregnancy. The ultrasound also helps the doctor or nurse to know if the fetus is alive and normal. It also helps the health worker to see how many fetuses there are in the womb. Therefore:
* Every pregnant woman should one ultrasound scan before six (6) months
* You can get an ultrasound done at the following health facilities: all health centers and hospitals.

heading_path: 9.2 Data management
text:
## 9.2 Data management

Good Data Management is essential for the effective use of the information resources. All service providers must fully collect ANC related data for reporting on the ANC activities through the HMIS and CMIS. The data needs to be analyzed and presented by facility and regions to inform progress at all levels. Higher level indicator data should be collected through population based national surveys at intervals that agreed upon from time to time. e.g MMR, ANC coverage (at least once by skilled health personnel, and at least four times by any provider). The data for any new indicator will be developed and integrated in the Health Sector M&E framework. The antenatal card and ANC registers and CMIS indicators will be reviewed to be in line with the new guidelines. Where required the data collection tools will be revised to ensure the requisite data is collected.

text:
## **CHAPTER 1**

## **PREVENTION, HEALTH EDUCATION AND ROUTINE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS**

In Eswatini, like many countries globally, there has been a notable increase in non-communicable diseases (NCDs) over the past two decades due to an epidemiological transition. This shift highlights the growing burden of diseases such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, respiratory diseases, diabetes, obesity, and musculoskeletal disorders. Evidence indicates that non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are largely preventable, with both modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors often emerging early in life. Addressing these factors is crucial for NCD prevention in Eswatini.

### NCD risk factors: non-modifiable and modifiable, with clinical relevance

| Category | Risk factor | Clinical relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-modifiable | Age | Risk increases significantly after age 40, especially for DM and HTN. |
| Non-modifiable | Gender | Specific risks (e.g., gender-specific cancers, cardiovascular disease patterns). |
| Non-modifiable | Family history | Genetic predisposition to HTN, DM, or premature coronary artery disease (CAD). |
| Modifiable | Overweight/obesity | High BMI is a primary driver for HTN and DM. |
| Modifiable | Tobacco use (smoking) | A leading preventable cause of cardiovascular and chronic respiratory diseases and lung cancer. |
| Modifiable | Alcohol use | Increases risk of liver disease, some cancers, and hypertension. |
| Modifiable | Unhealthy diet | High intake of salt, sugar, and saturated fats contributes to hypertension and dyslipidaemia and some cancers. |
| Modifiable | Lack of physical activity | A sedentary lifestyle is a key independent risk factor for all major NCDs. |

text:
### Screening protocol for modifiable NCD risk factors: screening method and frequency (initial assessment, all patients)

Target population for screening: all adults aged 18 years and above attending health facilities; priority screening for adults ≥40 years or those with risk factors; pregnant women (at first antenatal visit); people living with HIV (at each clinic visit).

| Risk factor | Screening method | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tobacco use | Ask all patients about current and past tobacco use | Every visit |
| Alcohol use | AUDIT-C questionnaire (3 questions) | Annually |
| Physical activity | Ask: 'How many days per week do you engage in moderate physical activity for at least 30 minutes?' | Annually |
| Diet assessment | Ask about fruit/vegetable intake and consumption of processed foods | Annually |
| Weight/BMI | Measure height and weight; calculate BMI | Every visit |
| Blood pressure | Measure BP using standardized technique | Every visit |
| Blood glucose | Random or fasting blood glucose; HbA1c if available | Age ≥18 years: every visit; high risk: annually |
| Cholesterol | Total cholesterol; LDL/HDL if available | Screening guidelines for lipid disorders differ among experts. Cholesterol screening is recommended in adult men aged ≥35 years, in women aged ≥40 years or menopausal, and all adults with any risk factors. |

### Blood pressure screening algorithm: BP categories and actions

| BP reading (mmHg) | Category | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <120/80 | Normal | Recheck in 1 year or at next clinic visit, whichever comes first; promote healthy lifestyle |
| 120-129/<80 | Elevated | Lifestyle modification; recheck in 3-6 months |
| 130-139/80-89 | Stage 1 hypertension | Confirm with 2 more readings; initiate lifestyle + medication if CVD risk ≥10% |
| ≥140/90 | Stage 2 hypertension | Confirm within 1 month; initiate lifestyle + medication |
| ≥180/120 | Hypertensive crisis | URGENT: assess for end-organ damage; immediate treatment |

### **Tobacco Cessation**

- Brief advice: Use the 5 A's (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange)
- Behavioural counselling at each visit
- Pharmacotherapy if available: nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, or varenicline

### **Alcohol Reduction**

- Brief intervention for hazardous drinking (AUDIT-C score 3-7)
- Refer to specialized services for AUDIT-C score ≥8
- Recommended limits: Men ≤14 units/week; Women ≤7 units/week

text:
### **Healthy Diet**

- Increase fruits and vegetables to at least 5 servings daily
- Reduce salt intake to <5g per day
- Limit saturated fats and trans fats
- Choose whole grains over refined carbohydrates
- Reduce sugar-sweetened beverages.

### **Physical Activity**

- Goal: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week
- Alternative: 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity per week
- Start slowly for sedentary patients; any increase in activity is beneficial.

## **Referral Criteria and Follow-Up**

## Referral to Specialist Care

### **Immediate/Urgent Referral:**

- Hypertensive emergency (BP ≥180/120 with symptoms or end-organ damage)
- Diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
- Severe hypoglycaemia with altered consciousness
- Acute cardiovascular event (chest pain, stroke symptoms)

## **Patient Education Priorities**

* Explain the link between risk factors and NCDs in simple terms.
* Emphasize that lifestyle changes can be as effective as medication.
* Provide written information in appropriate language.
* Encourage family involvement in lifestyle modifications.

## Physical Inactivity

### **Introduction**

Physical inactivity is the fourth leading risk factor for global mortality, accounting for 6% of deaths worldwide. In 2022, 31% of adults globally were physically inactive. This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for screening, counselling, and managing physical inactivity in primary care settings in Eswatini, based on the latest WHO guidelines (2020) and adapted for the Southern African context.

text:
# Key Definitions

**Physical Activity (PA):** Any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure, including leisure time, transportation, work, household chores, and recreational activities.

**Physical Inactivity:** Not meeting the WHO recommendations of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week.

**Sedentary Behaviour:** Any waking behaviour characterized by low energy expenditure (≤1.5 METs) while sitting, reclining, or lying down.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Physical Inactivity > WHO physical activity recommendations
text:
### WHO physical activity recommendations by age group (children, adults, older adults, pregnant and postpartum women)

Physical inactivity: not meeting the WHO recommendation of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. Sedentary behaviour: any waking behaviour with low energy expenditure (≤1.5 METs) while sitting, reclining, or lying down.

| Age group | Recommendations |
| --- | --- |
| Children & adolescents (5-17 years) | At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous intensity PA daily. Include vigorous-intensity aerobic activities at least 3 days/week. Include muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 days/week. |
| Adults (18-64 years) | At least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity PA per week, OR at least 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity PA per week, OR an equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous activity. Muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups on 2 or more days per week. |
| Older adults (≥65 years) | Same as adults (150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous). Muscle-strengthening activities 2 or more days per week. Multicomponent PA emphasizing functional balance and strength training 3 or more days/week to prevent falls. |
| Pregnant & postpartum women | At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity PA per week. Incorporate a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities. Add gentle stretching; may be beneficial to add pelvic floor muscle training. |

**Note:** Note: some activity is better than none. Inactive individuals should start with small amounts and gradually increase frequency, intensity, and duration. Screening for physical inactivity: who to screen: all patients attending primary care facilities, particularly those with risk factors (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression); routine screening at annual check-ups or chronic disease reviews.

# Simple Screening Questions

Use these quick questions during consultations:
- On how many days in a typical week do you do at least 30 minutes of physical activity?
- What type of activities do you do? (walking, household chores, sports, farming, etc.)
- How many hours per day do you spend sitting? (at work, watching TV, etc.)
**Classification:** If <150 minutes of moderate activity per week = **PHYSICALLY INACTIVE**

### Brief counselling intervention for physical inactivity: the 5 A's (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange)

Screening: if <150 minutes of moderate activity per week, the patient is physically inactive.

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| ASK | Ask about current physical activity levels using screening questions. |
| ADVISE | Provide clear, personalized advice on benefits of physical activity for their specific health condition. |
| ASSESS | Assess willingness and readiness to change. Identify barriers (time, safety, cost, cultural factors). |
| ASSIST | Help develop a realistic action plan. Start small and build gradually. Provide written guidance. |
| ARRANGE | Arrange follow-up to monitor progress and provide ongoing support. |

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Physical Inactivity > Special Considerations
text:
# **Special Considerations**

- Chronic diseases: Physical activity is safe and beneficial; adjust intensity based on individual capacity.
- HIV/TB patients: Encourage light-to-moderate activity; avoid vigorous activity during acute illness.
- Elderly: Focus on balance and fall prevention exercises; social group activities beneficial.

## <u>Key Messages for Patients</u>

**Some physical activity is better than none**

- Start slowly and gradually increase over time.
- Every minute counts - even 10 minutes at a time adds up.
- Choose activities you enjoy and can maintain long-term.
- Reduce sitting time - stand up and move every 30 minutes.
- Involve family and friends for motivation and support.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Nicotine Use > Smoking cessation approach
text:
### Smoking cessation approach in clinical practice (flowchart, with nicotine dependence table)

All smokers should be identified and their readiness to quit evaluated. If resistance to quitting exists, information and suitable follow-up should be provided. If the person is ready to make a quit attempt, evaluation of nicotine dependence, co-morbid and psychosocial factors should guide the choice of effective interventions.

1. Ask: do you smoke? do you know the risks? have you thought of quitting?
2. Alert: do you know the benefits of quitting? do you know that we can help you?
3. Assess: are you ready to quit?
4. Assist/arrange:
   - No or maybe: give a motivational pamphlet and encourage follow-up; return to Ask at the next visit.
   - Yes: arrange for cessation intervention.
5. Specific nicotine dependence review: Fagerstrom/CO levels; current smoking and history of quit attempts; social stressors/household smokers.
   Dependence level (already attempted to quit / cigarettes per day / time to first cigarette after waking):
   - Very high: yes / >30 / >5 min (printed)
   - High: yes / 20-30 / 5-30 min
   - Medium: yes / 10-20 / 30-60 min
   - Low: no / <10 / >60 min
6. By dependence:
   - Motivated, low dependence: could manage with counselling/support alone or NRT; support group, text/internet/smartphone-based support.
   - Motivated, high dependence: probably will need added pharmacological support; assess medical/psychiatric history; evaluate capacity to purchase medicine; review availability of medication. Medication options: nicotine replacement therapy (patch/gum/spray), varenicline, bupropion.
7. Set quit date: arrange appropriate support and medication if needed.
8. Follow-up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side-effects; evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors; identify potential for relapse.

CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.

text:
## **Health Harms of Alcohol Use**

Alcohol is causally linked to over 200 diseases and injuries. Even light-to-moderate drinking increases health risks.

## <u>Cancer Risk</u>

**Alcohol is a well-established cause of at least 7 types of cancer:**
- Mouth, Throat, and Oesophageal Cancer
- Liver Cancer
- Colon and Rectal Cancer
- Breast Cancer (women)

**Important:** Cancer risk begins with ANY amount of alcohol consumption and increases with higher intake.

text:
## **Other Major Health Consequences**

- **Cardiovascular disease:** Hypertension, stroke, heart disease, cardiomyopathy
- **Liver disease:** Fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis
- **Mental health:** Depression, anxiety, suicide, alcohol use disorder
- **Infectious diseases:** Increased risk of tuberculosis and HIV acquisition (through risky behaviors)
- **Injuries:** Road traffic accidents, falls, violence, burns
- **Pregnancy complications:** Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders, miscarriage, stillbirth
- **Gastrointestinal:** Pancreatitis, gastritis, malabsorption, malnutrition
- **Neurological:** Brain damage, memory impairment, dementia, peripheral neuropathy

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Alcohol Use > Screening tools > AUDIT-C
text:
### AUDIT-C alcohol screening questionnaire: questions, scoring and interpretation

| Question | Answer scoring | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. How often do you have a drink containing alcohol? | Never (0); monthly or less (1); 2-4 times/month (2); 2-3 times/week (3); 4+ times/week (4) | 0-4 |
| 2. How many drinks containing alcohol do you have on a typical day when drinking? | 1 or 2 (0); 3 or 4 (1); 5 or 6 (2); 7-9 (3); 10+ (4) | 0-4 |
| 3. How often do you have 5 or more drinks on one occasion? | Never (0); less than monthly (1); monthly (2); weekly (3); daily/almost daily (4) | 0-4 |

**Note:** AUDIT-C interpretation: men: score ≥4 = unhealthy alcohol use: provide brief intervention. Women: score ≥3 = unhealthy alcohol use: provide brief intervention. Score ≥8: possible alcohol use disorder: consider full AUDIT and referral.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Alcohol Use > Brief intervention: the 5 A's
text:
### Brief intervention for alcohol use: the 5 A's (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange)

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| ASK | Ask about alcohol use using AUDIT-C: 'How often do you drink alcohol?' 'How much do you typically drink?' |
| ADVISE | Provide clear, personalized advice: 'The safest choice is to not drink alcohol at all. There is no safe level of drinking.' Link to their health concerns: 'Alcohol is making your blood pressure worse' or 'Drinking increases your cancer risk.' |
| ASSESS | Assess readiness to change: 'How do you feel about quitting or cutting down?' 'What makes it difficult for you to stop?' |
| ASSIST | Help develop a quit/reduction plan: set a quit date or reduction goal; identify triggers and develop coping strategies; provide written educational materials; consider referral to counselling or support groups. |
| ARRANGE | Schedule follow-up in 2-4 weeks to monitor progress, provide support, and address challenges. |

text:
## Alcohol Use

## Special Populations

### **Pregnant Women and Women of Childbearing Age**

# **ABOLUTE RECOMMENDATION**: Complete abstinence during pregnancy and when planning pregnancy

- No amount of alcohol is safe during pregnancy
- Alcohol causes Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD): growth problems, facial abnormalities, brain damage, learning disabilities
- Screen ALL pregnant women at first antenatal visit and subsequent visits
- Counsel all women of childbearing age about risks

## Patients Living with HIV

- Alcohol reduces ART adherence and treatment effectiveness
- Increases HIV viral load and accelerates disease progression
- Associated with increased risky sexual behaviours
- Worsens liver disease (especially with hepatitis B co-infection)
- **RECOMMENDATION**: Strong advice to quit alcohol for optimal HIV treatment outcomes

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Alcohol Use > Special Populations > Patients on TB Treatment
text:
## Patients on TB Treatment

- Alcohol interferes with TB medication effectiveness
- Increases risk of liver toxicity from TB drugs
- Reduces treatment adherence and increases treatment failure
- **RECOMMENDATION**: Complete abstinence during TB treatment

## Adolescents and Young Adults

- Brain continues developing until age 25; alcohol impairs brain development
- Early alcohol use increases lifetime risk of alcohol use disorder
- Associated with risky behaviours, injuries, poor school performance
- **RECOMMENDATION**: Delay alcohol initiation as long as possible; abstinence is safest

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Alcohol Use > Special Populations > Older Adults (≥65 years)
text:
## Older Adults (≥65 years)

- Increased sensitivity to alcohol effects with aging
- Higher risk of falls, fractures, and injuries
- Interactions with multiple medications
- Worsens cognitive decline and increases dementia risk

## Practical Strategies for Patients

### **Tips for Quitting Alcohol**

- Set a clear quit date and tell family/friends for support
- Remove all alcohol from home
- Avoid places and situations where alcohol is present
- Find alternative activities (sports, hobbies, church/community groups)

- Practice saying 'no' to offers of alcohol
- Keep non-alcoholic drinks available
- Manage stress through exercise, prayer, meditation, talking to friends
- Join support groups or counseling services

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Alcohol Use > Practical Strategies for Patients > Managing Cravings and Triggers
text:
## **Managing Cravings and Triggers**

- Recognize triggers: stress, social pressure, certain places, emotions
- Use the '4 Ds': Delay, Distract, Deep breathing, Drink water
- Call a supportive friend or family member
- Remember health benefits: better sleep, more energy, improved health, saving money

## When to Refer

**Refer to **specialized alcohol treatment services** if:**
- AUDIT score ≥20 (likely alcohol dependence)
- Failed previous attempts to quit despite brief intervention
- Signs of withdrawal symptoms (tremors, sweating, anxiety, seizures)
- Co-occurring mental health disorders (depression, anxiety, psychosis)
- Severe alcohol-related medical complications (cirrhosis, pancreatitis)
- Patient requests specialized help

> - NO amount of alcohol is safe for your health.

text:
## Unhealthy Diet

Unhealthy dietary patterns contribute significantly to non-communicable diseases in Eswatini. Healthcare providers should screen patients for dietary habits and provide brief counseling emphasizing increased consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes, while limiting salt (less than 5g/day), sugar, and processed foods. The accompanying visual dietary guideline provides practical, culturally appropriate recommendations based on WHO guidelines and featuring locally available and affordable food options suitable for Eswatini's context.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Unhealthy Diet > Healthy eating guidelines
text:
### Healthy eating guidelines: food groups, foods to limit, counselling tips and health benefits

**Eat a variety of foods daily for good health**

| Food group | Advice | Details / examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vegetables & fruits | Eat PLENTY daily | At least 5 portions (400 g) per day. Examples: spinach, cabbage, tomatoes, carrots, pumpkin, oranges, bananas, mangoes |
| Starchy foods | Part of MOST meals | Choose WHOLE GRAINS. Examples: whole grain pap/maize meal, brown bread, rice, potatoes, sweet potatoes |
| Protein foods | Eat DAILY | Choose lean options. Examples: beans, lentils, peanuts, fish, chicken, lean meat, eggs |
| Milk & dairy | Have EVERY DAY | Good for bones & teeth. Examples: milk, maas, yoghurt, cheese |
| Clean water | Drink LOTS daily | 6-8 glasses per day; best choice for hydration |
| Fats & oils | Use SPARINGLY | Choose vegetable oils; avoid hard fats & excessive frying |

**Foods to limit**

| Food group | Advice | Details / examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salt | Less than 1 teaspoon (5 g) per day | Reduces blood pressure & heart disease |
| Sugar | Less than 6 teaspoons (25 g) per day | Reduces blood pressure & heart disease |
| Processed foods | Limit chips, soda, sweets, fast food | High in salt, sugar & unhealthy fats |

**Note:** Counselling tips: fill half the plate with vegetables; eat locally available seasonal foods; choose whole grains over refined; eat beans/legumes regularly; remove visible fat from meat. Health benefits: prevents heart disease & stroke; reduces diabetes risk; helps maintain a healthy weight; prevents some cancers; improves overall wellbeing.

Routine health examinations aim to identify risk factors and early signs of the disease as well as preventing future diseases using early interventions. heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Hypertension
text:
### **HYPERTENSION**

Hypertension is defined as systemic blood pressure of ≥140/90mmHg. Controlling hypertension is associated with a reduction in heart failure, strokes, chronic kidney disease, and myocardial infarctions. Therefore, routine screening for hypertension is recommended.

#### **Recommendations for BP measurements in the office and at home**

image: circular infographic of blood pressure measurement recommendations

**1.** Use validated automated electronic upper-arm cuff device

**2.** Quiet room with comfortable temperature

**3.** No smoking, caffeine, food, drug intake or exercise 30 min before measurement

**4.** Remain seated and relaxed for 3–5 min

**5.** No talking during or between measurements

**6.** Sitting with back supported by chair

**7.** Legs uncrossed, feet flat on floor.

**8.** Bare arm resting on table mid-arm at heart level

**9.** Office: Take 3 readings with 1 min interval between readings use average of the last 2 the last

**10.** Home: Take 2 readings with 1 min interval between and use average

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Hypertension > Algorithm for hypertension screening
text:
### Algorithm for hypertension screening in adults (18 years and above)

Adults (18 years and above), by office blood pressure:
- Optimal <120/80: repeat at least every 5 years.
- Normal 120-129/80-84: repeat at least every 3 years.
- High normal BP 130-139/85-89: consider masked hypertension; repeat annually. Consider out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM).
- Hypertension >140/90: repeated visits for office BP measurement, and consider out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM).

Adopted from ESC/ESH guidelines, 2023.
N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring blood pressure yearly for adults ≥18 years of age.

### Anthropometric measurements in adults (≥18 years): BMI, obesity class and disease risk by waist circumference

Overweight and obesity are abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that presents a risk to health. In adults, a BMI over 25 is overweight and over 30 is obese. BMI = body mass (kg) divided by the square of body height (m).

| Underweight | <18.5 |  | - |  |
| Normal\* | 18.5-24.9 |  | - |  |
| Overweight | 25-29.9 |  | Increased | High |
| Obesity | 30-34.9 | Class 1 | High | Very high |
| Obesity | 35-39.9 | Class 2 | Very high | Very high |

*Increased waist circumference can also be a marker for increased risk even in persons of normal weight.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Diabetes Mellitus > Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening
text:
### Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening in adults

All clients >18 years attending a health facility should be screened for diabetes using the known risk factors below.
- No risk factors: re-evaluate.
- Risk factors present: test (HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, or random glucose):
  - HbA1c <5.7% / FPG <100 mg/dl: encourage healthy lifestyle maintenance; retest at least annually.
  - HbA1c 5.6-6.4% / FPG 100-125 mg/dl / OGTT 140-199 mg/dl: encourage lifestyle modification and retest every 6-12 months.
  - HbA1c ≥ 6.5% / FPG ≥ 126 mg/dl: retest with a different test, and refer for treatment if still positive.

*Known risk factors for diabetes: physical inactivity; family history of diabetes; high-risk race or ethnicity (African, Indian); hypertension (≥ 140/90); HDL-C <35 or triglyceride > 250 mg/dL; history of gestational diabetes or gave birth to a baby ≥4.5 kg; history of heart disease; conditions associated with insulin resistance; polycystic ovary syndrome; malnutrition.

Adapted from the American Diabetes Association Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes. N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring glycaemia yearly in adults ≥ 18 years of age.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Lipids Disorders > Lipid management clinical decision pathway
text:
### Lipid management: clinical decision pathway (CV risk, comorbidities, lipid targets)

Obtain fasting lipids at baseline and annually. Then three parallel assessments, then treat to the target:
1. Calculate and categorize CV risk using the Framingham risk score (mdcalc.com - Framingham Risk Score). Risk categories: low risk < 10%; moderate risk 10%-19%; high risk > 20%.
2. Assess comorbidities: diabetes; CAD; previous CV event; atherosclerosis; aneurysm. *Any = high risk.
3. Determine lipid targets:
   - LDL-C: optimal <100 mg/dL; near or above optimal 100-129 mg/dL; borderline high 130-159 mg/dL; high 160-189 mg/dL; very high ≥190 mg/dL.
   - Total cholesterol: desirable <200 mg/dL; borderline high 200-239 mg/dL; high ≥240 mg/dL.
   - Triglycerides: normal <150 mg/dL; borderline high ≥150-199 mg/dL; high 200-499 mg/dL; very high ≥500 mg/dL.
Then: treat to the target.

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD clinical protocol (kidney health check)
text:
### Chronic kidney disease clinical protocol: kidney health check, confirmation and staging

Offer a kidney health check to people with: diabetes; hypertension; established CVD; family history of kidney failure; obesity (BMI ≥30); current or past smoker/vaper; history of AKI aged ≥60 years; high index of suspicion in clients, especially paediatrics, with oedema and recurrent puffiness.

Tests: uACR, eGFR, and trace protein on urine dipstick.
- uACR ≥3 mg/mmol (yes): repeat uACR within 3 months. If uACR normal, complete a third test (preferably first morning void). CKD if a minimum of two uACRs ≥3 mg/mmol over 3 months.
- eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m2 (yes): repeat eGFR within 7 days; if ≥20% reduction in eGFR, possible AKI: discuss with nephrologist. Repeat eGFR within 3 months. CKD if a minimum of two eGFRs <60 mL/min/1.73m2 over 3 months.
- No to both: repeat kidney health check (annually if aged ≥18, people with diabetes or hypertension).
If either (and/or) criterion is met: stage CKD with the staging table, using eGFR and uACR results.

text:
### Algorithm for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening

Target population:
- No markers of risk: do not screen.
- Risk factors (high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, family history, HIV): screen.

Screen: test (urine dipstick, blood glucose, blood pressure, family history) and measure kidney function (serum creatinine; estimate the eGFR).
Determine if test results indicate CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 or presence of albuminuria):
- No: rescreen based on the risks.
- Yes: lifestyle modification (smoking cessation; balanced diet; regular exercise; limit salt intake to <2 g/day); medical treatment (diabetes, BP and lipid control: SGLT2, ACEI/ARB, statins, metformin...); considerations (drug dosing; use of contrast media; CKD complications: anaemia, hyperkalaemia, bone disease, CVD...).
Then: retesting; follow-up visits; referral to nephrology when appropriate.

text:
### Diabetes mellitus: definition, classification and treatment targets

| Section | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Definition | Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition in which the pancreas no longer produces enough insulin (impaired insulin secretion) or cells stop responding to the insulin that is produced (insulin resistance), resulting in increased blood glucose. |
| Classification: common types | 1. Type 1 diabetes: due to autoimmune b-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood. 2. Type 2 diabetes: due to a progressive loss of b-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance. |
| Classification: specific types | Monogenic diabetes syndromes (neonatal diabetes; maturity-onset diabetes of the young). Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis). Drug- or chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoid use, treatment of HIV/AIDS, or after organ transplantation. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes before gestation. |
| Treatment target: HbA1c | HbA1c <7% for most adults. HbA1c <6.5% for type 1 diabetes without hypoglycaemia. HbA1c <8% for people with frequent hypoglycaemia, limited life expectancy, or cardiovascular complications. |
| Treatment target: glucose | All clients on treatment should aim for a glycaemia (random or fasting) ranging 5-10 mmol/L. |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Testing and Diagnosis of Diabetes > Criteria for Testing
text:
### Criteria for Testing

- Age 18 years and above to be screened annually **AND** as when new risk factors **AND** symptoms present themselves)
- Sustained blood pressure >130/ 80 mmHg or history of CVD
- HDL cholesterol level <35mg/dL/ 0.90mmol and or triglyceride level >250 mg
- Overweight
- Individuals with polycystic ovary syndrome (insulin resistance and other conditions)
- People with prediabetes (hba1c >5.7-6.4 or FBG >7mmol)/l should be testing yearly.
- People living with HIV.
- People with history of or current TB diagnosis
- People who have been diagnosed with gestational diabetes are to be **checked every year**

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diagnosis of Diabetes is Confirmed When
text:
## **Diagnosis of Diabetes is Confirmed When**

The diagnosis of diabetes is confirmed:
(a) In patients <u>*with symptoms*</u> of hyperglycaemia ( polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, weight loss) or metabolic decompetion (diabetic ketocidosisi or hyperosmolar non-ketotic state), when <u>any one single test</u> confirms that the:
* Random plasma glucose is ≥ 11.1 mmol/L
* Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L
* HbA<sup>1</sup>c ≥ 6.5%
* 2 hour post-load glucose is ≥ 11.1 mmol/L. However, GTT is rarely needed in this category of patient.

(b) In an <u>*asymptomatic individual*,</u> when <u>*any one*</u> of the following test, <u>*repeated*</u> on separate days within a 2 week period confirms that the
* Fasting plasma glucose is ≥ 7.0 mmol/L
* 2hr-post load glucose (OGTT) is ≥ 11.1 mmol/L
* HbA<sup>1</sup>c ≥ 6.5%

If the diagnosis of diabetes is not confirmed with the repeated test, institute lifestyle modification and retest in 3 to 6 months.

| Component | Initial visit | 3-6 monthly | Annually |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Blood glucose (fasting, random, or postprandial as appropriate) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
