text:
> **When to do a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria (decision tree)**
>
> Decision tree for considering a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria:
> - The kidney biopsy is the gold standard for diagnostic evaluation of glomerular diseases. Biopsy should be performed if the result is expected to modify treatment and/or if additional prognostic information is needed.
> - Patients classically treated without a kidney biopsy diagnosis (children): steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome ≤12 years old; post-streptococcal GN.
> - Examples of conditions for which treatment may be considered without diagnostic confirmation by kidney biopsy: PLA2Rab+ (membranous nephropathy); PR3+ ANCA vasculitis; anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; Alport disease; Fabry disease; familial focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis in families with well-characterised mutations; biopsy contraindicated as judged by history, physical exam and laboratory testing; systemic lupus erythematosus.
> 
> ANCA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; MPO, myeloperoxidase; PLA2Rab+, M-type phospholipase A2 receptor antibody positive; PR3, proteinase 3. Referral to a nephrologist may include immunosuppressive treatment such as prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, angiotensin blockade.
html:
When to do a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria (decision tree)

Decision tree for considering a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria:

- The kidney biopsy is the gold standard for diagnostic evaluation of glomerular diseases. Biopsy should be performed if the result is expected to modify treatment and/or if additional prognostic information is needed.

- Patients classically treated without a kidney biopsy diagnosis (children): steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome ≤12 years old; post-streptococcal GN.

- Examples of conditions for which treatment may be considered without diagnostic confirmation by kidney biopsy: PLA2Rab+ (membranous nephropathy); PR3+ ANCA vasculitis; anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; Alport disease; Fabry disease; familial focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis in families with well-characterised mutations; biopsy contraindicated as judged by history, physical exam and laboratory testing; systemic lupus erythematosus.

ANCA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; MPO, myeloperoxidase; PLA2Rab+, M-type phospholipase A2 receptor antibody positive; PR3, proteinase 3. Referral to a nephrologist may include immunosuppressive treatment such as prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, angiotensin blockade.

text:
### Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations

Letters before drugs (A, C, S, D) are the medicine level codes used in the guideline.

| Histological Pattern | Treatment Regime | Special Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid sensitive. Initial: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d [max 60 mg/d] for 6 weeks (complete 6 weeks of initial treatment if remission is attained at 4 weeks). Continue: A: prednisolone 40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg (alternate days) for 6 weeks if remission was attained by 4 weeks of initial treatment; after 6 weeks of alternate-day therapy taper and stop within 6 weeks (taper by 5-10 mg a week) | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Relapsing steroid sensitive: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 or 2 mg/kg [max 60 mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN A: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg per dose; maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks. S: levamisole (PO) 2.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 12 months | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent: S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/d for 10-12 weeks [max 168 mg/kg cumulative dose] OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: everolimus 0.5-2 mg 12-hourly OR S: sirolimus 1-3 mg 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses; S: rituximab 375-1000 mg/m2 | Monitor calcineurin inhibitor toxicity/levels |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome: S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone high dose |  |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg 24-hourly (maximum 80 mg) OR alternate-day single dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 120 mg) – 4 weeks if remission; continue to 16 weeks if complete remission is not achieved | Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Check HbA1c monthly. Screen for osteoporosis |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent/resistant (idiopathic only): D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg [max 80 mg] daily or alternate-day 2 mg/kg [max 120 mg] for 4-16 weeks. OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate) | Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Children: alternating monthly treatment with methylprednisolone + prednisolone (months 1, 3 & 5) and oral cyclophosphamide (months 2, 4 & 6): D: methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg for 3 days, then prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 27 days; S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg for 30 days. Alternative regimens: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg in two divided doses with prednisolone 0.15 mg/kg/day for 6 months; S: tacrolimus 0.2 mg/kg in two divided doses without prednisolone | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Adults: S: cyclophosphamide; A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; D: methylprednisolone IV monthly. Alternative regimens: S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 6 months OR S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses. If albumin <25 g/l + thrombosis risk: C: warfarin 5 mg PO [refer to DVT anticoagulation] | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranoproliferative GN | S: cyclophosphamide OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone |  |
| IgA Nephropathy | Initial supportive care for 3-6 months: C: enalapril (PO) 10-20 mg 24-hourly OR C: lisinopril (PO) 2.5-10 mg 24-hourly. For persistent proteinuria >1 g/d for 6 months (adults and children): A: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/day for 6 months (as printed) | Other registered ACEI or ARBs may be used as in the Hypertension section |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | All patients: S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 6 mg/kg/day maintenance. Class II with proteinuria >3 g/day: treat as minimal change disease above |  |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class III and class IV, initial 6 months: D: methylprednisolone (IV slow) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days monthly AND S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500-1000 mg/m2 monthly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly, titrating to 1.5 g 12-hourly if tolerated, OR S: mycophenolate sodium. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) for 6 months OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) | Oral prednisolone less effective; 60 mg/day may be given. A shorter, more frequent regimen (Euro-Lupus) may be used: cyclophosphamide 500 mg every two weeks x 6 doses |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class V + persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: as class III and IV |  |
| Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis | Initial: S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then every three weeks for 3-6 months, OR S: cyclophosphamide oral 1.5-2 mg/kg daily for 3-6 months; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg slowly over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg, tapered to 30 mg in one week and then to 5 mg by 4-6 months. Severe disease: S: rituximab 1 g followed 14 days later by another 1 g, OR S: rituximab 375 mg/m2 per week for 4 weeks; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered as above. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/d for 18 months OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium | S: haemodialysis. S: plasmapheresis in special indications |

Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations (part 3 of 6).
Minimal Change Disease: adults: Treatment Regime: Frequent relapse/steroid dependent/resistant (idiopathic only): D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg [max 80 mg] daily or alternate-day 2 mg/kg [max 120 mg] for 4-16 weeks. OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate); Special Considerations: Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels.
Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only): Treatment Regime: Children: alternating monthly treatment with methylprednisolone + prednisolone (months 1, 3 & 5) and oral cyclophosphamide (months 2, 4 & 6): D: methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg for 3 days, then prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 27 days; S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg for 30 days. Alternative regimens: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg in two divided doses with prednisolone 0.15 mg/kg/day for 6 months; S: tacrolimus 0.2 mg/kg in two divided doses without prednisolone; Special Considerations: Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated.

### Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations

Letters before drugs (A, C, S, D) are the medicine level codes used in the guideline.

| Histological Pattern | Treatment Regime | Special Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid sensitive. Initial: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d [max 60 mg/d] for 6 weeks (complete 6 weeks of initial treatment if remission is attained at 4 weeks). Continue: A: prednisolone 40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg (alternate days) for 6 weeks if remission was attained by 4 weeks of initial treatment; after 6 weeks of alternate-day therapy taper and stop within 6 weeks (taper by 5-10 mg a week) | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Relapsing steroid sensitive: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 or 2 mg/kg [max 60 mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN A: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg per dose; maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks. S: levamisole (PO) 2.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 12 months | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent: S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/d for 10-12 weeks [max 168 mg/kg cumulative dose] OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: everolimus 0.5-2 mg 12-hourly OR S: sirolimus 1-3 mg 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses; S: rituximab 375-1000 mg/m2 | Monitor calcineurin inhibitor toxicity/levels |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome: S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone high dose |  |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg 24-hourly (maximum 80 mg) OR alternate-day single dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 120 mg) – 4 weeks if remission; continue to 16 weeks if complete remission is not achieved | Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Check HbA1c monthly. Screen for osteoporosis |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent/resistant (idiopathic only): D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg [max 80 mg] daily or alternate-day 2 mg/kg [max 120 mg] for 4-16 weeks. OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate) | Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Children: alternating monthly treatment with methylprednisolone + prednisolone (months 1, 3 & 5) and oral cyclophosphamide (months 2, 4 & 6): D: methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg for 3 days, then prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 27 days; S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg for 30 days. Alternative regimens: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg in two divided doses with prednisolone 0.15 mg/kg/day for 6 months; S: tacrolimus 0.2 mg/kg in two divided doses without prednisolone | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Adults: S: cyclophosphamide; A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; D: methylprednisolone IV monthly. Alternative regimens: S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 6 months OR S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses. If albumin <25 g/l + thrombosis risk: C: warfarin 5 mg PO [refer to DVT anticoagulation] | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranoproliferative GN | S: cyclophosphamide OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone |  |
| IgA Nephropathy | Initial supportive care for 3-6 months: C: enalapril (PO) 10-20 mg 24-hourly OR C: lisinopril (PO) 2.5-10 mg 24-hourly. For persistent proteinuria >1 g/d for 6 months (adults and children): A: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/day for 6 months (as printed) | Other registered ACEI or ARBs may be used as in the Hypertension section |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | All patients: S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 6 mg/kg/day maintenance. Class II with proteinuria >3 g/day: treat as minimal change disease above |  |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class III and class IV, initial 6 months: D: methylprednisolone (IV slow) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days monthly AND S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500-1000 mg/m2 monthly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly, titrating to 1.5 g 12-hourly if tolerated, OR S: mycophenolate sodium. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) for 6 months OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) | Oral prednisolone less effective; 60 mg/day may be given. A shorter, more frequent regimen (Euro-Lupus) may be used: cyclophosphamide 500 mg every two weeks x 6 doses |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class V + persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: as class III and IV |  |
| Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis | Initial: S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then every three weeks for 3-6 months, OR S: cyclophosphamide oral 1.5-2 mg/kg daily for 3-6 months; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg slowly over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg, tapered to 30 mg in one week and then to 5 mg by 4-6 months. Severe disease: S: rituximab 1 g followed 14 days later by another 1 g, OR S: rituximab 375 mg/m2 per week for 4 weeks; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered as above. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/d for 18 months OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium | S: haemodialysis. S: plasmapheresis in special indications |

text:
### Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations

Letters before drugs (A, C, S, D) are the medicine level codes used in the guideline.

| Histological Pattern | Treatment Regime | Special Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid sensitive. Initial: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d [max 60 mg/d] for 6 weeks (complete 6 weeks of initial treatment if remission is attained at 4 weeks). Continue: A: prednisolone 40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg (alternate days) for 6 weeks if remission was attained by 4 weeks of initial treatment; after 6 weeks of alternate-day therapy taper and stop within 6 weeks (taper by 5-10 mg a week) | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Relapsing steroid sensitive: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 or 2 mg/kg [max 60 mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN A: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg per dose; maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks. S: levamisole (PO) 2.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 12 months | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent: S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/d for 10-12 weeks [max 168 mg/kg cumulative dose] OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: everolimus 0.5-2 mg 12-hourly OR S: sirolimus 1-3 mg 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses; S: rituximab 375-1000 mg/m2 | Monitor calcineurin inhibitor toxicity/levels |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome: S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone high dose |  |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg 24-hourly (maximum 80 mg) OR alternate-day single dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 120 mg) – 4 weeks if remission; continue to 16 weeks if complete remission is not achieved | Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Check HbA1c monthly. Screen for osteoporosis |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent/resistant (idiopathic only): D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg [max 80 mg] daily or alternate-day 2 mg/kg [max 120 mg] for 4-16 weeks. OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate) | Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Children: alternating monthly treatment with methylprednisolone + prednisolone (months 1, 3 & 5) and oral cyclophosphamide (months 2, 4 & 6): D: methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg for 3 days, then prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 27 days; S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg for 30 days. Alternative regimens: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg in two divided doses with prednisolone 0.15 mg/kg/day for 6 months; S: tacrolimus 0.2 mg/kg in two divided doses without prednisolone | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Adults: S: cyclophosphamide; A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; D: methylprednisolone IV monthly. Alternative regimens: S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 6 months OR S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses. If albumin <25 g/l + thrombosis risk: C: warfarin 5 mg PO [refer to DVT anticoagulation] | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranoproliferative GN | S: cyclophosphamide OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone |  |
| IgA Nephropathy | Initial supportive care for 3-6 months: C: enalapril (PO) 10-20 mg 24-hourly OR C: lisinopril (PO) 2.5-10 mg 24-hourly. For persistent proteinuria >1 g/d for 6 months (adults and children): A: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/day for 6 months (as printed) | Other registered ACEI or ARBs may be used as in the Hypertension section |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | All patients: S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 6 mg/kg/day maintenance. Class II with proteinuria >3 g/day: treat as minimal change disease above |  |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class III and class IV, initial 6 months: D: methylprednisolone (IV slow) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days monthly AND S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500-1000 mg/m2 monthly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly, titrating to 1.5 g 12-hourly if tolerated, OR S: mycophenolate sodium. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) for 6 months OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) | Oral prednisolone less effective; 60 mg/day may be given. A shorter, more frequent regimen (Euro-Lupus) may be used: cyclophosphamide 500 mg every two weeks x 6 doses |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class V + persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: as class III and IV |  |
| Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis | Initial: S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then every three weeks for 3-6 months, OR S: cyclophosphamide oral 1.5-2 mg/kg daily for 3-6 months; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg slowly over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg, tapered to 30 mg in one week and then to 5 mg by 4-6 months. Severe disease: S: rituximab 1 g followed 14 days later by another 1 g, OR S: rituximab 375 mg/m2 per week for 4 weeks; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered as above. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/d for 18 months OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium | S: haemodialysis. S: plasmapheresis in special indications |

## **Management in Special Populations**

(a) Glomerular disease in pregnancy and child-bearing age females (15yrs - 49yrs)
* Safer immunosuppression and adjuncts = azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), glucocorticoids, and hydroxychloroquine.
* Preferred contraception = products that do not contain estrogen

text:
### Coordinated care of pregnant patients with glomerular disease: prepregnancy, antenatal, delivery and postnatal actions Glomerular disease in pregnancy and women of child-bearing age (15-49 years): safer immunosuppression and adjuncts are azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), glucocorticoids, and hydroxychloroquine. Preferred contraception: products that do not contain estrogen. | Stage | Actions | | --- | --- | | Prepregnancy | - Discuss timing of contraception; contraception advice if needed; fertility assessment if needed
- Assess disease activity, with repeat biopsy confirmation if necessary; optimize blood pressure control
- Change to non-teratogenic medications and provide reassurance about continuation of safe medications
- Explain the risk of pregnancy complications and the need for heightened surveillance | | Antenatal | - Target BP <140/90 mmHg
- Oral glucose tolerance test (especially important in women taking glucocorticoids or calcineurin inhibitors)
- Start low dose aspirin; consider vitamin D and calcium supplements
- Frequent fetal monitoring if concerns about fetal well-being: up to twice weekly BPPs, up to placental Dopplers, 2-weekly growth scans
- Baseline and serial kidney function, proteinuria (albumin-creatinine or protein-creatinine ratios or 24h collections) and markers of disease activity
- Monitoring of calcineurin inhibitor levels if required
- Consider venous thromboembolism prophylaxis if risk factors, e.g. nephrotic syndrome, previous venous thromboembolic events, high body mass index | | Delivery | - Delivery if fetal or maternal decompensation
- NOT at a pre-specified gestation
- Glucocorticoids for fetal lung maturation at least 24 h and up to 7 d before anticipated delivery if <34 weeks gestation | | Postnatal | - Encourage breastfeeding
- Careful surveillance for active glomerulonephritis
- Calcineurin inhibitor level if dose changed in pregnancy
- Continue venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for at least 6 weeks if necessary
- Emotional support | Adapted from Blom K, Odutayo A, Bramham K, et al. Pregnancy and glomerular disease: a systematic review of the literature with management guidelines. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2017;12:1862-1872. BP, blood pressure; BPP, biophysical profile; q2, every 2.

Coordinated care of pregnant patients with glomerular disease: prepregnancy, antenatal, delivery and postnatal actions
StageActions
Prepregnancy- Discuss timing of contraception; contraception advice if needed; fertility assessment if needed<br/>- Assess disease activity, with repeat biopsy confirmation if necessary; optimize blood pressure control<br/>- Change to non-teratogenic medications and provide reassurance about continuation of safe medications<br/>- Explain the risk of pregnancy complications and the need for heightened surveillance
Antenatal- Target BP <140/90 mmHg<br/>- Oral glucose tolerance test (especially important in women taking glucocorticoids or calcineurin inhibitors)<br/>- Start low dose aspirin; consider vitamin D and calcium supplements<br/>- Frequent fetal monitoring if concerns about fetal well-being: up to twice weekly BPPs, up to placental Dopplers, 2-weekly growth scans<br/>- Baseline and serial kidney function, proteinuria (albumin-creatinine or protein-creatinine ratios or 24h collections) and markers of disease activity<br/>- Monitoring of calcineurin inhibitor levels if required<br/>- Consider venous thromboembolism prophylaxis if risk factors, e.g. nephrotic syndrome, previous venous thromboembolic events, high body mass index
Delivery- Delivery if fetal or maternal decompensation<br/>- NOT at a pre-specified gestation<br/>- Glucocorticoids for fetal lung maturation at least 24 h and up to 7 d before anticipated delivery if <34 weeks gestation
Postnatal- Encourage breastfeeding<br/>- Careful surveillance for active glomerulonephritis<br/>- Calcineurin inhibitor level if dose changed in pregnancy<br/>- Continue venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for at least 6 weeks if necessary<br/>- Emotional support

text:
# CHAPTER 8

## Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder

**Clinical Guidelines Diagnosis and Management of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Abbreviations**
- ADHD: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
- DSM 5: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5th Edition
- MDD: Major Depressive Disorder

## Definition and Classification of ADHD

### Definition

- Is a neuropsychiatric disorder classified under developmental disorders
- Characterized by ongoing pattern of inattention and/ or hyperactivity- impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development.
- **Inattention:** difficulty staying on a task, sustaining focus, and staying organized, and these problems are not due to defiance or lack of comprehension.
- **Hyperactivity:** constant mobility including situations when it is not appropriate or excessively fidgets tap or talks. In adults may present with extreme restlessness or talking too much.
- **Impulsivity:** may act without thinking or have difficulty with self-control. It may include an inability to delay gratification, interrupting others, making important decisions without consideration of consequences.
Onset is usually before the age of 12

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder > Classification; Screening for ADHD
text:
## Definition and Classification of ADHD

### Classification

- Predominantly inattentive
- Predominantly impulsive/hyperactive
- Combined presentation

## Screening and Diagnosis of ADHD

### Screening for ADHD

- ADHD should be suspected in children and adults with history of inattentive, impulsive, or hyperactive symptoms.
- Commonly used tools include:
- The Adult Self Report Scale (ASRS)

- ADHD Rating Scale-IV (ADHD-RS-IV) for children
- Definitive diagnosis of ADHD is made by a specialist.

text:
## **Diagnostic Criteria (DSM5):**

May be reported by carer, self-reported or observed during the assessment process

(a) **Inattention:** Six or more symptoms of inattention for children up to age 16 years, or five or more for adolescents aged 17 years and adults; symptoms of inattention have been present for at least 6 months, and they are inappropriate for developmental level:
- Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes in schoolwork, at work, or with other activities.
- Often has trouble holding attention on tasks or play activities.
- Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
- Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace (e.g., loses focus, side-tracked).
- Often has trouble organizing tasks and activities.
- Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to do tasks that require mental effort over a long period of time (such as schoolwork or homework).
- Often loses things necessary for tasks and activities (e.g. school materials, pencils, books, tools, wallets, keys, paperwork, eyeglasses, mobile telephones).
- Is often easily distracted.
- Is often forgetful in daily activities.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder > Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5): Hyperactivity and Impulsivity
text:
(b) **Hyperactivity and Impulsivity:** Six or more symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity for children up to age 16 years, or five or more for adolescents aged 17 years and adults; symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity have been present for at least 6 months to an extent that is disruptive and inappropriate for the person's developmental level:
- Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet, or squirms in seat.
- Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
- Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is not appropriate (adolescents or adults may be limited to feeling restless).
- Often unable to play or take part in leisure activities quietly.
- Is often “on the go” acting as if “driven by a motor”.
- Often talks excessively.
- Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
- Often has trouble waiting their turn.
- Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations or games)

(c) In addition, the following conditions must be met:
* Several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were present before age 12 years.
* Several symptoms are present in two or more settings, (such as at home, school, or work; with friends or relatives; in other activities).
* There is clear evidence that the symptoms interfere with, or reduce the quality of, social, school, or work functioning.
* The symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder (such as a mood disorder, anxiety disorder, dissociative disorder, or a personality disorder). The symptoms do not happen only during the course of schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder > Non-Pharmacological Management of ADHD
text:
## **Non-Pharmacological Management of ADHD**

* Social skills training
* Psychoeducation to parents
* Cognitive- behavioural training
    - Set up very firm and clear routines
    - Set up good rewards system for good behaviour
    - Learn how to speak to a hyperactive kid

text:
## **For care givers**

* Acceptance of the child’s condition
* Involving the child in everyday life activities
* Develop and maintain routine
* Rewarding good behaviour
* Respecting the child’s right to have a safety zone
* Protecting the child from abuse
* Joining support groups and seeking professional advice

## **For teachers**

* Education structured to meet the child’s unique educational needs
* Providing an appropriate place in the classroom and giving proper attention.
* Inclusive education: children with mild to moderate symptoms must remain in mainstream school to receive education in normal environment
* Protection from bullying and abuse

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder > Complications and Prevention of ADHD
text:
# **Complications of ADHD**

- Impaired long-term work or school functioning, school dropout, bullying
- Social challenges: poor social interactions, social isolation from peers
- Financial instability
- Increased risk of injury; motor vehicle accidents, etc

# **Prevention of ADHD**

- No prevention for ADHD. However, early identification and intervention have positive impact.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Autism Spectrum Disorder > Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5)
text:
## **Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5)**

To meet diagnostic criteria, a child must have persistent deficits in each of three areas of social communication and interaction (see A.1. through A.3. below) plus at least two of four types of restricted, repetitive behaviors (see B.1. through B.4. below).

a. Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as manifested by the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text):
1. Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions.

2. Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication.

3. Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers.

b. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, as manifested by at least two of the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text):
1. Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypes, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases).

## **Management of ASD Treatment Targets**

* Improve social functioning and play skills
* Improve communication skills (both functional and spontaneous)
* Improve adaptive skills
* Decrease non- functional or negative behaviours
* Promote academic functioning and cognition
* Promote independent living

## **Non-Pharmacological Management of ASD**

* Speech therapy
* Occupational therapy
* Music therapy
* Art therapy
* Sport therapy

* Psychotherapy and psychoeducation for parents and care takers
* Education assessment, school placement
* Child Support assistance
* Sexual reproductive health needs

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Autism Spectrum Disorder > Non-Pharmacological Management > For care givers and teachers
text:
## **For care givers**

* Acceptance of the child’s condition
* Involving the child in everyday life activities.
* Develop and maintain routine
* Rewarding good behaviour
* Respecting the child’s right to have a safety zone
* Protecting the child from abuse
* Joining support groups and seeking professional advice

## **For teachers**

* Education structured to meet the child’s unique educational needs
* Providing an appropriate place in the classroom and giving proper attention.
* Inclusive education: children with mild to moderate symptoms must remain in mainstream school to receive education in normal environment
* Protection from bullying and abuse

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Classification
text:
### Classification of seizures: generalised (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, epileptic spasms) and focal (aware, impaired awareness): consciousness, duration, features, typical age

Epilepsy is a chronic noncommunicable brain disorder characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures (two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart). This module covers convulsive epilepsy. With proper treatment, most people can be seizure-free.

| Category | Type | Consciousness | Duration | Key Clinical Features | Typical Age/Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Generalized | Tonic–clonic | Lost | 2–5 min | Fall, stiffening → jerking, frothing, tongue bite, incontinence, postictal sleep/confusion | Most common |
| Generalized | Absence | Briefly lost | 5–30 sec | Blank stare, stops activity, eye rolling, no fall, no confusion after | School-aged children, frequent, provoked by hyperventilation |
| Generalized | Myoclonic | Usually preserved | Seconds | Sudden shock-like jerks of limbs/body | Often in epileptic syndromes |
| Generalized | Epileptic spasms (infantile spasms) | Variable | Seconds (clusters) | Head/trunk flexion, arm abduction, knee bending | Infants <1 yr, developmental delay |
| Focal | Focal aware (simple partial) | Preserved | Seconds | Local twitching, sensory changes, déjà vu, hallucinations | Patient aware of event |
| Focal | Focal impaired awareness (complex partial) | Impaired | 1–3 min | Aura, staring, automatisms (lip smacking, picking clothes), confusion, amnesia | Slow recovery, may appear aggressive |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Diagnosis of Epilepsy
text:
## **Diagnosis of Epilepsy**

According to NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) guidelines, April 2022:
1. **History Taking and Physical Examination** - better with video record.
2. **Cardiac assessment** - 12-lead ECG- to rule out cardiac diseases which might mimic seizures.
3. **Blood test** - full blood count, electrolytes, random blood glucose, HIV testing, toxicology screen, renal profile, liver function test, serum corrected calcium, magnesium, and phosphate.
4. **Specific investigations** - CSF analysis, connective tissue disease screening
5. **Neuroimaging - Brain CT or MRI**
6. **Electroencephalogram (EEG)**

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Epilepsy Algorithm of Assessment and Management
text:
> **Epilepsy assessment and management algorithm: 8 assessment steps, emergency management of seizures >5 min, when to refer, first aid at home**
>
> Assessment:
> 1. Person presents with episodes of convulsions (fits, shaking, stiffening), witnessed or reported.
> 2. Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency?
> 3. Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal.
> 4. Assess: postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history?
> 5. Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age.
> 6. Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life.
> 7. Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety).
> 8. Diagnosis: epilepsy confirmed → proceed to management.
> 
> EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT (seizure > 5 min): call for emergency help immediately; diazepam 10-20 mg IV/PR or lorazepam 4 mg IV for status epilepticus; airway – place in recovery position, ensure breathing; DO NOT restrain; DO NOT put anything in the mouth; monitor blood glucose; give thiamine if alcohol-related.
> 
> When to refer: first seizure (confirm diagnosis); seizures not controlled after 2 drug trials; pregnancy + epilepsy (specialist input needed); status epilepticus; suspected structural cause (tumour, stroke).
> 
> First aid at home (advise carers): lay the person on their side, head turned to the side; ensure the airway is clear, loosen tight clothing; time the seizure and stay until fully conscious; no food/water until fully alert; seek help if the seizure lasts >5 min, there is no recovery, or injury; epilepsy is NOT contagious.
html:
Epilepsy assessment and management algorithm: 8 assessment steps, emergency management of seizures >5 min, when to refer, first aid at home

Assessment:

1. Person presents with episodes of convulsions (fits, shaking, stiffening), witnessed or reported.

2. Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency?

3. Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal.

4. Assess: postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history?

5. Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age.

6. Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life.

7. Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety).

8. Diagnosis: epilepsy confirmed → proceed to management.

EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT (seizure > 5 min): call for emergency help immediately; diazepam 10-20 mg IV/PR or lorazepam 4 mg IV for status epilepticus; airway – place in recovery position, ensure breathing; DO NOT restrain; DO NOT put anything in the mouth; monitor blood glucose; give thiamine if alcohol-related.

When to refer: first seizure (confirm diagnosis); seizures not controlled after 2 drug trials; pregnancy + epilepsy (specialist input needed); status epilepticus; suspected structural cause (tumour, stroke).

First aid at home (advise carers): lay the person on their side, head turned to the side; ensure the airway is clear, loosen tight clothing; time the seizure and stay until fully conscious; no food/water until fully alert; seek help if the seizure lasts >5 min, there is no recovery, or injury; epilepsy is NOT contagious.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Epilepsy Management — Pharmacological Treatment
text:
### Antiepileptic medicines: sodium valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine: adult and child doses, contraindications, side effects; principles of AED treatment

Antiepileptic medications: start one medication at the lowest dose and increase slowly until seizures are controlled. 1. Start low and go slow with a single AED as monotherapy, chosen by seizure type and epilepsy syndrome; titrate to the maximal dose. 2. If the first AED is ineffective at the maximum tolerated dose, introduce an alternative AED slowly without tapering the first. 3. If there is a good response to the second AED, consider withdrawing the original gradually. 4. If the first add-on AED is ineffective or has undesirable side effects, withdraw it slowly and replace it with another add-on AED. 5. If seizures are not controlled on two AEDs, some patients may benefit from a third. 6. Prefer an add-on AED with a different mode of action. 7. Review the diagnosis if seizures continue despite this approach and 2-3 years have elapsed.

| Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anticonvulsant | Sodium valproate | Adults: 200 mg TDS PO; maintenance 400-1800 mg/day divided into 3 doses. Children: 10-15 mg/kg/day PO divided into 2 doses; maintenance <20 kg: 20-40 mg/kg/day; >20 kg: 20-30 mg/kg/day | Hepatic impairment; von Willebrand disease | Tremor, dizziness, weight gain, alopecia, diuresis, thrombocytopenia, impaired hepatic function |
| Anticonvulsant | Carbamazepine | Adults: 200 mg BD PO; maintenance 800-1200 mg/day divided into 2 doses. Children: 10-20 mg/kg/day PO divided into 2 doses; maintenance 20-30 mg/kg/day | Absence and myoclonic seizures; bone marrow suppression; hypersensitivity to tricyclic antidepressants | Blurred/double vision, nystagmus, ataxia, drowsiness, hyponatremia, rash, cytopenia, liver dysfunction, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis |
| Anticonvulsant | Phenytoin | Adults: 100 mg TDS PO; maintenance 300-900 mg/day divided into 3 doses. Children: 5-8 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses | Absence and myoclonic seizures; febrile convulsions | Gingival hypertrophy, rash, confusion, fever, slurred speech, double vision, ataxia, bone marrow depression, hepatitis |
| Barbiturate | Phenobarbital | Adults: 30 mg NOCTE PO; maintenance 30-120 mg/day divided into 2 doses. Children: 3-5 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses | Airway obstruction; dyspnea; marked hepatic impairment | Nausea, rash, sedation, lethargy, dependence, alteration of sleep cycle, hyperactivity, ataxia, liver dysfunction |
| Anticonvulsant | Lamotrigine | Adults: 25 mg every other day [with valproate], 25 mg OD [without valproate]; maintenance 100-200 mg/day [with valproate], 100-400 mg/day [without valproate]. Children: 0.15 mg/kg/day [with valproate], 0.3 mg/kg/day [without valproate]; maintenance 1-3 mg/kg/day [with valproate], 4.5-7.5 mg/kg/day [without valproate] | Hypersensitivity to the drug or its ingredients. Be cautious and titrate slowly if used with sodium valproate | Drowsiness, dizziness, diplopia, rash, cytopenia, liver injury, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis |

text:
### Antiepileptic medicines: sodium valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine: adult and child doses, contraindications, side effects; principles of AED treatment

Antiepileptic medications: start one medication at the lowest dose and increase slowly until seizures are controlled. 1. Start low and go slow with a single AED as monotherapy, chosen by seizure type and epilepsy syndrome; titrate to the maximal dose. 2. If the first AED is ineffective at the maximum tolerated dose, introduce an alternative AED slowly without tapering the first. 3. If there is a good response to the second AED, consider withdrawing the original gradually. 4. If the first add-on AED is ineffective or has undesirable side effects, withdraw it slowly and replace it with another add-on AED. 5. If seizures are not controlled on two AEDs, some patients may benefit from a third. 6. Prefer an add-on AED with a different mode of action. 7. Review the diagnosis if seizures continue despite this approach and 2-3 years have elapsed.

text:
> **Epilepsy psychoeducation and psychosocial interventions, cautions and special populations (drug interactions, pregnancy, children, PLHIV), and follow-up**
>
> Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions:
> - Epilepsy is caused by abnormal electrical brain activity, NOT spirits or witchcraft.
> - Chronic condition: medication controls seizures in most if taken daily.
> - People with epilepsy can marry, work, have children and lead normal lives.
> - Avoid open fires, swimming alone, heights, heavy machinery, alcohol excess.
> - Observe local driving laws; may qualify for disability benefits.
> - All AEMs: taper slowly; an abrupt stop causes breakthrough seizures.
> - Review every 3-6 months; check adherence and side effects.
> 
> Cautions & special populations:
> - Check drug-drug interactions: AEMs reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives and antiretrovirals.
> - Rare: severe bone marrow depression, Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
> - Pregnancy: consult a specialist; supplement folate; valproate contraindicated.
> - Children: weight-based dosing; monitor growth and development.
> - PLHIV: check interactions with antiretrovirals before prescribing.
> - (Printed in the same cell:) minimum 2 years seizure-free before [stopping AEMs].
> 
> Follow-up (every 1-3 months initially, then 3-6 monthly): review seizure frequency (decreased or stopped?); check medication adherence and side effects; assess functional status (school, work, daily activities); screen for depression/anxiety comorbidity; if no seizures for 2+ years, discuss gradual tapering with a specialist; if seizures continue despite an adequate dose, increase the dose, check adherence, or refer to a specialist.
html:
Epilepsy psychoeducation and psychosocial interventions, cautions and special populations (drug interactions, pregnancy, children, PLHIV), and follow-up

Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions:

- Epilepsy is caused by abnormal electrical brain activity, NOT spirits or witchcraft.

- Chronic condition: medication controls seizures in most if taken daily.

- People with epilepsy can marry, work, have children and lead normal lives.

- Avoid open fires, swimming alone, heights, heavy machinery, alcohol excess.

- Observe local driving laws; may qualify for disability benefits.

- All AEMs: taper slowly; an abrupt stop causes breakthrough seizures.

- Review every 3-6 months; check adherence and side effects.

Cautions & special populations:

- Check drug-drug interactions: AEMs reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives and antiretrovirals.

- Rare: severe bone marrow depression, Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

- Pregnancy: consult a specialist; supplement folate; valproate contraindicated.

- Children: weight-based dosing; monitor growth and development.

- PLHIV: check interactions with antiretrovirals before prescribing.

- (Printed in the same cell:) minimum 2 years seizure-free before [stopping AEMs].

Follow-up (every 1-3 months initially, then 3-6 monthly): review seizure frequency (decreased or stopped?); check medication adherence and side effects; assess functional status (school, work, daily activities); screen for depression/anxiety comorbidity; if no seizures for 2+ years, discuss gradual tapering with a specialist; if seizures continue despite an adequate dose, increase the dose, check adherence, or refer to a specialist.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Systematic approach to long-term pharmacological treatment
text:
### Systematic approach to long-term pharmacological treatment of epilepsy: when to start AEDs, monotherapy, second AED, referral, re-evaluation, surgery and other options

When to start AEDs: immediate AED therapy is usually not necessary after a single seizure; it is generally started after two or more unprovoked seizures.

1. Initial AED monotherapy. Select the AED based on seizure type/syndrome, age, sex, childbearing potential, comorbidities, concomitant medications, adverse effects, interaction profile.
2. If failure: second AED, as monotherapy or add-on.
3. If failure: referral to a tertiary care centre (a).
4. Diagnostic re-evaluation (epilepsy yes/no, seizure types, syndrome, adherence, dosing), then: resective surgery; additional drug trials; neurostimulatory and dietary approaches (b).
Options at tertiary level: epilepsy surgery; ketogenic diet; vagus nerve stimulation; deep brain stimulation.

text:
# Complications of Epilepsy

- High mortality- sudden death, injury, and motor vehicle accidents.
- Fall- it might lead to fractures, head contusion or internal bleeding
- Dropout of school or unemployment
- Adverse effects or intoxication of AEDs

# Epilepsy Emergencies

There are two common Epilepsy emergencies:
(i) Acute repetitive seizures and
(ii) Status epilepticus.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Status Epilepticus > Treatment Algorithm for Status Epilepticus
text:
### Management algorithm for status epilepticus in adults (ICU): stabilisation 0-5 min, first-line benzodiazepines 5-15 min, second-line valproate or phenytoin 15-30 min, third-line anaesthetic infusions after 30 min

Epilepsy emergencies: (i) acute repetitive seizures; (ii) status epilepticus.

0-5 minutes (stabilisation):
1. Stabilise the patient: assess airway, breathing, circulation.
2. Time the seizure onset; monitor vital signs (ECG, BP, HR, temperature).
3. Finger-stick blood glucose. If glucose <60 mg/dl, give 50 ml of 50% dextrose IV.
4. Laboratory investigations: electrolytes, CBC, liver and renal function tests.
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

5-15 minutes (first-line therapy): IV diazepam ('0.5 - 0.2 mg/kg/dose' as printed), max 10 mg, OR IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max not printed).
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

15-30 minutes, on ward (second-line therapy): valproate (VPA) 30 mg/kg loading dose and 4-8 mg/kg every 8 hr maintenance, OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading dose and '1.5 mg' every 8 hr maintenance (as printed).
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

After 30 minutes, on ward (third-line therapy):
1. Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg bolus and 1-2 mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for a minimum of 24 hr.
2. Propofol 1-3 mg/kg bolus and 5-10 mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for 24 hr.
3. Thiopental 3-5 mg/kg bolus and '3-3 mg/kg/hr' continuous infusion for 24 hr (as printed).

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Introduction
text:
### **ONCOLOGY**

These guidelines will concentrate on the following cancers. Cervical cancer , prostate cancer, colorectal cancers, adult lymphomas, breast cancer, childhood cancer screening and oral-maxillofacial cancers. For further reading please REFER TO Eswatini National Cancer guidelines.

#### **Cervical Cancer**

Cervical cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related death among women in Eswatini, with an incidence rate of 84.5 per 100,000 female population - the highest in the world. The high HIV prevalence in Eswatini (approximately 40% among sexually active women) significantly contributes to this burden, as women living with HIV have a six-fold increased risk of developing cervical cancer.

These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for cervical cancer screening, triage, and treatment of pre- cancerous lesions in Eswatini, with specific considerations for women living with HIV.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Cervical Cancer > Cervical Cancer Screening & Treatment Algorithm
text:
### Cervical cancer screening and treatment algorithm: HIV-negative women vs women living with HIV (HPV DNA testing, VIA/VILI triage, screen-and-treat, stop age)

A. General population (HIV-negative women):
1. Age 25-50 years: HPV DNA testing; screen every 5 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 5 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every 2 years (rescreen in 2 years):
   - Negative: rescreen in 2 years.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/colposcopy.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

B. Women living with HIV:
1. HIV positive, age 25+ OR at diagnosis: HPV DNA testing; screen every 3 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 3 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every year or VILI every year (return in 1 year):
   - Negative: return in 1 year.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/oncology.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

Single-visit screen-and-treat: SCREEN → TRIAGE → TREAT (same day) → FOLLOW-UP; same-day care when feasible.
VIA: visual inspection with acetic acid. VILI: visual inspection with Lugol's iodine.

   - Negative: rescreen in 2 years.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/colposcopy.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

B. Women living with HIV:
1. HIV positive, age 25+ OR at diagnosis: HPV DNA testing; screen every 3 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 3 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every year or VILI every year (return in 1 year):
   - Negative: return in 1 year.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/oncology.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

Single-visit screen-and-treat: SCREEN → TRIAGE → TREAT (same day) → FOLLOW-UP; same-day care when feasible.
VIA: visual inspection with acetic acid. VILI: visual inspection with Lugol's iodine.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Cervical Cancer > Management by VIA result
text:
### Management by VIA screening result: negative, positive eligible for ablation, positive ineligible (LEEP), suspicious for cancer: eligibility, action and follow-up

| VIA Screening Result | Treatment Eligibility / Findings | Clinical Action & Procedure | Follow-Up Timeline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VIA Negative | No lesions or suspicious areas identified | Discharge: return to routine screening (annual for HIV+; 2 years for HIV-) | 12 - 24 months (based on HIV status) |
| VIA Positive (eligible for ablation) | Lesion ≤75% of ectocervix; TZ fully visible (type 1); no endocervical extension; no suspicion of cancer | Ablative treatment (same visit): thermal ablation or cryotherapy | 12 months (repeat VIA) |
| VIA Positive (ineligible for ablation) | Large lesion (≥75% coverage); high-grade lesion suspected; tissue diagnosis needed | Refer for LEEP | 6 months (VIA or HPV) |
| Suspicious for Cancer | Visible mass/cauliflower growth; bleeds easily on contact; extension to vaginal walls | Urgent referral to secondary/tertiary level for colposcopy and biopsy | Immediate (per specialist) |

text:
### Cervical cancer screening in special populations: women living with HIV (on ART/PrEP), pregnant women, HIV-negative women

Because HIV significantly increases the risk of cervical cancer, screening must be integrated into routine care.

| Population | Screening Rule | Key Clinical Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HIV-positive women | Annual VIA screening | Integrate into ART initiation and routine follow-up. |
| On ART / PrEP | Annual VIA screening | Adherence reduces but does not eliminate risk. |
| Pregnant women | Screen per HIV status | VIA is safe. Defer treatment until post-delivery unless cancer is suspected. |
| HIV-negative | Every 2 years | Use community health workers and registries for recall. |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Adult Lymphomas > Definition and Classification
text:
### **Definition(s) and Classification of Adult Lymphomas:**

Lymphoma is a broad term for cancer that begins in cells of the lymph system. The two main types are Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

Though some NHL subtypes are not easy to categorize as such, NHL are often classified as

* Indolent (Low grade)
* Intermediate Grade
* High grade (Aggressive)

HL is divided in to:
* Classical (95% of HL)
* Nodular Lymphocyte predominant HL(NLPHL)

# BREAST CANCER

Breast cancer is a malignant tumor that starts in the cells of the breast. Most breast cancers begin in the cells that line the ducts (ductal cancers). Some begin in the cells that line the lobules (lobular cancers), while a small number start in other tissues.

## **Classification of Breast Cancer**

Breast cancer is grossly divided into:
1. Carcinoma-in-situ (CIS) :in particular Ductal carcinoma-in-situ(DCIS)
2. Invasive cancer: main histology being invasive/infiltrating ductal carcinoma and invasive lobular carcinoma.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Metastases and Risk Factors
text:
## Breast Cancers are further categorised based on metastases

### **Isolated Tumour Cells (ITCs):**

- Micro-metastases are single cancer cells or small clusters of cells (0.2 - 2mm).
- Macro-metastases are cancer cells larger than 2mm.
- Three or more sentinel nodes with macro-metastases, will need further treatment to the axilla.

## **Risk Factors for Breast Cancer**

Modifiable risk factors are mainly (Life-style related risk factors). However nulliparous women and women who have used hormonal birth control as well as hormone replacement therapy post-menopause are at higher risk.

Non-modifiable risk factors specific to breast cancer include:
- Family or personal history of breast or ovarian cancer.
- Inheriting genetic mutations such as **BRCA1, BRCA2**
- Previous radiation exposure to the chest for other conditions in childhood or early adulthood

### Breast cancer risk stratification by family history and genetics: above average, moderately increased, high risk | Risk Level | Criteria | | --- | --- | | Above Average Risk | - No family history
- One first-degree relative or 1–2 second-degree relatives diagnosed at age 50 or older | | Moderately Increased Risk | - A first-degree relative diagnosed before age 50

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > How to Advise Client on Breast Self-Examination
text:
> **Breast self-examination: how to advise clients (looking, touching, lying down, lymph nodes)**
>
> 1. By looking: stand before a mirror and look at both breasts and nipples – once with both arms beside your body; once with both hands on your hips; once with both arms raised and arms behind your head.
> 2. By touching: raise your left arm. Use the pads of 3 or 4 fingers of the right hand to examine your left breast; repeat on the right side. Examine once in lines up and down the breast from outside and inside; once in circles around the breast, making smaller circles towards the nipple; once in wedges starting from outside towards the nipple and back again.
> 3. While lying down: lie on your back, left arm over your head and a pillow under your left shoulder. Examine your left breast with your right hand as described before; repeat for the right side. This position flattens the breast and makes it easier to examine.
> 4. Lymph nodes: place your left hand on your waist. With your right hand try to find enlarged lymph nodes in the left underarm area and around your collar bone; repeat on your right side. An enlarged lymph node feels like a corn kernel or a bean.
html:
Breast self-examination: how to advise clients (looking, touching, lying down, lymph nodes)

1. By looking: stand before a mirror and look at both breasts and nipples – once with both arms beside your body; once with both hands on your hips; once with both arms raised and arms behind your head.

2. By touching: raise your left arm. Use the pads of 3 or 4 fingers of the right hand to examine your left breast; repeat on the right side. Examine once in lines up and down the breast from outside and inside; once in circles around the breast, making smaller circles towards the nipple; once in wedges starting from outside towards the nipple and back again.

3. While lying down: lie on your back, left arm over your head and a pillow under your left shoulder. Examine your left breast with your right hand as described before; repeat for the right side. This position flattens the breast and makes it easier to examine.

4. Lymph nodes: place your left hand on your waist. With your right hand try to find enlarged lymph nodes in the left underarm area and around your collar bone; repeat on your right side. An enlarged lymph node feels like a corn kernel or a bean.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Clinical Breast Examination (CBE) > Step 1: Visual Inspection
text:
#### **Clinical Breast Examination (CBE)**

It is an examination of both breasts performed by a trained health professional.

#### **Step 1: Visual Inspection**

Identify any visible abnormalities or asymmetry or nipple retraction

1. Patient should be naked from the waist up.
2. Patient sitting up, hands on either side of hips and pushing into hips down.
3. The patient has to raise her arms and press her hands together over her head.
4. Pay attention to the size, form, symmetry of the breast tissue, color and changes on the skin, condition of the nipple and nipple discharge.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Early Referral Flow Chart for Suspected Breast Cancer
text:
### Early referral flowchart for suspected breast cancer: urgent referral to the specialised breast unit, booking, or surgical clinic, by likelihood of malignancy

Suspected lump → provider-initiated clinical breast exam (PI-CBE) and direct referral to the specialised breast unit (SBU):
- High likelihood of malignancy → URGENT REFERRAL TO SBU (call and inform the SBU): suspicious lump (fixed, hard, irregular); palpable axillary lymph node; ulceration; nodules on the skin; skin tethering; nipple retraction; nipple discharge (e.g. bloody).
- Unsure → book SBU: palpable lump in women >25 years; non-lactational breast infection/abscess.
- Unlikely to be malignant → book for surgical clinic: palpable lump in women <25 years; breast pain with normal PI-CBE; family history with normal PI-CBE; lactation-associated infection with non-resolution/recurrence.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Treatment Targets and Management
text:
### **Treatment Targets**

Treatment for breast cancer is stage dependent and relies on a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.

The aims are:
* Control the primary disease with an optimum 5-year survival rate
* Control the symptoms and pain and improve the patients daily living (Palliative care)

### **Management of Breast Cancer**

Several factors are considered when planning the treatment for an individual breast cancer patient. Ideally, an MDT team comprised of surgeon, oncologist and other experts meet to discuss the outline and plan of care.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Management in Special Populations (pregnancy)
text:
#### **Management in Special Populations:**

**ALL PREGNANT WOMEN WITH BREAST CANCER SHOULD BE REVIEWED BY AN MDT TEAM INCLUDING AN ONCOLOGIST, OBGYN AND OR OBGYN ONCOLOGIST**

#### **Breast Cancer in Pregnancy**

* **Chemotherapy in pregnant patients after the first trimester**
    - **Anthracyclines, Cyclophosphamide and Taxanes can be used in both 2nd and 3rd Trimesters**

* **If in 3rd trimester, it is preferable to have upfront surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy after delivery.**
* **No radiotherapy or radiation-related investigations are to be offered at any stage of the pregnancy.**

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Definition and Common Childhood Cancers
text:
## **Childhood Cancers**

Cancer that arises between birth and 19 years of age. Pediatric malignancies differ greatly from adult malignancies in both prognosis and distribution by histology and tumor site. Lymphohematopoietic cancers (i.e., Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphomas) account for approximately 40%, central nervous system cancers for approximately 30%, and embryonal tumors and sarcomas for approximately 10% among the broad categories of childhood cancers.

The most common cancers of children are:
* Leukemias (about 28% of all childhood cancers)
* Brain and spinal cord tumors (about 26% of childhood cancers)
* Neuroblastoma (about 6% of childhood cancers)
* Wilms tumor (5%)
* Lymphoma (including both Hodgkin’s and Non-Hodgkin’s)
* Rhabdomyosarcoma
* Retinoblastoma
* Bone cancer (including osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma)<sup>2</sup>

### **Diagnostic Criteria**

High index of suspicion and early detection of childhood cancers is critical. The main warning signs are summarized as ‘**SILUAN signs**’.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Warning Signs of Childhood Cancers (St. Siluan's signs)
text:
### Warning signs of childhood cancers (St. Siluan's signs): seek help, eye, lump, unexplained symptoms, aches, neurological signs, with likely cancers and actions

Childhood cancers arise between birth and 19 years. The most common are leukaemias (about 28%), brain and spinal cord tumours (about 26%), neuroblastoma (about 6%), Wilms tumour (5%), lymphomas, rhabdomyosarcoma, retinoblastoma and bone cancers (osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma). A high index of suspicion and early detection are critical.

| Letter | Category | Key Signs & Symptoms | Actions/Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S | Seek | Seek medical help early for ongoing symptoms: prolonged symptoms; symptoms persist after treatment; symptoms return after initially disappearing | Seek medical help; return to the same clinic/doctor for follow-up |
| I (E) | Eye | White spot in the eye (leukocoria) → possible retinoblastoma; loss of red eye reflex; new squint or sudden blindness → possible brain tumour; bulging eyeball → possible eye cancer or retro-orbital tumour | Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist or paediatrician |
| L | Lump | Lump in the abdomen, pelvis, head, arms, legs, testicle or glands; Wilms' tumour (age 3–4 years); consider neuroblastoma, lymphoma | Refer every lump to a doctor. If treated for TB without confirmation and not improving after 2 weeks → re-evaluate, consider biopsy |
| U | Unexplained | Unexplained fever for over two weeks; weight or appetite loss; fatigue; pallor; easy bruising and bleeding | Possible leukaemia or solid tumours; requires thorough clinical assessment |
| A | Ache | Aching bones, joints, back and easy fractures. Aches and pains in bones and back are not common in children and should raise suspicion | Possible leukaemia or sarcoma; needs critical evaluation |
| N | Neurological | Change in walk, balance or speech; regression of milestones; slurred speech; continuous headaches (>1 week) with or without vomiting; early morning vomiting; cranial nerve palsy; enlarged head (hydrocephalus) | Possible brain tumour; prompt referral and neuroimaging as needed |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Warning Signs of Childhood Cancers (St. Siluan's signs)
text:
### Warning signs of childhood cancers (St. Siluan's signs): seek help, eye, lump, unexplained symptoms, aches, neurological signs, with likely cancers and actions

Childhood cancers arise between birth and 19 years. The most common are leukaemias (about 28%), brain and spinal cord tumours (about 26%), neuroblastoma (about 6%), Wilms tumour (5%), lymphomas, rhabdomyosarcoma, retinoblastoma and bone cancers (osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma). A high index of suspicion and early detection are critical.

| Letter | Category | Key Signs & Symptoms | Actions/Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S | Seek | Seek medical help early for ongoing symptoms: prolonged symptoms; symptoms persist after treatment; symptoms return after initially disappearing | Seek medical help; return to the same clinic/doctor for follow-up |
| I (E) | Eye | White spot in the eye (leukocoria) → possible retinoblastoma; loss of red eye reflex; new squint or sudden blindness → possible brain tumour; bulging eyeball → possible eye cancer or retro-orbital tumour | Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist or paediatrician |
| L | Lump | Lump in the abdomen, pelvis, head, arms, legs, testicle or glands; Wilms' tumour (age 3–4 years); consider neuroblastoma, lymphoma | Refer every lump to a doctor. If treated for TB without confirmation and not improving after 2 weeks → re-evaluate, consider biopsy |
| U | Unexplained | Unexplained fever for over two weeks; weight or appetite loss; fatigue; pallor; easy bruising and bleeding | Possible leukaemia or solid tumours; requires thorough clinical assessment |
| A | Ache | Aching bones, joints, back and easy fractures. Aches and pains in bones and back are not common in children and should raise suspicion | Possible leukaemia or sarcoma; needs critical evaluation |
| N | Neurological | Change in walk, balance or speech; regression of milestones; slurred speech; continuous headaches (>1 week) with or without vomiting; early morning vomiting; cranial nerve palsy; enlarged head (hydrocephalus) | Possible brain tumour; prompt referral and neuroimaging as needed |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Warning Signs of Childhood Cancer: suspicious clinical features
text:
### Warning signs of childhood cancer: signs and symptoms with the clinical features that make them suspicious (pallor, fever, infections, lymphadenopathy, bleeding, headache, masses, bone pain and others)

| Signs and Symptoms | Suspicious Clinical Features |
| --- | --- |
| Paleness, fatigue, and malaise | Especially if persistent and associated with signs of bone marrow infiltration (unexplained fever, recurrent infections, bleeding diathesis) and/or lymphadenopathy |
| Fever | Prolonged (>2 weeks) without apparent cause, associated with weight loss, night sweats, paleness, petechiae, mass, bone pain and lymphadenopathy |
| Recurrent or persistent infections | Associated with paleness, petechiae, weight loss, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or palpable mass |
| Anorexia and weight loss | Prolonged and unjustified, especially with other warning signs (recurrent infections, fever, paleness, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly) |
| Localized lymphadenopathy | Persistent or progressive, not resolving in 4-6 weeks or unresponsive to antibiotics; size >2 cm, hard, painless, supraclavicular or epitrochlear |
| Generalized or localized (lymphadenopathy) | Associated with fever, night sweats, weight loss, malaise, paleness and hepatosplenomegaly |
| Hemorrhagic manifestations (petechiae, ecchymosis, recurrent epistaxis, bleeding gums) | Persistent or combined with other signs of bone marrow infiltration (paleness, fatigue, recurrent infections) |
| Headache | Recent onset, in the morning or waking the child at night, without a history of migraine, associated with vomiting or neurological symptoms (cranial palsy, motor or sensory signs), occipital location, worse when lying down |
| Impaired school performance and mood changes | Recent onset, progressive and not explained |
| Palpable abdominal mass | Any mass (except in the neonatal period) is suspicious for malignancy, especially with vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, hematuria or hypertension |
| Hepatomegaly | Must always be investigated, even in asymptomatic cases |
| Vomiting | Persistent or recurring; associated with morning headache or abdominal mass |
| Bone pain, arthralgia/arthritis, limp or refusal to walk | Bone pain that wakes the child at night, duration >2 weeks, localized, associated with inflammation, no improvement with NSAIDs |
| Back pain, kyphoscoliosis, lordosis and torticollis | Back pain of sudden onset, age <4 years, worse at night, associated with fever or neurological symptoms, without trauma, not improving with NSAIDs |
| Mass or lump in extremities, head, neck, or trunk | Any palpable mass of recent appearance, deep to the fascia, not painful, hard, >2 cm in diameter and associated with regional lymphadenopathy |
| Urinary retention/enuresis | Recent; associated with neurological symptoms or abdominal mass |
| Scrotal mass or swelling | Recent; isolated right varicocele |
| Swollen/bleeding gums | Not explained |
| Dermatological manifestations | Eczema that does not respond to treatment; subcutaneous nodules |

NSAIDs: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Childhood Cancer Referral Pathway
text:
### Childhood cancer referral pathway: primary clinic identification, urgent referral, workup, MDT, confirmation, paediatric oncology

1. Primary clinic (e.g. GP, school nurse): identify suspected cancer using the SILUAN signs (significant, unexplained, rapid onset, ongoing symptoms, night sweats).
2. Urgent referral to a health centre/regional hospital.
3. Initial workup and assessment: physical exam, blood tests, imaging as needed.
4. Multidisciplinary team (MDT): paediatric oncologist, radiology, radiotherapy (as printed 'ratiology'), pathology, surgery.
5. Confirmation of diagnosis.
6. Referral to paediatric oncology for management (treatment planning, supportive care).

#### **Definition(s) and Classification of Colorectal Cancer**

There are no defined classifications of colorectal cancer, however it may be described based on local disease or metastatic disease.

#### **Risk Factors for Colorectal Cancer**

Factors that increase the risk of developing colorectal cancer are as follows: They are grouped into modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Colorectal Cancer > Risk Factors for Colorectal Cancer
text:
### Colorectal cancer risk factors: modifiable vs non-modifiable

| Modifiable Risk Factors | Non-modifiable Risk Factors |
| --- | --- |
| Excess body fat | Family history of colorectal cancer |
| Sedentary lifestyle | Advanced polyps |
| Westernized diet including processed/pre-packed meats, fried foods, fast food etc. | Polyposis syndrome (FAP, MAP) |
| Processed meats | Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) |
| Red meats | Black race |
| Smoking | Older age |
| Alcohol | Male gender |

## **Prevention**

Lifestyle changes and regular screening can help prevent colorectal cancer. Lifestyle changes to help prevent colorectal cancer include:
* Eating a healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables
* Not smoking tobacco
* Keeping an active lifestyle
* Limiting alcohol consumption
* Diet low in red meat

## Screening and Diagnosis of Colorectal Cancer

### **Screening helps in**

* Detection and removal of polyps and sessile serrated lesions
* Early-stage detection of CRC

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Colorectal Cancer > Screening and High-Risk Patients
text:
### **High risk patients**

* Family history of colon cancer, aged < 60 years
* Benign colon disease, e.g. polyps
* History of abdominal or pelvic radiation
* Previous history of colon cancer in index patient
* Having inherited syndromes; Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis
* Inflammatory bowel syndrome

The high-risk population will be screened with scheduled colonoscopy and stool occult blood tests. It is advised that a baseline colonoscopy at age 50(at 45 or younger in high risk as per the discretion of the clinician) is offered; to be repeated t least every ten years.

text:
# Patient Assessment

This will be done based on clinical presentation with one of the following or those who have significant risk factors as outlined above.

- A change in bowel habits, such as more frequent diarrhea or constipation.
- Rectal bleeding or blood in the stool.
- Ongoing discomfort in the belly area, such as cramps, gas, or pain.
- A feeling that the bowel doesn't empty all the way during a bowel movement.
- Weakness or tiredness.
- Weigh loss
  ✓ Any rectal bleeding should be seriously investigated as colorectal cancer can be mistaken for hemorrhoids, anal fissures, and other benign conditions.
  ✓ Cancer on the left part of the colon is more likely to present with bowel obstructive symptoms; while right sided once may present
