heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Colorectal Cancer > Diagnostic Work Up
text:
## Diagnostic Work Up

**Fecal Occult Blood Test** - Blood in the stool may be a sign of polyps, cancer, or other conditions.

Types of Fecal Occult Blood Test:
1. Guaiac test
2. Fecal Immunochemical test
3. DNA stool test

If any of these tests are abnormal, then a colonoscopy should be performed.
- **Colonoscopy** - the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening. It works as both a diagnostic and therapeutic measure.
- **Sigmoidoscopy** - Sigmoidoscopy is less invasive and easier. It only looks at the lower part of the colon.

Other additional diagnostic methods for colorectal cancer include:
- Clinical presentation
- Basic blood workup (FBC/KFT/LFT/Blood glucose etc.)
- Imaging (ultrasound, X-ray, CT scan, and MRI),
- Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy for biopsy & histopathology examination
- Molecular testing to identify specific genetic mutations or biomarkers to guide the best treatment option.
- Tumor markers (CEA in particular)

text:
## <u>Staging of Colorectal Cancer (TNM)</u>

- Once the diagnosis is established, the local and distant extent of disease spread is determined to provide a framework for discussing therapy and prognosis.
- The TNM (AJCC) stage of a colon cancer has three components:
  - ✓ Primary tumor (T) in the layers of the colon wall (mucosa, submucosa, muscular layer and serosa)
  - ✓ Number of regional lymph nodes involved(N)
  - ✓ Distant metastasis (M)
- The T, N, and M combined to form stage groupings from I to IV.
- Stage groupings permit the stratification of prognosis, which is useful for the selection of treatment.

There are two types of TNM staging:
1. Clinical/Preoperative:
  - ✓ Based on preoperative imaging and other assessments
  - ✓ Indicated by the prefix 'c'

2. Surgical/Postoperative/pathologic staging:
  - ✓ After surgical removal of primary tumor and lymph nodes; and combines this with the preop imaging and other assessments
  - ✓ Indicated by the prefix 'p'

- Preoperative staging is based on findings from:
  - ✓ Physical examination
  - ✓ CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
  - ✓ Chest X-ray
  - ✓ Colonoscopy
  - ✓ Transrectal endoscopic ultrasound
  - ✓ MRI
  - ✓ Biopsy
  - ✓ PET/CT if available and indicated

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Colorectal Cancer > Staging Summary; Non-Pharmacological Management (aspirin)
text:
# **Staging Summary of Colorectal Cancer**

- For staging, please refer to the latest version of the TNM/AJCC staging system. The current Stage groups include from stage 0(carcinoma in situ) to stage IV-C. (stage four-C)

## **Non-Pharmacological Management of Colorectal Cancer**

Aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been shown to reduce the risk of colonic adenomas by 20-40% in those individuals with average risk. A clinical trial showed that high dose aspirin 600mg/day was beneficial to patients with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer<sup>3</sup>.

text:
# **Treatment Targets**

Treatment for breast cancer is stage dependent and relies on a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.

The aims are:
- Control the primary disease with an optimum 5-year survival rate
- Control the symptoms and pain and improve the patients daily living (Palliative care)

## **Management of Colorectal Cancer**

Treatment is based on the location of the cancer within the bowel (e.g. rectum vs rest of colon), stage, intention of treatment, individual performance status, comorbidities, and patient desire.

Early detection leads to less intensive treatment and better outcomes.

The surgeon, the oncologist and others come up with a plan of treatment in view of the above. Treatments modalities include:
- Surgery
- Radiotherapy (radiation)
- Chemotherapy
- Targeted therapy
- Immunotherapy

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Colorectal Cancer > Management: rectal and anal cancers
text:
## **NOTE:**

- Surgery might be the only treatment needed in early stages.
- In rectal tumors, the exact location of the cancer is quite critical in determining the treatment. There is a stark contrast in the management of lower rectal tumors and the rest of the colon, as these need radiotherapy as an integral component of the treatment in the former and patients are likely to need permanent colostomy.
  ✓ Anal Cancers:
  ✓ *The treatment of anal (the last part of the colon) cancers is much more different, as the standard treatment for most patients is concurrent chemoradiotherapy except for very early diseases that can be resected without harming the anal sphincter.*

- ✓ The most common histology of anal cancer is squamous cell carcinoma
- ✓ The common chemotherapy regimens used with radiotherapy in anal cancer are 5-FU/capecitabine + Mitomycin-C/Cisplatin/Carboplatin
- ✓ Some patients may need temporary or permanent colostomy<sup>4</sup>

- Most colon cancer cases need a combination of cytotoxic chemotherapy in adjuvant (or sometimes Neoadjuvant) setting depending among others on the stage. The cancer drugs most used for these cancers are:
  - ✓ 5-Fluorouracil(5-FU) [ with leucovorin/Folinic acid as a potentiator)
  - ✓ Capecitabine('Xeloda')
  - ✓ Oxaliplatin
  - ✓ Irinotecan
  - ✓ Bevacizumab
  - ✓ Others: Cetuximab, Panitumumab

- Some of the widely used combination regimens include
  - ✓ FOLFOX (5-FU +FOLINIC ACID+OXALIPLATIN) +/- Bevacizumab
  - ✓ FLOX
  - ✓ FOLFIRI (5-FU + IRINOTECAN + LEUCOVORIN)
  - ✓ FOLFOXIRI (FOLFOX +IRINOTECAN) +/- BEVACIZUMAB
  - ✓ XELIRI (XELODA + IRINOTECAN)
  - ✓ IROX (IRINOTECAN + OXALIPLATIN)
  - ✓ 5-FU + LEUCOVORIN etc.<sup>5</sup>

- Single agents could also be used, especially in metastatic setup
- The most common histology of colorectal cancer is adenocarcinoma
- As in all cancer types, monitor for side effects and adjust doses as indicated based on organ-function tests, FBC and other parameters

## <u>Survivorship and Follow-up</u>

- Recurrence is most common in the first 2 to 3 years after surgery.
- If treated by surgery alone, the surgeon is to follow-up with colorectal cancer patients for five years. A CEA test should be done at every follow-up visit, and a colonoscopy at one-year post-surgery and every 3-5 years thereafter.

- If the patient received adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy, they must be jointly followed-up by the surgeon and oncologist.
- Patients under the age of 50 must be followed up for the duration of their lifetime, and family counseling and screening are required, regardless of treatment.

text:
### Definition(s) and Classification of Oral & Maxillofacial Cancers

**Oral Cavity Cancer Anatomic Classifications**
This includes cancers of the lips, the tongue, floor of mouth, buccal mucosa, retromolar trigone, hard-palate, and gums.

**Etiopathology Established Risk Factors**
Use of tobacco in **ANY form** smoking, chewing, snuff, snus, vaping, hubbly High alcohol consumption (synergistic with tobacco)
Viral infections, e.g. certain types of Human Papilloma Virus (HPVs) 16,18particularly for oropharyngeal cancers
Prior history of the oral cavity or other aerodigestive tract cancer
Excessive exposure to sunlight or radiation (for lip cancer)
Age, in conjunction with other risks listed

**Other Possible Risk Factors**
Diet lacking in fresh fruits and vegetables
Immune deficiency disease or immune suppression
Chronic wounds in the mouth (especially in those with major risk factors)

### Clinical Features

The clinical presentation of oral cancer is highly variable, and the presentation of oral cavity cancer is most often related to the primary tumour, with symptoms and signs from cervical lymphadenopathy or distant metastases much less common. Any oral cavity lesion (including a patch or an ulcer), which fails to resolve in 2–3 weeks, should raise the suspicion of the treating clinician.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Oral & Maxillofacial Cancers > Visual Screening Examination
text:
## Visual Screening Examination

**Head and Neck:** Head and neck examination for cervical lymph glands is carried out by standing behind the individual and slightly flexing and bending the neck to the side so that the sternocleidomastoid muscle becomes relaxed and palpation and identification of any enlarged nodes will be easier. The presence of neck masses is not an uncommon finding, especially in subjects with oral infections or cancer.

**Lips:** Oral examination commences with the visual examination of the lips and the vermilion border and by palpation after removing any lipstick. The lip is usually smooth and pliable. Evert the lips and carefully inspect the labial mucosa. It should be smooth, soft and well-lubricated by minor salivary glands that can be palpated.

**Buccal Mucosa:** The buccal mucosa is examined by stretching it with a pair of tongue depressors or mouth mirrors after the subject partially opens the mouth.

**Tongue-Dorsal Surface:** The dorsal surface of the tongue is examined by asking the subject to protrude the tongue and attempt to touch the tip of the chin; alternatively, the tip of the tongue may be held gently by the fingers and a gauze sponge.

**Ventral Surface of Tongue and Floor of Mouth:** The ventral surface of the tongue and the floor of the mouth are most easily visualized by having the person touch the tip of the tongue to the roof of the mouth. A high level of clinical alertness is required when examining these sites, where oral cancers may be missed as red or white innocuous-looking lesions.

**Gingivae:** The gingivae are examined with the mouth partially opened and the lips retracted with a mouth mirror, fingers or plastic lip retractor.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Oral & Maxillofacial Cancers > Diagnostic Algorithm
text:
### Oral lesion diagnostic algorithm: clinical diagnosis, follow-up vs biopsy, adjuvant diagnostic techniques and urgent referral

Photographs show the steps of the oral examination.

1. Oral lesion → previous clinical diagnosis based on clinical data.
2. Lesion resolves with or without therapy → follow-up.
3. Lesion changes, persists or progresses → perform a biopsy → identification of the histological entity, with or without malignancy → follow-up (or repeat biopsy).

Adjuvant diagnostic techniques: 1. oral cytology; 2. salivary biomarkers; 3. light-based techniques (auto-fluorescence, spectroscopy, chemiluminescence); 4. tissue staining.

Diagnostic workup: if there is any suspicion that a lesion may be oral cavity cancer, document the lesion site and size, take a clinical photograph if possible, and make an urgent referral to an oral & maxillofacial surgeon who is part of a head and neck oncology MDT. Any oral lesion (including a patch or ulcer) that fails to resolve in 2-3 weeks should raise suspicion.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Prostate Cancer > Definition, Classification and Screening
text:
### **Definition(s) and Classification of Prostate Cancer**

(i) Screen-detected asymptomatic, microscopic, well-differentiated tumor, that may never become clinically significant OR
(ii) Screen-detected clinically symptomatic, aggressive, high-grade cancer that causes metastases, morbidity, and death

## Screening and Diagnosis of Prostate Cancer

#### **Screening**

Prostate screening should be done every two years for all men above age 50 with any of the following risk factors:
* Discussion should take place at age 45 for men at high risk (African American, 1st degree relative with prostate cancer at early age)
* Discussion should take place at age 40 (age at which AUA recommends routine screening) for men at very high risk (several 1st degree relatives with prostate cancer at early age)

**Digital Rectal Examination (DRE):** should be done by a trained healthcare worker. The healthcare worker should feel the surface of the prostate for any irregularities, in conjunction with annual PSA readings and rectal or pelvic ultrasound.

Those with above average risk start screening at an earlier age at the discretion of the clinician.

#### **PSA Levels:**

Risk stratification based on PSA screening for those under 4ng/ml (EAU 2022 guideline)

text:
### PSA-based prostate cancer screening: risk stratification for PSA under 4 ng/ml by age (EAU 2022), and recommendations for PSA 4-10 and >10 ng/ml in men 50-75

Prostate screening every two years for men above 50 with risk factors. Discuss screening at age 45 for men at high risk (African American, first-degree relative with prostate cancer at an early age) and at age 40 for very high risk (several first-degree relatives with early prostate cancer). DRE by a trained health worker, with annual PSA and rectal or pelvic ultrasound. Those with above-average risk start earlier at the clinician's discretion.

**PSA under 4 ng/ml: risk stratification (EAU 2022)**

| Category / PSA level | Definition | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low Risk | PSA <1 in those <40 years; PSA <2 in those 41-60 years | Repeat screening after 5 - 8 years |
| High Risk | PSA >1 in those <40 years; PSA >2 in those 41-60 years | Repeat screening after 2 years |

**PSA above 4 ng/ml in men 50-75 years**

| Category / PSA level | Definition | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4-10 ng/ml |  | 1. If DRE is normal, repeat after 4-6 weeks; if it increases, refer for urologist review. 2. If DRE abnormal, refer to urologist. 3. If available, determine the free to total PSA ratio and PSA density, and consult |
| > 10 ng/ml |  | Refer to urologist |

### Prostate cancer diagnosis and staging investigations: biopsy, pathology, PSA tests, radiology, other

Signs and symptoms: may be asymptomatic; LUTS (urgency/frequency, dysuria, nocturia, poor stream, straining); haematuria, poor erectile function, bone pain, bladder outlet obstruction, urinary retention, chronic renal failure, rectal bleeding.

| Diagnostic Category | Investigation |
| --- | --- |
| Biopsy | Biopsy (trans-rectal ultrasound-guided biopsy is the current standard) |
| Pathology | A full histology report |
| Laboratory Tests | Prostate specific antigen (PSA) test and its isoforms: PSA doubling time; PSA density; PSA velocity; PSA ratio, free to bound |
| Radiology | Ultrasound pelvis and abdomen; chest X-ray; if PSA >20, bone scan, or MRI DWI (high risk) if bone scan unavailable; CT scan; MRI pelvis (prostate-specific sequences) |
| Other | Endoscopy and other specialized tests as indicated and available |

text:
#### **Prostate Cancer Staging (TNM)**

* *Refer to the* latest TNM staging and the national cancer guideline.
* It is important to note that the latest TNM/AJCC staging of prostate cancer takes PSA level and the Gleason score into account, in addition to the TNM parameters.
* The latest stage group spans from Stage 1 to Stage IV-B

#### **Treatment Targets**

Treatment for Prostate Cancer is stage dependent and relies on a combination of chemotherapy, and radiation.

The aims are:
* ✓ Control the primary disease with an optimum 5-year survival rate
* ✓ Control the symptoms and pain and improve the patients daily living (Palliative care)

text:
# **Management of Prostate Cancer**

Management of prostate cancer considers several factors, including
- ✓ Stage
- ✓ Risk category
- ✓ Age, comorbidities, and life expectancy
- ✓ Performance status
- ✓ Resources
- ✓ Hormone sensitivity status in metastatic disease
- ✓ Patients' wishes

Depending on the above factors there are options in the management of prostate cancer. Some prostate cancer patients may not need active treatment against cancer, while others need combinations of multiple modalities of treatment)
- ✓ Watchful waiting
- ✓ Active surveillance
- ✓ Surgery (including radical prostatectomy, tunneling TURP etc.)
- ✓ Radiotherapy (external beam, brachytherapy)
- ✓ Hormonal therapy (including medical or surgical castration (bilateral orchiectomy))
- ✓ Chemotherapy
- ✓ Miscellaneous
- ✓ Supportive care (including pain management, bisphosphonates like Zoledronate)

text:
## General Principles of Management by Category

Once the decision has been made to treat a patient with prostate cancer, some of the principles include:
1. For Localized disease: Radical prostatectomy, Radiotherapy (RT) with or without hormones or other medical therapy

2. Metastatic prostate
   a. Hormone Sensitive:
      - ✓ Bilateral orchiectomy is by far the cheaper option than the expensive medical therapy
      - ✓ Hormonal therapy is often given as an ADT (Androgen Deprivation Therapy) or CAB (Combined Androgen Blockade)
   b. Castration Resistant:
      These would need second line hormonal agents (e.g. Enzalutamide, Abiraterone) and /or cytotoxic chemotherapy (e.g. Docetaxel)

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Prostate Cancer > Summary Guideline for Management by Risk Category
text:
### Prostate cancer management by risk category (very low, low, high risk): observation, active surveillance, radiotherapy, radical prostatectomy, hormone therapy

Management depends on stage, risk category, age, comorbidities and life expectancy, performance status, resources, hormone sensitivity in metastatic disease, and the patient's wishes. Options: watchful waiting; active surveillance; surgery (radical prostatectomy, TURP etc.); radiotherapy (external beam, brachytherapy); hormonal therapy (medical or surgical castration, bilateral orchiectomy); chemotherapy; supportive care (pain management, bisphosphonates such as zoledronate). Localised disease: radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy with or without hormones. Metastatic hormone-sensitive: bilateral orchiectomy (cheaper than medical therapy) or hormonal therapy as ADT or combined androgen blockade (CAB). Castration-resistant: second-line hormonal agents (enzalutamide, abiraterone) and/or chemotherapy (docetaxel).

| Risk category | Recommended Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Very Low Risk | Life expectancy <10 yrs: observation. Life expectancy 10-20 yrs: active surveillance. Life expectancy >20 yrs: active surveillance, radiotherapy (EBRT or brachytherapy), or radical prostatectomy (RP) +/- pelvic lymph node dissection (LND) if >2% risk of LN involvement (Roach or Partin tables) |
| Low Risk | Life expectancy <10 yrs: observation. Life expectancy >10 yrs: RT alone, RP +/- pelvic LND, or active surveillance. If RP with positive margins → adjuvant RT (preferred) or expectant management |
| High Risk | Radiotherapy (3DCRT/IMRT with IGRT +/- brachytherapy boost) + long-term hormone therapy (2-3 yrs; neoadjuvant, concurrent and adjuvant). 4-6 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) considered for select patients with a single adverse feature with Gleason score 6-7. Consider whole pelvis radiotherapy. Consider RP with pelvic LND only for selected patients with low-volume disease and no fixation. Adjuvant RT +/- short-term ADT for positive margins or pT3 disease |

ADT: androgen deprivation therapy; CAB: combined androgen blockade; EBRT: external beam radiation therapy; IGRT: image-guided radiation therapy; IMRT: intensity-modulated radiation therapy; LN: lymph node; LND: lymph node dissection; RP: radical prostatectomy; RT: radiotherapy; 3DCRT: three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy.

# **Supportive Care**

- Hot flushes
  ✓ Depot Provera 1 Amp 3 monthly if significant
- Obstructive bladder symptoms
  ✓ Oral selective α1 blockers e.g. Alfuzosin 10mg daily, Tamsulosin 0.4mg daily
- Irritative bladder
  ✓ Oxybutynin 5mg tds PO
- Bone mineral density preservation
  ✓ After Bilateral Orchidectomy or on Zoladex
  ✓ Calcium 2 tabs TDS PO
  ✓ Vit D 50 000 Units every 2 weeks PO
    - Caution: Discontinue if high number of lytic bone metastases i.e. risk of hypercalcemia
- Incontinence
- Erectile dysfunction
- Psychosexual support

text:
## <u>Complications of Prostate Cancer</u>

**Common Complications<sup>7</sup>:**
(a) Functional
  ✓ Urinary incontinence
  ✓ Urethral strictures
  ✓ LUTS
  ✓ Erectile dysfunction
(b) Surgical: Sserious complications include myocardial infarction and thromboembolic, infectious, and neurologic events

## **Follow Up and Survivorship**

Follow-up post-surgery is done using PSA testing, symptomatology, and clinical examination for non- metastatic cancers. The frequency of follow-ups should be every six months for the first two years and annually for up to five years following surgery.

Metastatic patients are to be followed by oncologists and surgeon on an individualized basis.

## <u>Management in Special Populations</u>

Older males: In the management of Prostate Cancer in older male patients, there are certain factors that are more important that chronological age. Management decisions is therefore guided with these in mind. As such, clinicians must carefully consider:
(i) Comorbidity,
(ii) Dependency,
(iii) Functionality and activities of daily living,
(iv) Nutritional status

## Classification of Cataract<sup>2</sup>

Cataract can be classified according to Aetiology:
- ✓ **Acquired Cataract** i.e., Age-related, cataract in systemic disease, secondary cataract, traumatic cataract,
- ✓ **Drug-induced** corticosteroids, phenothiazines, tamoxifen
- ✓ **Traumatic:** penetrating, concussion and electric shock
- ✓ **Endocrine /Metabolic cataract:** diabetic, galactosemia, hypocalcaemia, Downs Syndrome, Neurofibromatosis
- ✓ **Congenital Cataract**
- ✓ **Secondary Cataract:** uveitis, ionizing radiation, tumour, acute angle-closure glaucoma

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Cataract > Screening and Diagnosis of Cataract
text:
### Cataract screening, diagnosis and management workflow: assessment, ruling out other causes, impact on daily life, referral, early vs significant cataract, surgery; referral rules

1. Patient presents with visual complaints: gradual, painless vision loss; glare, haloes, blurred vision.
2. Clinical assessment: visual acuity; lens exam (cloudiness); red reflex.
3. Rule out other causes of vision loss: retinal disease; glaucoma; refractive errors.
4. Confirm the cataract diagnosis.
5. Assess the impact on daily life: daily activities; bilateral/unilateral; uncorrectable with glasses.
6. Refer to an ophthalmologist: full evaluation; biometry.
   - Mild/early cataract: monitor; improve lighting; adjust glasses.
   - Affects daily life (significant cataract): surgery (phacoemulsification + IOL); post-operative care: eye drops, follow-up, patient education.

REFER ALL SEVERE/SIGNIFICANT CATARACT CASES TO AN EYE SURGEON FOR CATARACT SURGERY. Refer clients with comorbidities such as HTN/DM, and pregnant women with cataract, to an ophthalmologist once a year from diagnosis for routine screening. Refer children immediately: a white pupil in a child may be an eye tumour, and late referral may lead to permanent loss of vision, squint, loss of the eye or loss of life.

text:
# **Non-Pharmacological Management of Cataract**

Risk of cataract can be lowered by:
1. Protect your eyes from Ultra-Violet (UV) radiation
2. Quit smoking
3. Eat lots of fruits and vegetables that are rich in antioxidants, Vitamins C and E
4. Manage chronic conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure
5. Limit alcohol consumption
6. Avoid long term use steroids (both oral and eye drops)
7. Get regular eye check up

text:
### Diabetic retinopathy classification by severity (no DR, mild/moderate/severe NPDR, PDR, DME): defining features, management and follow-up interval

| DR Severity | Defining Features | Management | Follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No DR | No microvascular abnormalities | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 1-2 yrs |
| Mild NPDR | Microaneurysms only | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 6-12 mo |
| Moderate NPDR | Microaneurysms and other signs (dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots), but not severe NPDR | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 3-6 mo |
| Severe NPDR | Intraretinal haemorrhages (>20 in each of 4 quadrants), definite venous beading (in at least 2 quadrants), or apparent IRMA (in at least 1 quadrant), but not PDR | Consider PRP | <3 mo |
| PDR | Neovascularization of the optic disc or elsewhere, preretinal haemorrhage, or vitreous haemorrhage | Strongly consider PRP; consider vitrectomy for persistent vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment | <1 mo (variable) |
| DME | Retinal thickening in the macula | Consider focal laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF therapy, or corticosteroid therapy for centre-involving DME | 1-3 mo |

No DR: no apparent retinopathy; NPDR: non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy; PDR: proliferative diabetic retinopathy; DME: diabetic macular oedema. Fundus photographs show normal fundus, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR and PDR (courtesy of Medscape Education).

text:
### Diabetic retinopathy screening schedule: timing of first and subsequent retinal examination by risk factor (type 1, type 2, complications, poor control, other)

| Risk Factors | 1st retinal examination | Subsequent examination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 DM | Within 5 years of diagnosis and after onset of puberty | Annually |
| Type 2 DM | At time of diagnosis | Annually |
| Evidence of other diabetic complications, e.g. CVD, renal disease (nephropathy), foot ulcers (neuropathy) | Immediately | As recommended by eye care provider |
| Poor glycaemic control | Immediately | As recommended by eye care provider |
| Other risk factors: hyperlipidemia, smoking, cataract surgery, obesity, anaemia, leukaemias etc. | At time of diagnosis / immediately | As recommended by eye care provider |

**Note:** Screening by health care workers (medical officers and nursing staff): visual acuity with a Snellen or illiterate E chart; penlight torch to examine the external eye, pupillary reaction etc. Symptoms are absent early; later fluctuating or blurred vision, spots or floaters, dark or empty areas in vision, total loss of vision.

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Diabetic Retinopathy > Screening flowchart for diabetic retinopathy
text:
### Diabetic retinopathy screening flowchart: visual acuity and fundus findings → routine re-examination, non-urgent referral, or urgent referral

1. Diabetes history, medical history, current medication, biochemical parameters.
2. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) with current spectacles, and ophthalmoscopy or fundus photography.
   - VA better than 6/12 (20/40) and no DR → routine re-examination.
   - VA 6/12 (20/40) or worse, or mild or moderate NPDR → non-urgent referral for refraction and assessment.
   - Severe NPDR, DME, or PDR → urgent referral.
*Need to optimise medical treatment: glycaemic control, hypertension, and lipids.
DME = diabetic macular oedema; NPDR = non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy; PDR = proliferative diabetic retinopathy; VA = visual acuity.

## **Non-Pharmacological Management of Diabetic Retinopathy**

Risk of diabetic retinopathy can be lowered by keeping blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol levels under control. This can be done by adopting healthy lifestyle changes, which include:
- Eating a healthy, balanced diet – cut down on salt, sugar, and fat intake
- Maintain an appropriate weight (according to BMI or waist circumference)
- Exercise regularly
- Quit smoking
- Limit alcohol consumption
- Regular eye check ups

## Clinical Guidelines Diagnosis and Management of Glaucoma

### Defination of Glaucoma

Glaucoma represents a group of diseases defined by a characteristic optic neuropathy that is consistent with excavation and undermining of the neural and connective tissue elements of the optic disc and by the eventual development of distinctive patterns of visual dysfunction. Although elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is one of the primary risk factors, its presence or absence does not have a role in the definition of the disease.

text:
## **Classification of Glaucoma<sup>2</sup>**

**Glaucoma** is traditionally classified as open angle or closed angle glaucoma and as primary or secondary glaucoma. Glaucoma can also be congenital / developmental. It is usually bilateral, but maybe unilateral or asymmetrical.
Screening and Diagnosis of Glaucoma

## **Who must be screened (Risk Factors)**

* Adults ≥40 years
* Family history of glaucoma
* High IOP
* Persons with history of diabetes, hypertension, migraines, sickle cell anaemia
* Persons with history of eye injuries or certain types of eye surgery
* Prolonged use of corticosteroid medicines especially eyedrops

## **Screening for Glaucoma**

1. All healthcare workers should take visual acuity using Snellen’s Chart
2. Use pen-light torch to examine the external the eye

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Glaucoma > Screening and Diagnosis of Glaucoma
text:
### Acute (angle-closure) vs chronic (open-angle) glaucoma: onset, pain, redness, vision, pupil, cornea, IOP, optic nerve, age, family history, urgency; who to screen

Who must be screened (risk factors): adults ≥40 years; family history of glaucoma; high IOP; diabetes, hypertension, migraines, sickle cell anaemia; eye injuries or certain eye surgery; prolonged corticosteroid use, especially eye drops. Screening: all health workers take visual acuity with a Snellen chart and examine the external eye with a penlight torch.

| Feature | Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure) | Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Sudden | Gradual |
| Pain | Severe eye pain | Usually painless |
| Redness | Present, typically unilateral | Usually absent |
| Vision Changes | Sudden vision loss; haloes around lights | Gradual peripheral vision loss (tunnel vision) |
| Headache | Unilateral, temporal | Rare |
| Nausea/Vomiting | Common | Rare |
| Pupil | Mid-dilated, fixed, non-reactive | Usually normal |
| Cornea | Cloudy or hazy | Clear |
| Anterior Chamber | Shallow | Normal depth |
| Intraocular Pressure (IOP) | Markedly elevated; eye feels hard on palpation | Elevated; eye may feel tense on palpation |
| Optic Nerve | May appear swollen in acute phase | Shows cupping/damage on fundoscopy |
| Age Group | Usually >40 years | Usually >40 years, earlier in Black individuals |
| Family History | Not prominent | First-degree relatives at higher risk |
| Urgency | Ophthalmological emergency – urgent referral | Chronic, but requires monitoring and long-term management |

Primary open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms in early stages, so routine intraocular pressure checks and fundus examination should be done in everyone aged 40 and above by qualified eye care personnel.
All suspected cases of glaucoma should be referred to qualified eye care personnel for confirmation of diagnosis and a treatment plan.

Redness: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Present, typically unilateral; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Usually absent.
Vision Changes: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Sudden vision loss; haloes around lights; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Gradual peripheral vision loss (tunnel vision).
Headache: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Unilateral, temporal; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Rare.
Nausea/Vomiting: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Common; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Rare.
Pupil: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Mid-dilated, fixed, non-reactive; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Usually normal.
Cornea: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Cloudy or hazy; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Clear.
Anterior Chamber: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Shallow; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Normal depth.
Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Markedly elevated; eye feels hard on palpation; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Elevated; eye may feel tense on palpation.
Optic Nerve: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): May appear swollen in acute phase; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Shows cupping/damage on fundoscopy.
Age Group: Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure): Usually >40 years; Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle): Usually >40 years, earlier in Black individuals.

text:
### Acute (angle-closure) vs chronic (open-angle) glaucoma: onset, pain, redness, vision, pupil, cornea, IOP, optic nerve, age, family history, urgency; who to screen

Who must be screened (risk factors): adults ≥40 years; family history of glaucoma; high IOP; diabetes, hypertension, migraines, sickle cell anaemia; eye injuries or certain eye surgery; prolonged corticosteroid use, especially eye drops. Screening: all health workers take visual acuity with a Snellen chart and examine the external eye with a penlight torch.

| Feature | Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure) | Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Sudden | Gradual |
| Pain | Severe eye pain | Usually painless |
| Redness | Present, typically unilateral | Usually absent |
| Vision Changes | Sudden vision loss; haloes around lights | Gradual peripheral vision loss (tunnel vision) |
| Headache | Unilateral, temporal | Rare |
| Nausea/Vomiting | Common | Rare |
| Pupil | Mid-dilated, fixed, non-reactive | Usually normal |
| Cornea | Cloudy or hazy | Clear |
| Anterior Chamber | Shallow | Normal depth |
| Intraocular Pressure (IOP) | Markedly elevated; eye feels hard on palpation | Elevated; eye may feel tense on palpation |
| Optic Nerve | May appear swollen in acute phase | Shows cupping/damage on fundoscopy |
| Age Group | Usually >40 years | Usually >40 years, earlier in Black individuals |
| Family History | Not prominent | First-degree relatives at higher risk |
| Urgency | Ophthalmological emergency – urgent referral | Chronic, but requires monitoring and long-term management |

Primary open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms in early stages, so routine intraocular pressure checks and fundus examination should be done in everyone aged 40 and above by qualified eye care personnel.
All suspected cases of glaucoma should be referred to qualified eye care personnel for confirmation of diagnosis and a treatment plan.

text:
### **Patient Assessment:**

To make a diagnosis of glaucoma, one needs to
* Take detailed history on medications used, systemic disease, ocular trauma, ocular disease and ocular surgery
* Take patients visual acuity using relevant chart e.g., Snellen’s or E-Chart
* Do anterior segment eye examination using penlight torch (for Level 1 and Level 2)
* Pupillary examination, refraction and dilated slit lamp examination to view optic nerve properly (level 2 with ophthalmic nurse or optometrist, level 3/ Tertiary hospital)
* OCT at level 3 facility

text:
### **Non-Pharmacological Management of Hypertension**

* If there is any suspicion of glaucoma, the patient must be referred for accurate testing.
* Patients over the age of 35 years should be encouraged to have their eye pressure tested routinely if possible (e.g., when going to opticians to buy glasses).
* Patients who have been put onto maintenance therapy with specific medicines that decrease intraocular pressure (such as acetazolamide) must be encouraged to take their treatment regularly

text:
### Glaucoma medicines: acute glaucoma (acetazolamide, glycerol, timolol) and chronic glaucoma stepwise (timolol/betaxolol, latanoprost/bimatoprost, brimonidine, pilocarpine, acetazolamide): dose, frequency, duration

**Acute glaucoma (refer to ophthalmologist immediately)**

| Step | Medicine | Dose | Frequency | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First | Acetazolamide PO | 250-500 mg | Once |  |
| Or | Glycerin as glycerol | 1 ml/kg | Once |  |
| Plus | Timolol 0.25-0.5% | Instil 1 drop | Twice daily | 2 weeks |

**Chronic glaucoma**

| Step | Medicine | Dose | Frequency | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First line | Timolol 0.25 or 0.5% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily | Long term |
| Or | Betaxolol 0.25 or 0.5% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily | Long term |
| If adherent with no good response, add (or first line if beta-blockers contraindicated) | Latanoprost 0.005% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily (as printed) | Long term |
| Or | Prostamide bimatoprost 0.03% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily (as printed) | Long term |
| If intolerant of or not responding to prostaglandin analogue | Brimonidine 0.15-0.2% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily | Long term |
| Failure to respond (consult a specialist first) | Pilocarpine hydrochloride 2% or 4% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Four times daily | Review |
| Severe cases or while waiting for surgery | Acetazolamide PO | 250 mg | Four times daily | Review |

**Note:** Acute glaucoma: also treat pain and nausea/vomiting. Acetazolamide contains sulphur: do not use in patients allergic to sulphur. Glycerol is a concentrated sugar solution: do not give to diabetic patients. Prostaglandin analogues may be first line when beta-blockers are contraindicated, or second line on beta-blockers if the target IOP reduction is not reached. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in overt asthma (may cause an acute asthma attack soon after instillation). Pilocarpine causes long-standing pupil constriction; use only when the patient is prepared for glaucoma surgery, or as an alternative when timolol is contraindicated.

## **Complications of Glaucoma**

## **CHAPTER 11**

## PALLIATION

### **Palliation**

Palliative Care for both children and adults is an approach that improves the Quality of Life of patients and their families facing the problems associated with a life-threatening illness, through the prevention and relief of suffering by means of early identification and impeccable assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, including physical, psychosocial and spiritual wellness.

Palliative care is required throughout the course of illness regardless of access to disease modifying treatment.

* Causes patients to spend more time at home and reduces the number of hospital inpatient days
* Improves symptom management
* Provides patient, family and care takers satisfaction
* Reduces overall cost of disease
* Prolongs survival
* Improves quality of life of patients and family

text:
### Types of pain (nociceptive somatic, visceral, inflammatory; neurogenic; functional): characteristics, mechanisms and example drug treatments

Pain is 'an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage' (IASP).

| Type of Pain | Subtype | Characteristics | Mechanisms | Examples of pharmacologic treatments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nociceptive | Somatic (tissue injury) | Superficial (skin) or deep pain (muscle, fascia, tendon) | Mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli | Acetaminophen, Na+ blockers, NSAIDs, steroids, opioids |
| Nociceptive | Visceral (irritable bowel, cystitis) | Constant or cramping. Poor localization. Autonomic responses | Visceral distension | NSAIDs, antispasmodics, opioids |
| Nociceptive | Inflammatory (musculoskeletal) | Localized or diffuse pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia | Associated with localized inflammation | NSAIDs, steroids |
| Neurogenic | Neuralgia, radiculopathy, causalgia, CNS lesions | Spontaneous, paroxysmal pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia | Peripheral or CNS lesions | Anticonvulsants, opioids, antidepressants |
| Neurogenic | Functional (FM, thalamic syndromes, irritable bowel syndrome) | Diffuse deep pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia | Dysregulation of excitatory or inhibitory mechanisms in CNS | Antidepressants, anticonvulsants, opioids, cannabinoids |

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Pain Assessment
text:
## **Pain Assessment**

Pain should be considered as the “fifth vital sign.” As with the other vital signs: pulse, blood pressure, respiration and temperature, pain needs to be assessed regularly. All patients should be evaluated for the presence of pain at every visit, and any new pain should be thoroughly evaluated. Initial assessment should always start with the patient history, examination and occasionally, diagnostic examinations.

Questions to be included in the pain assessment are as follows:
* Where is the pain? (There may be more than one pain)
* How severe is the pain?
* What does it feel like? (e.g. aching, stabbing, cramping, burning, etc.)
* When did it start?
* Timing - Is the pain there all the time or does it come and go?
* Treatment - Has any treatment been tried and has it helped?
* Changing - What makes it better or worse (e.g. movement, eating, time of day, etc.)?
* Causing - What do you (the patient) think is causing the pain?

* Changing - What makes it better or worse (e.g. movement, eating, time of day, etc.)?
* Causing - What do you (the patient) think is causing the pain?

## Pain Scoring Tools

### **Numerical Rating Scale (NRS)**

This is the most used pain assessment tool. This enables the clinician to assess how severe the pain is and whether it is improving over time or getting worse.

image: Wong-Baker Faces Pain Rating Scale color gradient

## **Wong-Baker Faces Pain Rating Scale**

If the patient has difficulty in understanding the NRS e.g. children or the very old, the Wong-Baker Faces Pain Rating Scale may be used. Ask the patients to score their pain with these facial expressions: “On a scale of zero to five, where zero is no hurt and five is the hurts worst.”

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Pain Scoring Tools > Wong-Baker, Five Fingers, FLACC
text:
## **Five Fingers Scale**

This can be particularly useful for patients who are being monitored for pain over several days as they learn how to measure their pain. Ask the patients to show how much pain they have by holding up different numbers of fingers. “On a scale of zero to five, where zero is no hurt and five is the hurts worst.”

## **Revised FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability)**

This tool is used to assess pain in non-verbal children and neurological impaired patients. This assessment is done by their behaviors. Behaviors associated with pain in this population include:
* Vocalizations (crying, moaning)
* Facial expression (grimacing)
* Consolability
* Interactivity(withdrawn)
* Diminished sleep
* Movement (restless, increased movement of extremities)

* Tone and posture (arching, stiffening)
* Physiological responses (diaphoresis, pallor, tachycardia)

Core pain behaviors are consistently identified in this population, yet each child will display a unique set of behaviors. It is important to be vigilant about the possibility of pain in children with neurological impairments.

## **Management of Pain**

The Management of Pain in adults is referred from WHO Analgesic Ladder

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Management of Pain > WHO Analgesic Ladder
text:
### WHO analgesic ladder for adult pain: step 1 non-opioid (mild), step 2 weak opioid (moderate), step 3 strong opioid (severe), with drug categories

Pain scores on the numerical rating scale: none 0; mild 1-3; moderate 4-6; severe 7-10.
- Step 1, mild pain (0-3): non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
- Step 2, moderate pain (4-6): weak opioid +/- non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
- Step 3, severe pain: strong opioid +/- non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
Step up if pain persists or increases; step down if pain decreases.

Categories of drugs:
- Non-opioids: ibuprofen or other NSAID, paracetamol (acetaminophen), or aspirin.
- Weak opioids: codeine, tramadol, or low-dose morphine.
- Strong opioids: morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, buprenorphine.
- Adjuvants: antidepressant, anticonvulsant, antispasmodic, muscle relaxant, bisphosphonate, or corticosteroid.
Combining an opioid and a non-opioid is effective, but do not combine drugs of the same class. Time doses by drug half-life ('dose by the clock'); do not wait for pain to recur.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Analgesics: doses and cautions
text:
### Analgesics for palliative pain management: non-opioids (paracetamol, ibuprofen, diclofenac), weak opioids (tramadol, codeine), strong opioid (morphine): doses, cautions and contraindications

| Category | Drug and Dosage | Caution and Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-Opioid | Paracetamol: 500 mg-1 g 6-8 hourly | Hepatotoxicity. Maximum dose 4 g per day |
| Non-Opioid | Ibuprofen: 400 mg 6-8 hourly | Give with food. Maximum dose 1.2 g. Avoid in asthma and peptic ulcer. Lower dose if liver impairment |
| Non-Opioid | Diclofenac: 50 mg 8-12 hourly | Give with food; avoid in asthma and peptic ulcer. Maximum dose 150 mg |
| Weak Opioid | Tramadol: 50-100 mg 4-6 hourly | Caution in epileptic patients. Maximum dosage 240 mg daily (as printed). Give laxatives to avoid constipation unless the patient has diarrhoea |
| Weak Opioid | Codeine: 30-60 mg 4 hourly | Caution in epileptic patients. Maximum dosage 240 mg daily (as printed). Give laxatives to avoid constipation unless the patient has diarrhoea |
| Strong Opioid | Morphine: start with 2.5-20 mg q4h (immediate release); give 8-24 hourly for slow release. 5%-20% of the daily dose is used as the starting dose for breakthrough pain | Low-dose morphine is given if the maximum weak-opioid dose does not work. No ceiling dose for morphine (increase gradually until pain is controlled). Pethidine can be used for acute pain (NOT for chronic pain) |

Less commonly used strong opioids in our settings: fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Palliative Care in the Trajectory of the Patient's Illness
text:
### Palliative care across the illness trajectory, and palliative care tasks by level (referral hospital, regional hospital, health centre/primary clinic, home)

Trajectory (diagram): from presentation/diagnosis, therapies to modify disease (curative, restorative intent) decrease over time while therapies to relieve suffering and/or improve quality of life (palliative care) increase; palliative care continues through life closure and active dying to death, followed by bereavement care.

Palliative care by level:
- Referral hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; holistic care with specialised management (radiotherapy, chemotherapy, surgery).
- Regional hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; initiate or adjust the PC regimen for mild, moderate or severe symptoms; plan continued PC after discharge to a lower level or home; refer to referral hospitals for specialised management.
- Health centre/primary care clinic: visit the patient at home in the first week after discharge if possible; holistic pain assessment; pain and symptom management using the WHO ladder; emotional support; liaise with CHWs who visit patients at home; request oral morphine solution for PC patients in the HC catchment area; request advice from the regional hospital if needed; refer complicated cases to the regional hospital.
- Home: recognise and report inadequately relieved pain or other physical, psychological or social distress, and improper use of morphine or other medicines; provide emotional support; educate the family on daily care (feeding, hygiene, mobility, medications).

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Morphine: dose calculation, paediatric dose, side effects, naloxone
text:
## **How to calculate the dose of morphine PR:**

Add up all the morphine given in the past 24 hours. That gives the total dose required in 24 hours. Then divide by 2 to give the 12 hourly doses. E.g. morphine 10mg given every 4 hours = 6x10mg in 24 hours = 60mg in 24 hours = 30mg every 12 hours. The dose of morphine PR is 30mg twice daily.

Pediatric dose: 0.2 to 0.3 mg /kg (10-15mg) initial dose, 4hrly PO/SL and IV/SC 0.1mg/kg.
Side effects of morphine include are constipation, nausea, and vomiting, sedation, dry mouth, sweating, hallucinations, myoclonus, urinary retention, pruritus, hyperalgesia etc.

**Constipation is the most common side effect. The hand that writes opioids should also write laxatives.**
Morphine reduces gastrointestinal motility and secretion leading to constipation. A stimulant laxative like Bisacodyl, reduces the ring contraction and facilitate propulsive activity.

Sedation and nausea usually resolve after a few days. A patient will need to be reassured and given an antiemetic if they experience nausea.

Physical dependence may develop but drug addiction to morphine in patients with palliative care is very rare. Withdrawal symptoms when morphine is stopped or the dose is reduced are due to physical dependence.

Therefore the morphine dose should only be reduced slowly whilst the patient adjusts to coming off morphine.

**Respiratory depression is a very rare side effect in pain management when morphine is correctly titrated in palliative care. Naloxone is an antidote if respiratory depression develops. Dilute 400 micrograms (1amp) in 9ml normal saline and give 2.5ml (100 micrograms) IV every 1-2 minutes for titrating response**

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Adjuvant Analgesics for Bone and Neuropathic Pain
text:
### Adjuvant analgesics for bone and neuropathic pain: dexamethasone, amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin: indications, doses and key notes

| Class | Indications | Common Drugs & Doses | Key Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Steroids | Pain caused by pressure (e.g. stretched liver capsule, raised ICP, Pancoast tumour) | Dexamethasone: 8–16 mg once daily before noon; if effective, reduce by 2 mg/day after 3 days | Stop after 5 days if no response |
| Antidepressants | Neuropathic pain | Amitriptyline: 10–75 mg at night; start low, increase every 2–3 days until pain controlled or side effects limit use | Sedating – useful at night; caution in elderly |
| Anticonvulsants | Neuropathic pain | Gabapentin: start 300 mg at night → increase by 300 mg every 2–3 days (night → BD → TDS → 600 mg BD); max 2400 mg/day; if no benefit after 900 mg/day, unlikely to be effective | Titrate slowly to minimise dizziness & somnolence. Caution: renal impairment |
| Anticonvulsants | Neuropathic pain | Pregabalin: start 50 mg TDS or 75 mg BD; doses >300 mg/day rarely give extra benefit | Titrate slowly to minimise dizziness & somnolence. Caution: renal impairment |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Classification > Wagner grades
text:
### Diabetic foot ulcer classification (Wagner grades 0-5): description and category

Diabetic foot: infection, ulceration or destruction of tissues of the foot associated with neuropathy and/or peripheral arterial disease in people with diabetes. About 80% of non-traumatic lower limb amputations in diabetes are preceded by a foot ulcer.

| Ulcer Grade | Description | Category |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | No ulcer but high-risk foot (e.g. deformity, callus, or ischaemia) | Non-ulcer stage |
| 1 | Superficial ulcer involving only the skin | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| 2 | Deep ulcer, extending into tendon, bone, or joint capsule, but without bony involvement or abscess | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| 3 | Deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis (confirmed clinically or by X-ray) | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| 4 | Localized gangrene (e.g. toe, heel, forefoot) | Gangrenous ulcer |
| 5 | Extensive gangrene involving the whole foot | Gangrenous ulcer |

text:
### Diabetic foot algorithm A: foot assessment in all patients with diabetes, active foot problems, and risk stratification (high, moderate, low) with actions

All patients with diabetes → foot assessment: skin; neurological; vascular; musculoskeletal.
1. Active foot problem? (any of: ulceration; spreading infection; critical limb ischaemia; gangrene; suspicion of acute Charcot neuroarthropathy or an unexplained hot, red, swollen foot with or without pain)
   - Yes → Algorithm B.
   - No → 2.
2. Previous history of ulceration, amputation, or on renal replacement therapy? Yes → HIGH RISK: early referral to podiatrist/surgical department for further care.
3. Deformity/neuropathy/non-critical limb ischaemia → MODERATE RISK: refer to NCD clinic/podiatrist/surgical department for further review.
4. Callus alone → LOW RISK: total contact insole; foot care education; yearly screening.
5. Normal findings → foot care education; yearly screening.
*Risk categories as in the diabetic foot risk stratification table.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Algorithm B: active foot problems
text:
### Diabetic foot algorithm B: management of active foot problems by ulcer type, infection and ischaemia (outpatient, oral antibiotics, multidisciplinary foot care team)

Active foot problems*:
- Without ulcer (UT grade 0): manage as outpatient by foot protection services.
- With ulcer:
  - Superficial (UT IA): manage as outpatient by foot protection services.
  - Infection:
    - Superficial ulcer not requiring surgical intervention (UT IB): oral antibiotics (outpatient, foot protection services).
    - Deep ulcer requiring surgical intervention (UT IIB/IIIB): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
  - Ischaemia (pulses not palpable) (UT IC/IIC/IIIC): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
  - Infection and ischaemia (UT ID/IID/IIID): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
*Refer urgently for admission if the patient presents with general illness (e.g. sepsis or diabetic [emergency]).

Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Examination (SWME) is easy to perform. The examination uses a 5.07/10-g monofilament which exerts a buckling force when it bends. Inability to sense the touch/pressure indicates Loss of Protective Sensation (LOPS).

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Screening > Tuning Fork Examination
text:
> **How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy**
>
> 1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.
> 2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.
> 3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).
> 4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.
> 5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).
> 6. Repeat on the other leg.
> Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe.
html:
How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy

1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.

2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.

3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).

4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.

5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).

6. Repeat on the other leg.

Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe.

How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy.
1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Diabetic Foot Ulcers: Non-pharmacological and Pharmacological Treatment
text:
## **Non-pharmacological Treatment**

- Metabolic control
- Relieve pressure: non-weight bearing
- Smoking cessation is essential.
- Wound care
- Frequent (e.g. weekly) removal of excess keratin and allow efficient drainage of the lesion.

## **Pharmacological Treatment**

**B:** ceftriaxone (IV) 1-2g 24 hourly for 7-10 days  
**AND**  
**B:** metronidazole (IV) 500mg 8 hourly for 7-10 days Depending on culture results  
**S:** piperacillin-tazobactam (IV) 4.5g 6-8 hourly 7-10 days (for severe/complicated cases)  
**OR**  
**S:** meropenem (IV) 1g 8 hourly 7-10 days

## **Surgical Management**

- Surgical debridement
- Amputation depending on Wagner's classification

text:
### Key steps in diabetic foot ulcer management: risk stratification, MDT, assessment, debridement, infection, moist healing, advanced therapies, offloading, metabolic control, monitoring, referral

1. Risk stratification (Wagner, UT, SINBAD).
2. Multidisciplinary team (endocrinology, podiatry, surgery, nursing, dietitian).
3. Comprehensive assessment (wound, vascular, neuropathy, labs).
4. Debridement (sharp, enzymatic, autolytic, etc.).
5. Infection management (antibiotics, osteomyelitis care).
6. Moist wound healing (appropriate dressings).
7. Advanced therapies (NPWT, skin substitutes, HBOT, PRP).
8. Offloading (total contact cast is the gold standard; walkers; footwear).
9. Glycaemic & metabolic control.
10. Monitoring & documentation (weekly to biweekly, photos).
11. Referral criteria (no healing, infection, ischaemia).

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Importance of Off-Loading in DFU Management
text:
## **Importance of Off-Loading in DFU Management**

* **Pressure Reduction:** Chronic pressure on ulcerated areas prevents the natural healing process, leading to further tissue damage, infection, and even amputation in severe cases.
* **Healing Promotion:** By off-loading the ulcerated site, the blood flow improves, inflammatory responses are regulated, and collagen formation is supported.
* **Infection Prevention:** Reduced pressure minimizes the risk of infection due to less friction and moisture retention at the wound site.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Off-Loading Techniques for DFUs
text:
### Off-loading techniques for diabetic foot ulcers: total contact cast, removable cast walkers, cushioned footwear, custom orthotics, wheelchair/bed rest: indications, advantages, disadvantages, care

Off-loading reduces chronic pressure on the ulcer (which prevents healing and can lead to tissue damage, infection and amputation), promotes healing (better blood flow, regulated inflammation, collagen formation), and lowers infection risk (less friction and moisture).

| Technique | Description | Indications | Advantages | Disadvantages | Care Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total Contact Cast (TCC) | Cast that encompasses the foot & ankle, redistributing pressure | Moderate–severe plantar DFUs; no infection or significant ischaemia | Gold standard for off-loading; promotes wound healing; reduces recurrence & re-ulceration | Hard to monitor wound; skin maceration risk; fall/ambulation difficulty | Keep dry & intact; weekly reviews for skin breakdown or infection |
| Removable Cast Walkers (RCWs) / Braces | Custom-fitted, removable devices for off-loading | Mild–moderate DFUs, or if TCC not feasible | Allows wound inspection & hygiene; more comfortable & easier to use | Less effective than TCC; compliance issues if removed too often | Use with proper footwear; patient education on strict off-loading |
| Cushioned Footwear | Shoes with cushioned insoles, rocker soles, or extra depth | Mild DFUs; patients needing frequent ambulation | Comfortable & non-invasive; redistributes pressure, especially combined with other techniques | Not effective for moderate–severe ulcers; requires consistent use | Regular podiatry inspection & fitting |
| Custom Orthotics | Tailored insoles/orthotics to redistribute pressure | DFUs on forefoot or heel | Individualized to foot anatomy; less cumbersome than casts/walkers | Requires precise fitting; wear out & need replacement | Educate patients on maintenance; ensure proper shoe fit |
| Wheelchair / Bed Rest | Eliminates weight-bearing through immobilization | Severe DFUs, or with major vascular/neuropathic issues | Removes pressure completely; can combine with NPWT | Reduces mobility & quality of life; risk of pressure sores from immobility | Monitor skin, nutrition, and mental health closely |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT)
text:
**Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT)** NPWT uses a vacuum dressing to promote wound healing by applying sub-atmospheric pressure to the wound bed, removing excess exudate, and reducing oedema.

**Indications:** NPWT can be used in conjunction with off-loading devices for DFUs, particularly when there is significant exudate or deep tissue involvement.

**Advantages:** Reduces wound size and promotes tissue granulation and contraction. Can be used with other off-loading devices, increasing overall effectiveness.

**Disadvantages:**
- Requires specialized equipment and training.
- May be costly and less accessible in resource-limited settings.
- Care Considerations:
- Regular monitoring to ensure proper vacuum pressure and to prevent leakage, which can result in loss of therapeutic efficacy.

text:
## **Post-Amputation Management of Patients**

<u>Key Components of Post-Amputation Care</u>
Post-amputation management includes a multidisciplinary approach involving the following key areas:
**Immediate Post-Operative Care**

**(a) Wound Care and Healing**

- **Criteria for Wound Monitoring:**
  ✓ Assess wound daily for signs of infection (e.g., redness, warmth, purulent drainage, and fever).
  ✓ Evaluate wound healing progress using tools like the Wound Healing Score (WHS), considering factors like wound size, exudate levels, and presence of infection.
  ✓ Non-healing or chronic wounds should be managed with advanced dressing materials (e.g., hydrocolloids, foam dressings) and, if needed, NPWT (Negative Pressure Wound Therapy).

**(b) Pain Management**

- **Pain Assessment Criteria:**
  ✓ Use standardized pain assessment scales such as the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) or McGill Pain Questionnaire.
  ✓ Early post-operative pain should be managed with opioids (short-term use) combined with NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for inflammation control.
  ✓ Phantom limb pain may be managed with medications like gabapentin, amitriptyline, or pregabalin.
  ✓ Ensure regular reassessment of pain intensity and adjust analgesia accordingly.

(c) **Infection Prevention**
- Antibiotic Therapy Criteria:
  ✓ Prophylactic antibiotics should be administered during the first 24-48 hours post-surgery, particularly in diabetic and immunocompromised patients.
  ✓ If infection is suspected, cultures should be taken from the wound bed, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or vancomycin) should be initiated until culture results guide de-escalation.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Post-Amputation Management > Infection Prevention; Rehabilitation and Mobility Support
text:
## <u>Rehabilitation and Mobility Support</u>

**(a) Early Mobilization and Physical Therapy**
- Criteria for Initiation:
  ✓ Early post-operative mobilization should begin within 48-72 hours to prevent complications such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pneumonia.
  ✓ Initiate physical therapy (PT) with an emphasis on strengthening remaining muscles, improving balance, and preventing contractures.

**(b) **Prosthetic Fitting and Training****
- Criteria for Prosthesis Fitting:
  ✓ Prosthetic fitting should begin once the surgical wound has healed adequately (usually after 4-6 weeks, depending on the type of amputation).
  ✓ Consider the patient's physical activity level, lifestyle, and comorbid conditions in the choice of prosthetic.
  ✓ Prosthetic Training should be initiated after fitting, with a focus on ambulation, balance, and functional use.
  ✓ Prosthesis Maintenance: Ensure regular check-ups to monitor fit and function of the prosthesis.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Post-Amputation Management > Long-Term Rehabilitation and Psychological Screening
text:
## <u>Long-Term Rehabilitation</u>

**Criteria for Long-Term Rehabilitation:**
- Multidisciplinary teams should be involved in creating individualized rehabilitation plans.
- Set clear goals for mobility, independence, and reintegration into daily activities.
- Occupational therapy should also be included to assist with adaptations in daily living (e.g., use of assistive devices, home modifications).

**Psychological Screening Criteria:**
- Regular screening for depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) using validated tools like the PHQ-9 or HADS.
- Psychological support should be provided to help the patient cope with the emotional and mental impact of amputation.
- Referral to mental health professionals (e.g., psychologists, psychiatrists) should be made as needed for long-term psychological counselling.

text:
### **Pressure Ulcer Prevention**

- Criteria for Pressure Ulcer Prevention:
  - ✓ Regular position changes for non-ambulatory patients and the use of pressure-relieving mattresses and heel cushions to reduce the risk of developing pressure sores.

### **Post-Amputation Follow-Up**

- Criteria for Follow-Up Visits:
  - ✓ Weekly visits for the first month post-amputation to monitor wound healing and prosthetic fitting.
  - ✓ Monthly visits during the first six months, and then quarterly follow-ups for ongoing monitoring of prosthesis use, rehabilitation progress, and the prevention of complications.
  - ✓ Blood pressure, glucose, and cholesterol should be routinely monitored to ensure optimal cardiovascular health and prevent complications like further amputations.

### **Peripheral Neuropathy**

Peripheral neuropathies encompass disorders of peripheral nerve cells and fibers which manifest secondary to a wide range of pathologies that can affect motor, sensory, and autonomic fibers. Peripheral neuropathies can be classified as mononeuropathies, multifocal neuropathies, and poly- neuropathies. Further sub classifications categorize peripheral neuropathies as axonal, demyelinating, or mixed types, which is essential for treatment and management purposes.

## Special Considerations

### **Clinical Presentation**

* Numbness and paresthesia
* Neuropathic pain
* Extremities weakness

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Guide to Clinical diagnosis of Peripheral Neuropathies
text:
### Peripheral neuropathy types: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, mononeuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex, hereditary neuropathies: clinical features and common causes

Peripheral neuropathies are disorders of peripheral nerve cells and fibres affecting motor, sensory and autonomic fibres; classified as mononeuropathies, multifocal neuropathies and polyneuropathies, and as axonal, demyelinating or mixed.

| Type | Clinical Features | Common causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy | Length-dependent: diffuse involvement affects distal segments first; symptoms occur below the knees before affecting the fingertips | Most common cause: diabetes. Chronic idiopathic axonal polyneuropathy, alcohol, chemotherapy induced |
| Mononeuropathy | Symptoms restricted to the distribution of a single nerve, myotome, or dermatome; asymmetric reflexes | Entrapment neuropathies, e.g. carpal tunnel, peroneal nerve entrapment; post-traumatic neuropathies; diabetes |
| Mononeuropathy multiplex | Occurrence of several concurrent mononeuropathies | Autoimmune vasculitis etiologies |
| Hereditary neuropathies | Distal calf atrophy, hammertoes, pes cavus; motor deficits ≥ sensory deficits; diffuse areflexia | Genetic diseases |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Treatment of Neuropathic Pain in Diabetic Foot
text:
### Treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy (flowchart): first-line anticonvulsants or antidepressants, second-line SNRIs, opioid-like drugs, topicals, third-line SSRIs and opioids

Patient presenting with painful neuropathy → rule out other causes of neuropathy → establish treatment goals → optimise glycaemic control.
- First-line therapy: anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin) or antidepressants (TCAs and SNRIs: amitriptyline, duloxetine).
- Second-line therapy: SNRIs (venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine); opioid-like drugs (tramadol or tapentadol ER); topical treatments (lidocaine 5% patch or capsaicin 0.075% cream).
- Third-line therapy: SSRIs (citalopram or paroxetine or escitalopram); opioids (oxycodone controlled release).
ER = extended release; SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant. Adapted from Snyder MJ, Gibbs LM, Lindsay TJ. Treating Painful Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: An Update. Am Fam Physician. 2016;94(3):227-34.

- Second-line therapy: SNRIs (venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine); opioid-like drugs (tramadol or tapentadol ER); topical treatments (lidocaine 5% patch or capsaicin 0.075% cream).
- Third-line therapy: SSRIs (citalopram or paroxetine or escitalopram); opioids (oxycodone controlled release).

text:
### Medicines for painful diabetic neuropathy: SNRIs, opioid-like drugs, topicals, anticonvulsants, amitriptyline: doses, maximum doses and cautions

**Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duloxetine | 60 mg daily or divided twice daily | 120 mg daily or divided twice daily |
| Venlafaxine | 150 mg daily | 225 mg daily |
| Desvenlafaxine | 200 mg daily | 400 mg daily |

**Notes (applies to every row in this section):** Side effects: nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, constipation, decreased appetite, insomnia, dizziness, somnolence, blurred vision, increased sweating and fatigue. Advise taking with food to reduce nausea

**Opioid-like medications**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tramadol | 50 mg every 4 to 6 hours | 100 mg every 6 hours; maximum 400 mg daily | Lowers seizure threshold; avoid in epilepsy or at risk of seizures |
| Tapentadol ER | 100 mg twice daily | 250 mg twice daily | Lowers seizure threshold; avoid in epilepsy or at risk of seizures |

**Topical medications**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lidocaine 5% patch | 1 patch daily | 3 patches daily |  |
| Capsaicin 0.075% cream | Four times daily | NA |  |
| Isosorbide dinitrate spray | 30 mg at bedtime applied to the bottom of the feet | NA |  |

**Anticonvulsants**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pregabalin | 300 mg divided twice daily | 600 mg divided twice daily | Side effects: dizziness, sedation, GI symptoms and mild peripheral oedema. Use cautiously in heart failure and with thiazolidinediones (cases of decompensated heart failure reported); renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance ≤30 ml/min/1.73 m2) requires dose adjustment |
| Gabapentin | 1,200 mg divided three times daily | 3,600 mg divided three times daily | Side effects: dizziness, sedation, GI symptoms and mild peripheral oedema. Dose adjustment recommended in renal impairment |

**Tricyclic antidepressant**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Amitriptyline | 25 mg daily at bedtime | 150 mg daily at bedtime or divided twice daily | Side effects: dry mouth, sedation, disturbed vision, arrhythmia, palpitations, postural hypotension, urinary retention and constipation. Contraindicated in cardiovascular disease (unstable angina, recent MI, heart failure, abnormal cardiac conduction) and glaucoma. Caution in elderly patients |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)
text:
# Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)

Screening of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) should be done annually in all patients with diabetes. This includes a minimum of history taking and complete physical examination especially palpating foot pulses.

Use of bedside non-invasive tests to exclude PAD is recommended. Among the tests that can be used are ankle brachial index (ABI), toe brachial index (TBI) and continuous wave Doppler (CWD). PAD can be excluded when:
- ✓ Ankle Brachial Index (ABI) is 0.9 - 1.3
- ✓ Toe Brachial Index is ≥0.75
- ✓ There is presence of triphasic Pedal Doppler Arterial Waveforms (PDAW

text:
## **CHAPTER 13**

## PSYCHIATRY

Clinical Guidelines for Management of Major Depressive Disorder in Adults - Diagnosis and Management. Depressive Disorder is a common mood disorder characterized by negative changes in feelings, thinking, and behaviour resulting in loss of normal functioning.

There are different classes of Depressive Disorders
* Persistent Depressive Disorder
* Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
* Substance/Medication Induced Depressive Disorder
* Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition
* Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder

Major Depressive Disorder is the commonest Depressive Disorder in Eswatini. This guideline focuses on Major Depressive Disorder( MDD)

#### **Screening and Diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder**

* Screening for Major Depressive Disorder is done to all clients accessing services using Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)
* PHQ-9 can be self-administered or administered by a healthcare provider.

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Screening and Diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder
text:
> **Major depressive disorder: 8-step assessment, DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9 for 2+ weeks), severity classification and when to refer urgently**
>
> Assessment steps:
> 1. Screen: 'Have you felt sad/depressed most of the time for the past 2 weeks?' AND 'Have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?'
> 2. Assess core symptoms: 5 or more of 9 criteria present for 2+ weeks.
> 3. Assess functional impairment: work, relationships, self-care, daily activities.
> 4. RULE OUT: bipolar disorder (past mania?), psychosis, medical causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV, stroke, diabetes).
> 5. Screen for suicide/self-harm: 'Do you have thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to live?'
> 6. Assess alcohol and substance use (may co-occur or cause symptoms).
> 7. Determine severity: mild / moderate / severe (any psychotic features?).
> 8. DIAGNOSIS confirmed if 5+ criteria are met, at least 1 being depressed mood or anhedonia.
> 
> DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9, lasting 2+ weeks): depressed mood most of the day (or irritability in children/adolescents); markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia); significant weight loss/gain or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day; psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable by others); fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day; feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; difficulty concentrating or making decisions; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.
> 
> Severity: mild – few symptoms beyond the minimum, mild functional impairment; moderate – between mild and severe, moderate impairment; severe – most symptoms, marked impairment, may have psychotic features.
> 
> When to refer urgently: active suicidal ideation with plan or intent; psychotic features (hallucinations, delusions); severe self-neglect or inability to care for self; no response after 2 adequate medication trials; suspected bipolar disorder.

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Depression Management – Pharmacological Treatment
text:
### Antidepressants for moderate-severe depression: fluoxetine, amitriptyline, imipramine, sertraline, escitalopram: starting and usual doses and notes; psychoeducation and cautions

Consider antidepressants for moderate-severe depression. Discuss with the person: not addictive; takes 2-4 weeks for effect; must be taken for 9-12 months minimum after remission.

| Drug | Starting Dose | Usual Dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fluoxetine (SSRI) | 10-20 mg mane | 20-60 mg/day | First-line; only SSRI recommended for adolescents ≥12 yrs; avoid with MAOIs |
| Amitriptyline (TCA) | 25-50 mg nocte | 75-150 mg/day | Effective; caution in cardiac disease, elderly, overdose risk |
| Imipramine (TCA) | 25-50 mg nocte | 75-200 mg/day | Alternative TCA; monitor ECG if cardiac risk present |
| Sertraline (SSRI) | 25-50 mg/day | 50-200 mg/day | Good tolerability; preferred in elderly and cardiac disease |
| Escitalopram (SSRI) | 5-10 mg/day | 10-20 mg/day | Well tolerated; fewer drug interactions; good for elderly |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Suicide Risk Assessment and Follow-up
text:
> **Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening**
>
> SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?
> - HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.
> - MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.
> - ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.
> 
> FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):
> - Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).
> - Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.
> - Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).
> - After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.
> - 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.
> - Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.
> 
> PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit.
html:
Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening

SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?

- HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.

- MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.

- ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.

FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):

- Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).

- Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.

- Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).

- After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.

- 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.

- Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.

PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit.
