heading_path: 12 Health Management Information System (hmis)
text:
## **12. HEALTH MANAGEMENT INFORMATION SYSTEM (HMIS)**

Health Management Information System (HMIS) involves recording and custody of information to facilitate future planning and reference. Reports involve filling out, compiling specific information on data for use at a certain level. the Documentation remains important in FP service provision, for report writing and monitoring purposes as well as research purposes where applicable.

Health provider should ensure that all FP records are fully taken, including;

* Client’s demographic details
* Detailed history (past and present); medical, surgical, gynaecological, etc.
* Appointment card which is given to the client for follow up.
* CMIS, FP and PNC registers
* A national referral forms
* A supply stock card which records FP methods and quantity stock balances.
* FP ordering and reporting form
* FP summary reports: monthly, quarterly and annual. This provides a summary of the number and type of clients served, number of contraceptives received and dispensed and the projected requirement of contraceptives by method

text:
## **Family Planning Indicators**

Indicators are measures used to track changes in a programme over time and provide information on the status of programme activities, targets and progress toward achieving programme objectives. They are as follows:
* Number of health facilities providing FP services.
* Total population catchment area.
* Total population of reproductive age.
* Types of FP methods available and offered
* Number of first FP attendance.
* Number of re-attendants.
* Number of FP clients tested for HIV.
* Number of FP clients who tested HIV positive.
* Number of FP clients taking condoms for dual protection.
* Number of FP clients discharged for intended pregnancy
* Number of crude dropouts.
* Number of clients who got pregnant while on contraceptives.
* Number of clients accessing FP services through MNCH services.
* Number of FP commodities distributed.

text:
## **Challenges in Documentation**

* Multiple records (too many registers). Shortage of human resource. · Stock out of the data tools
* Lack of knowledge by staff on the importance of data.
* Continuous increase of workload.
* Poor quality data (sometimes the data collected does not help to inform programmers and policy makers).
* Poor network affects operations of CMIS, thus leading to using down time data forms which are later not captured into the system
* Poor maintenance of computers
* Some information not captured e.g., outreaches, mobile clinics

Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4)** | Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) can use the following *hormonal* contraceptive methods without restriction: *COCs,* CICs, combined contraceptive patches and *rings,* POPs, POIs (DMPA and NET-EN), and LNG and ETG implants (MEC Category 1).

Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) generally should not initiate use of the LNG-IUD (MEC Category 3) until their illness has improved *to asymptomatic* or mild HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 1 or 2).

Women who already have an LNG-IUD inserted and who develop severe or advanced HIV clinical disease *need* not have their IUD removed (MEC Category 2 for *continuation).* | |

heading_path: Background
text:
# **Background**

# **Eswatini National Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and Viral Hepatitis (VH) Guidelines**

STIs affect both men and women, and <mark>almost</mark> half of all STIs occur in people younger than 25 years old. Exposure to an STI can <mark>occur</mark> any time you have sexual contact with anyone that involves the genitals, the mouth (oral), or the rectum (anal). Exposure to STIs is more likely if you have more than one sex partner or do not use condoms. Some STIs can be transmitted through other routes, such as by sharing needles or needle pricks, during pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding. Others may be asymptoms but still infectious.

STIs remain a priority in the HIV response. They constitute a major health and economic burden worldwide, and account for a substantial number of economic losses that are sustained in developing nations due to various morbidities. Globally, WHO estimates that more than one million curable STIs are acquired every day among people aged 15-49 years, amounting to 374 million new infections of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis in 2020. An estimated 8 million adults aged 15-49 years acquired syphilis in 2022, and approximately 520 million people in this age group are living with herpes simplex virus type 2 [15]. Prevalence of these infections is highest in the WHO African Region.

They constitute a major health and economic burden worldwide, and account for a substantial number of economic losses that are sustained in developing nations due to various morbidities. Globally, WHO estimates that more than one million curable STIs are acquired every day among people aged 15-49 years, amounting to 374 million new infections of chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis in 2020. An estimated 8 million adults aged 15-49 years acquired syphilis in 2022, and approximately 520 million people in this age group are living with herpes simplex virus type 2 [15]. Prevalence of these infections is highest in the WHO African Region.

heading_path: Background
text:
In Eswatini, the number of clients presenting with STIs at health facilities more than doubled between 2021 and 2024, rising from 11,129 to 25,351, and remained at a similar level of 25,221 in 2025. Women accounted for 62% of 2025 presentations and men 38%. The highest caseloads were recorded in Manzini (8,542; 33%) and Hhohho (6,478; 25%), followed by Lubombo (5,362; 21%) and Shiselweni (5,253; 21%). The burden is concentrated in young adults: adolescent girls and young women aged 15-24 years accounted for 5,483 presentations, women aged 25-34 years for 5,368, and men aged 15-34 years for 6,508 [16]. Eswatini also carries one of the world's highest adult HIV burdens, with adult HIV prevalence of 24.8% and incidence of 0.62% [17], and 6,701 new HIV diagnoses among 213,516 people tested in 2024 [18]. This overlapping epidemiology makes the STI consultation one of the highest-yield entry points for HIV prevention, testing and treatment [19].

The factors that determine healthy sexual behaviour are complex and context-specific. In Eswatini, behaviours that pose high risks for STI and HIV transmission include; Low levels of knowledge about STIs and HIV; Inconsistent condom use; Multiple sexual partners; Gender disparities leading to unequal power in sexual decision-making and Inappropriate health seeking behaviour for STIs. The 2025 national programme review [16,20] further identified inadequate syphilis and hepatitis B screening and treatment in antenatal care, and voluntary medical male circumcision coverage of 48% against a 70% target, as persisting service-delivery gaps in STI and viral hepatitis prevention.

heading_path: Background
text:
# **Eswatini National Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and Viral Hepatitis (VH) Guidelines**

The use of standardized national **protocols** is strongly recommended to ensure adequate treatment at all levels of the *health care delivery*. All health facilities that provide STI services should implement the STI service package as outlined in this guideline.

The growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) necessitates a shift in STI management strategies, particularly for gonorrhea and *Mycoplasma genitalium*, which have shown resistance to commonly used antibiotics, limiting treatment options. The emergence of multi-drug-resistant *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, a WHO-designated priority pathogen of public health concern, underscores the urgent need for **bacteriology testing** to identify resistance patterns and guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. Laboratory confirmation nonetheless remains limited: fewer than 200 detections of *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* and *Chlamydia trachomatis* combined were recorded nationally through molecular (GeneXpert) testing in 2025, concentrated in the 15-29 year age bands, against more than 25,000 clinical STI presentations in the same period [16]. These counts reflect the current reach of molecular testing rather than the true burden of infection, and the gap between clinical presentations and confirmed diagnoses underlines the need to expand testing coverage and strengthen STI laboratory reporting. While syndromic management remains fundamental, Eswatini's approach now emphasizes specimen collection and bacteriology testing where feasible, ensuring pathogen-specific treatment to optimize antibiotic use, reduce treatment failures, and curb AMR development.

heading_path: Background > Rationale for the STIs guidelines
text:
## **Rationale for the STIs guidelines**

There are several challenges to providing effective STI services to the people who need them. Many people with STIs do not seek treatment because they are asymptomatic or have mild symptoms and do not realize that anything is wrong. Others who have symptoms due to stigma associated with STI's may prefer self-medication or seek treatment at pharmacies or from traditional healers. Even those who come to a clinic may not be properly adhere or complete treatment course. In the end, only a small proportion of people with an STI may be cured and avoid reinfection. This Guideline aims to help increase the proportion of STI patients that are treated and cured through assisting health care providers to:
- Raise awareness in the community about STIs and how they can be prevented - especially among populations who may be at high risk.
- Promote safer sexual practices, including delaying sexual onset, consistent condom use and having one or fewer partners.

## **Target audience**

These guidelines will be part of a consolidated set of guidelines for the prevention of STIs and management of people with STIs that are intended for programme managers for STI prevention and control at the national level and the health-care providers at the frontline in primary, secondary and tertiary health-care facilities. For the programme managers, the guidelines will assist in deciding how to organize the services for providing STI care and to determine the distribution of equipment and commodities that ensure access to high-quality STI care for people. The guidelines can also be used as an advocacy tool for the financial and human resources required to deliver adequate, acceptable and equitable STI care for everyone who needs STI services. Similarly, these guidelines can offer guidance to policy-makers other stakeholders and partners in providing services for STI prevention, treatment and care.

heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.1 Rational of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases
text:
## 1.1 Rationa**l** of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases

Effective management is one of the cornerstones of STI control. It prevents the development of complications, sequela and decreases the spread of these diseases in the community. Offers a unique opportunity for targeted education about HIV prevention and other STI's. Appropriate treatment of STI at the first contact between patient and health care provider is therefore an important public health measure.

The use of standardized national protocols is strongly recommended in order to ensure adequate treatment at all levels of the health care system delivery. Standardized treatment facilitates training and supervision of health providers and, this in turn delays the development of antimicrobial resistance in STIs.

**Etiological diagnosis:** Ideally, the diagnosis of an STI is made by knowing exactly what organism is present by performing laboratory tests. Unfortunately, this method of e diagnosis is often expensive and requires sophisticated equipment and skilled personnel to carry out. This places constraints on time, resources, costs and access to treatment for the patients. In addition, test results may not be available during the consultation, thus requiring patients to return in one or two days. This is not feasible in many settings. The risk of developing complications is high and the period of infectivity is prolonged by this delay in therapy.

heading_path: 1.0 National STIs Case Management > 1.1 Rational of national management of STI and Viral Hepatitis (VH) cases
text:
To enhance etiological diagnosis, sample collection should be integrated into routine STI care, where feasible. Specimen collection methods vary depending on the suspected STI and the site of infection. The following approaches can be used:
- Urine samples: Used for Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAATs) to detect Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in both males and females.
- Urethral or endocervical swabs: Collected for gram stain, culture, and NAATs, aiding in identifying gonorrhea, chlamydia, and Mycoplasma genitalium.
- Vaginal swabs: Self-collected or clinician-obtained samples can be used for bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and candidiasis testing.
- Blood samples: Used for serological tests (e.g., RPR or TPHA for syphilis, HSV IgG/IgM for herpes, and HIV screening).
- Lesion or ulcer swabs: Collected for herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR testing, syphilis dark-field microscopy, or Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) culture.

- Rectal and pharyngeal swabs: <mark>Recommended</mark> for high-risk populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM), to diagnose extragenital gonorrhea and chlamydia infections.

By incorporating sample collection into clinical workflows, healthcare providers can increase diagnostic accuracy, improve antibiotic stewardship, and contribute to AMR surveillance efforts.

NB: Please refer to the relevant Specimen Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for detailed guidelines.

**Clinical diagnosis:** This involves using clinical experience to match identified symptoms and signs to a specific STI. However, even experienced specialists often misdiagnose STIs when they rely only on clinical experience. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies found that a clinical (syndromic) diagnosis of genital ulcer disease detected only about half of syphilis cases (pooled sensitivity 52.8%) and fewer than half of herpes cases (43.5%), while being somewhat better for chancroid (71.9%); the authors concluded that relying on clinical diagnosis alone results in significant numbers of missed cases and that affordable point-of-care diagnostics are urgently needed (Loh et al., 2022).

### **Genital Ulcer Syndrome**

1. **Chancroid:** raised rough edges, beefy.
2. **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV):** itchy, burning and tingling sensation, painful blisters, ulcer.
3. **Syphilis:**
   - Primary stage firm: painless lesions (chancre) and self-limiting, may last up to 3 weeks.
   - Secondary stage: non itchy pigmented lesions can show up on the palms of your hands and soles of your feet, all over your body, or in just a few places. You may also have mucous membrane lesions.
   - Latent/late stage: gumma, and may affect the central nervous system.

text:
# Other STIs

1. **Human Papilloma virus (HPV) warts:** raised or papillary skin colored growth with a cauliflower like appearance, soft to the touch usually painless but may itch.
2. **Mycoplasma genitalium:** Mycoplasma genitalium (Mgen) is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) that can infect your cervix, urethra and/or rectum. Because Mgen often doesn't cause symptoms, many people who have it don't know it and unknowingly infect other people. Mgen is treatable with antibiotics
3. **Neonatal Conjunctivitis:** thick, often sticky, muco-purulent discharge, hyperaemia
4. **Syphilitic Warts:** flat, extensive clustered lesions, mostly on moist areas.
5. **Ingual bubo:** unilateral or bilateral swelling in the inguinal region, its fluctuant, painful.
6. **Pediculosis pubis:** whitish nits on the base of hairs accompanied by itchiness.

7. **Genital Scabies:** burrows, itchiness erythematous lesions
8. **Hepatitis B:** Many people have no symptoms during the initial infection. Some develop a rapid onset of sickness with vomiting, yellowish skin, feeling tired, dark urine and abdominal pain.
9. **Hepatitis C:** Every long term of Hepatitis c starts with an acute. ## 1.3 Syndromic Approach:

A syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms. The numerous and different STI pathogens produce a number of syndromes, hence a syndromic diagnosis is made when the patient's signs and symptoms are matched to a particular STI syndrome. Syndromic approach offers treatment for more than one pathogen so that antimicrobial therapy is effective against all the pathogens that commonly cause the syndrome.

This approach to diagnosis and treatment reduces costs and increases access to treatment. This provides a more practical and cost-effective intervention for reaching the majority of patients with STI's, especially in resource-limited settings. Syndromic STI management has some advantages which include the following:
Improved diagnosis

text:
## **Challenges**

- Overdiagnosis and overtreatment can increase drug costs
- Risk of multiple-drug side effects, drug interactions, altered vaginal flora, and antimicrobial resistance - WHO now treats overtreatment as increasingly undesirable given worsening resistance and limited treatment options.
- Not useful for detecting infections in asymptomatic individuals
- Vaginal discharge poorly predicts cervical gonococcal/chlamydial infection; WHO acknowledges its vaginal discharge flowcharts have limitations for cervical infections.
- Leaves a gap in establishing antimicrobial susceptibility for patients failing first-line therapy, especially gonococcal infections.

<mark> The Ministry of Health recommends that all patients presenting with STI's are treated using the syndromic management approach, but when available, guided with quality-assured rapid tests, bacteriological and molecular assays for STI laboratory diagnosis </mark>

text:
## **2.0 Essential Components**

- History taking: Includes demographic information, a behavioural risk assessment, and medical history to identify potential exposures and risk factors.
- Physical examination: Focuses on the genital, anal, and oral areas, along with a skin assessment, to identify lesions, discharge, ulcers, or other STI-related signs.
- Establishing a syndromic and/or etiological diagnosis: Syndromic management remains a key approach in STI care, but etiological diagnosis is increasingly emphasised through laboratory testing. Where feasible, specimen collection (e.g. urethral, vaginal, cervical, or lesion swabs, urine samples, and blood tests) should be undertaken to confirm the causative pathogen, enable targeted treatment, and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, thereby helping to limit antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
- Curative therapy: Effective antimicrobials should be administered at the first point of contact to reduce transmission and complications. Given the rise in drug-

resistant STIs, treatment regimens <mark>should</mark> be reviewed and updated periodically in line with local AMR surveillance data to maintain efficacy.

- Health promotion package: Education on STI prevention, condom use, partner notification, and risk-reduction strategies should be integrated into patient consultations. Patients should also be informed about AMR and the importance of completing the prescribed treatment course.

## **2.2 Physical examination**

Before examining a patient, obtain consent, explain each step in advance, and ensure privacy and comfort throughout the examination. Adhere to safety precautions like hand hygiene, glove use, and safe disposal of sharps. Conduct examinations in a well-lit room, exposing only the area needed while keeping the patient covered. Communicate findings using language the patient understands, and perform all procedures gently with minimum discomfort. Have consideration of the client's choice in the sex/gender of the attendant as per provisions in the Health Act of 2023.

text:
## **2.2.1 Physical examination of the female**

Conduct a systematic general examination, inspecting the skin, palms, hair, lymph nodes (cervical, axillary, inguinal), and external genitalia for rashes, ulcers, warts, discharge, or swellings, documenting the size, location, and appearance of all lesions. For female patients, perform a speculum examination to inspect the vaginal walls and cervix for ulcers, warts, and discharge, and offer cervical cancer screening (Pap smear or VIA) if not performed within the recommended interval. Follow with a bimanual examination to assess for adnexal masses, tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness. Note that speculum and bimanual examinations may need to be deferred if the patient has extensive, painful genital ulcers.

text:
## **2.2.2 Physical examination of the male**

Inspect the skin of the neck, chest, back, hands, palms, lower abdomen, inguinal areas, and thighs for rashes and sores, and palpate the cervical, axillary, supraclavicular, epitrochlear, and inguinal lymph nodes for enlargement or buboes. Inspect the pubic hair for lice or nits, and examine the penis, including the meatus with foreskin retraction, looking for ulcers, warts, discharge, or other abnormalities. If no discharge is visible, gently squeeze and massage the urethra forward to express any discharge. Palpate the scrotal contents and inguinal regions, and document the size, location, and appearance of all lesions found.

text:
Key counselling messages should cover:
- **Diagnosis and treatment adherence:** Explain the patient's diagnosis, its implications, and the prescribed treatment. Emphasise the importance of completing the full course of medication (the right drug, right dose, right route, right time) and explain how poor adherence contributes to antimicrobial resistance, making future infections harder to treat.
- Risk reduction and safer sex: Discuss methods for lowering STI and HIV acquisition risk, including abstinence, mutual faithfulness, and correct and consistent use of male or female condoms with lubricants. Explore any barriers the patient @perceives to practising safer sex and identify realistic behavioural changes they are willing to make.
- Partner notification and treatment: Stress the importance of ensuring all sexual partners are notified, tested, and fully treated to prevent reinfection and onward transmission.
- HIV and related services: Discuss the risk of HIV co-acquisition, offer HIV counselling and testing, and refer to additional prevention services (PrEP, voluntary medical male circumcision) as per national guidelines.
- Follow-up: Encourage prompt health-seeking behaviour for any recurrent symptoms, and reinforce that reinfection is possible if partners are not treated or risk behaviours continue.
- Before closing, confirm three commitments with the patient: to complete their treatment, to reduce risky sexual activities, and to ensure their sexual partners are fully treated.

text:
## 3.3 **Notification and management of sexual partner(s)**

Partner notification and treatment is one of the most important components of STI case management. It breaks the cycle of transmission, prevents complications, and identifies asymptomatic individuals who would not otherwise seek care. All partner notification must be conducted confidentially, voluntarily, and without coercion.

**Partner treatment strategies:**

- Offer immediate treatment to all sexual partners of the index patient, even if *asymptomatic*, using the same treatment regimen.
- Where a partner is unlikely to attend in person, consider providing the index patient with a prescription or medication for their partner (expedited partner therapy), particularly for populations with casual partners.
- Assess all partners for additional STIs beyond the presenting infection.

**Approaches to partner notification:**

- Patient referral (passive): The index patient takes responsibility for notifying and referring their partner(s) for treatment, either through direct conversation, accompanying them to a facility, or providing a contact/notification slip. Success depends on the quality of counselling the index patient receives and the provider's communication skills.
- Provider referral (active): A health care worker contacts the partner(s) directly. This may be necessary when patient referral is unlikely to succeed, but requires the index patient's informed consent to protect confidentiality.
- Providers should discuss both approaches with the patient and agree on the most appropriate method. In some cases, a combination of both may be used.

text:
# STI and Viral Hepatitis prevention interventions

**STI and Viral Hepatitis Prevention:**

- Promote abstinence, delayed sexual debut, and mutual faithfulness as key prevention strategies.
- Ensure availability and correct use of male and female condoms for all sexually active individuals, particularly high-risk groups.
- Encourage periodic STI screening for sexually active individuals, especially those not using protection consistently.
- Provide education on STI and viral hepatitis prevention and risk reduction.
- Reinforce universal precautions when handling hazardous waste and infectious materials.

**Priority populations for hepatitis B vaccination:**

- Health care workers and frontline personnel (police, firefighters)
- Pregnant women (from second trimester until delivery)
- Newborns (birth dose) and children under five
- Key populations, including people who inject drugs
- HBV seronegative individuals receiving dialysis or kidney transplant
- Unvaccinated sexual abuse survivors

text:
# 4.0 Laboratory Diagnosis of STIs and VH

Syndromic management remains the foundation of STI care in Eswatini, but WHO recommends that treatment be guided by quality-assured laboratory or point-of-care testing wherever such testing is available. Molecular tests - nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) - are the reference standard for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis and Mycoplasma genitalium, and may be performed either in a laboratory or at the <u>point</u> of care using platforms already deployed in the Eswatini network, such as GeneXpert.

Culture retains a specific and irreplaceable role for *N. gonorrhoeae*: it remains the only method that yields an isolate for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and is therefore essential to national AMR surveillance. Where no aetiological test is accessible, syndromic treatment should still be given at the first point of contact and the specimen referred onward where feasible.

The tests set out in this section are drawn from the WHO manual Laboratory and point-of-care diagnostic testing for sexually transmitted infections, including HIV (fourth edition, 2023), the 2024 WHO updated recommendations for the treatment of *N. gonorrhoeae*, *C. trachomatis* and *T. pallidum* and new recommendations on syphilis testing, and the 2025 WHO guidelines for the management of asymptomatic STIs.

text:
## **4.2 Specimen collection and transport**

Correct specimen collection determines the validity of every result that follows. Use only the swab and transport medium supplied with the test platform in use, label each specimen at the patient's side, and record the anatomical site sampled on the request form so that the laboratory can interpret the result correctly.

Self-collected vaginal swabs perform as well as clinician-collected swabs for NAAT and should be offered where privacy allows. For extragenital infection, sample the site of exposure: a genital specimen will not detect pharyngeal or rectal infection. Where testing is not performed on site, transport specimens within the time and temperature range specified by the manufacturer and refer them to the nearest testing laboratory without delay.

text:
## 4.3 **Antimicrobial resistance surveillance**

N. gonorrhoeae has developed resistance to nearly every antibiotic used to treat it, and molecular tests cannot yet provide reliable susceptibility results from non-culture specimens. Sentinel facilities should therefore continue to collect urethral and endocervical specimens for culture and susceptibility testing, and results should be reported to the national AMR surveillance system so that first-line regimens in these guidelines can be reviewed against local data.

Patients whose symptoms persist or recur after correctly completed treatment should be re-tested, and an isolate sought for susceptibility testing where possible, rather than being treated empirically a second time.

## 4.3 **Antimicrobial resistance surveillance**

N. gonorrhoeae has developed resistance to nearly every antibiotic used to treat it, and molecular tests cannot yet provide reliable susceptibility results from non-culture specimens. Sentinel facilities should therefore continue to collect urethral and endocervical specimens for culture and susceptibility testing, and results should be reported to the national AMR surveillance system so that first-line regimens in these guidelines can be reviewed against local data.

Patients whose symptoms persist or recur after correctly completed treatment should be re-tested, and an isolate sought for susceptibility testing where possible, rather than being treated empirically a second time.

text:
## 4.4 **Testing asymptomatic people**

Most STIs are asymptomatic, and syndromic management cannot reach them. WHO recommends targeted screening for gonorrhoea and chlamydia in high-prevalence settings where resources allow, prioritising pregnant women, sexually active adolescents and young people aged 10-24 years, sex workers, and men who have sex with r. Screening for sex workers and men who have sex with men should be offered at least annually, and six-monthly where feasible.

Syphilis and HIV testing should be offered to every person attending for STI care, irrespective of symptoms, and to every pregnant woman at her first antenatal visit. Hepatitis B surface antigen testing should likewise be offered to all pregnant women to allow timely antiviral prophylaxis and birth-dose vaccination.

For a person with urethral discharge from the penis, take a medical and sexual history, assess STI risk, and do a physical and genital examination. narrative: Point-of-care workflow for anorectal discharge (STI/VH guidelines draft 2026, page 43). For a person with anorectal discharge who reports receptive anal sex, take a medical and sexual history, assess STI exposure risk, and inspect the genital and peri-anal area (anoscopy if available or digital exam if acceptable). Refer for other investigations if the discharge is not related to STIs. Where molecular assays are available, test: if NG/CT/MG (gonorrhoea, chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium) is positive, treat based on results; if there is pain, treat additionally for herpes simplex virus. With limited laboratory capacity: if anorectal discharge is present, treat for NG and CT, and treat additionally for herpes if there is pain. Offer HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services, and review in 1 week if symptoms persist or recur.

text:
## **5.3. Vaginal Discharge Syndrome (VDS)**

## **Description**

VDS is a vaginal discharge characterized by abnormal vaginal discharge in terms of increased quantity, and/or unusual color or malodor.

## **Etiology**

*N. gonorrhoea* and *C. trachomatis* can cause cervicitis Vaginal pathology: *T. vaginalis*, *C. albicans*, and bacterial vaginosis.

text:
## **Clinical features**

The symptoms of vaginal discharge syndrome include:
- Increased secretions,
- Change in the color or consistency, foul odor,
- Itching and soreness,
- Painful urination
- Pain during sexual intercourse.

## **Syndromic treatment of vaginal discharge syndrome (VDS)**

- Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT
  PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT
  PLUS
- Metronidazole 2g orally STAT.

**NB:** In case VDS is due to vaginitis, conduct risk assessment, if negative the treatment regimen should cover organisms causing bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis infections:
- Metronidazole** 2 g orally, STAT dose
  PLUS
- Clotrimazole pessary 500mg intra-vaginally once nocte

Patients taking Metronidazole should be cautioned to avoid taking alcohol while on these drugs and up to 24-48 hours after the last dose.

narrative: Syndromic treatment of vaginal discharge syndrome (STI/VH guidelines draft 2026, chart 4, page 46). A patient complains of vaginal discharge, burning micturition or vulval itchiness: take history, do a risk assessment, and examine with bimanual and speculum examination. If abnormal discharge or itching is confirmed: ceftriaxone 1 g IM stat plus azithromycin 1 g orally stat plus metronidazole 2 g orally stat; if candida is evident, add clotrimazole 500 mg pessaries intravaginally stat; follow up after 7 days. If not confirmed: another STI syndrome or illness present, treat by the appropriate flow chart; none, reassure, counsel and provide condoms. At follow-up: improved, reinforce the health promotion package; not improved, ask about re-infection or poor compliance: yes, repeat treatment and reinforce the package; no, refer for further management.

text:
## Management of cervical infections:

### **Examination findings - signs:**

Speculum examination may reveal a normal-looking cervix in the presence of endocervical infection. For those with abnormalities, the cervix may be erythematous or severely eroded and associated with a muco-purulent cervical discharge. The cervix may be friable and bleed easily on contact.

## **Syndromic treatment:**

- Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT OR Cefixime 400 mg orally STAT PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT (OR Erythromycin 500mg QID x 7 days) PLUS
- Metronidazole 2g orally STAT

Recommended treatment regimen for cervical infections in pregnant woman:
- Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT OR Cefixime 400 mg orally STAT PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1 g orally STAT (OR Erythromycin 500mg QID x 7 days) PLUS
- Metronidazole 2g orally STAT

<mark><u>If vulval oedema</u></mark>, itching, excoriations or curd-like discharge present ADD:
- Clotrimazole pessary 500mg intra-vaginally STAT

*Table 7: Treatment for cervical infections*

text:
## # 5.4 **Lower abdominal pain (LAP)**

## **Description**

Lower abdominal pain is one of the major signs of Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) which may be accompanied by cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination, a complaint of back pain, lower tenderness with or without guarding on abdominal examination.

All sexually active women presenting with a history of lower abdominal pain should be carefully evaluated for the presence of salphingitis and/or endometritis - elements of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). In addition, routine bimanual and abdominal examination should be carried out on all women with presumptive STI since some women with PID will not complain of lower abdominal pain. Hospitalization of patients with acute PID should be seriously considered when:
- The diagnosis is uncertain
- Surgical emergencies such as appendicitis and ectopic pregnancy cannot be excluded
- A pelvic abscess is suspected
- The patient is pregnant

Risk factors: women with IUD have a higher risk of PID, particularly if the IUD had been inserted recently.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Etiology
text:
## **Etiology**

*N. gonorrhea, C. Trachomatis* and bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis are most frequently responsible of this syndrome.

## **Clinical features**

Lower abdominal pain is a complex syndrome to identify. Several other important non-STI causes may produce similar symptoms and signs.

- In all suspected lower abdominal pain patients, bi-manual examination and speculum must be conducted.
- The physical examination should assess the general condition of the patient. In all cases, pregnancy-related conditions, as well as an acute abdominal tenderness, should be excluded.

- Elevated temperature, high pulse<sup>36</sup> rate, bleeding and low blood pressure, for example, should alert to the possibility of severe pelvic infection.

**NB:** Such patients should be referred urgently.

- On palpation, if signs of peritonitis such as lower abdomen guarding and rebound tenderness or if abdominal masses are present, the patient must be referred accordingly for further management.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.4 Lower abdominal pain (LAP) > Syndromic treatment of lower abdominal pain
text:
## **Syndromic treatment of lower abdominal pain**

- Ceftriaxone 1g IM STAT Stat
  PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1g orally weekly for 2 weeks
  PLUS
- Metronidazole, 400mg orally BID for 7 to 14 days

## **Treatment options for lower abdominal pain**

- Ceftriaxone, 1g I.M STAT, Gentamycin 240mg IM Stat and Spectinmycin 2 grams IM
  PLUS
- Azithromycin, 1g orally per week for 2 weeks, OR Doxycycline 100 mg orally BID for 14 days OR Erythromycin, 500 mg orally QID for 14 days
  PLUS
- Metronidazole, 400mg orally BID for 7 to 14 days

**NB:** Patients taking Metronidazole should be cautioned against taking alcohol while on these drugs and up to 24 - 48 hours after the last dose.

**Caution:** PID can be a serious condition. The patient must be referred: if she does not respond to treatment within 3 days and even earlier in case there is worsening of her condition. Because of the high risk for maternal morbidity, fetal wastage, and preterm delivery. Pregnant women who have suspected PID should be referred for hospitalization further management by an obstetrician.

text:
## **Description**

*M. genitalium* causes symptomatic and asymptomatic urethritis among men and is the etiology of approximately 15%-20% of NGU, 20%-25% of nonchlamydial NGU, and 40% of persistent or recurrent urethritis.

Among women, *M. genitalium* has been **associated** with cervicitis, PID, preterm delivery, spontaneous abortion, and infertility, with an approximately twofold increase in the risk for these outcomes among women infected with *M. genitalium*, infections among women are also frequently asymptomatic.

Rectal infection with *M. genitalium* has been reported among 1%-26% of MSM and among 3% of women (941). Rectal infections often are asymptomatic, although higher prevalence of *M. genitalium* has been reported among men with rectal symptoms. Similarly, although asymptomatic *M. genitalium* has been detected in the pharynx.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > Mycoplasma genitalium > Diagnostic Considerations
text:
## **Etiology**

- Mycoplasma Genitalium

## **Signs and Symptoms:**

- **Males:**
  - Urethritis
  - Epididymitis
  - Prostatitis
- **Females:**
  - Cervicitis
  - Endometriosis

## **Diagnostic Considerations**

*M. genitalium* is an extremely slow-growing organism. Culture can take up to 6 months, and technical laboratory capacity is limited to research settings. NAAT for *M. genitalium* is FDA cleared for use with urine and urethral, penile meatal, endocervical, and vaginal swab samples. *M. genitalium* should be suspected in cases of persistent or recurrent urethritis or cervicitis and considered for PID.

text:
## **Treatment**

*M. genitalium* lacks a cell wall, and thus antibiotics targeting cell-wall biosynthesis (e.g., β-lactams including penicillins and cephalosporins) are ineffective against this organism. Because of the high rates of macrolide resistance with treatment failures and efficient selection of additional resistance, a 1-g dose of azithromycin should not be used.

**Recommended Regimens**

41

Doxycycline 100 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days, substitute moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 7 days.

text:
## 5.5 Scrotal swelling (SSS)

**Description:**

Inflammation of the epididymis usually manifests itself by acute onset of unilateral testicular pain and swelling, often with tenderness of the epididymis, vas deferens, and occasionally with erythema and oedema of the overlying skin.

**Etiology:**

responsible micro-organism: E. coli, Klebsiella, and P. Aeruginosa. In pre-pubertal children, mumps epididymo-orchitis is usually noted within a week of parotid enlargement.

**Clinical features:**

- The patient usually complains of unilateral pain and swelling of the scrotum with a urethral discharge which develops over 1-2 days
- Scrotal swelling may be seen following trauma or testicular torsion and this required immediate referral for surgical or urological opinion.
- On inspection, the scrotal sac appears distended and on palpation, both testicles and the epididymis are swollen and tender. Differential Dx: Testicular torsion, testicular trauma, inguinal hernia, hydrocele and haematoccele

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Description
text:
## **Description**

Inguinal and femoral buboes are localized enlargements of the lymph nodes in the groin area, which are painful and may be fluctuant (soft with a feeling of liquid inside). Inguinal bubo is rarely the sole manifestation of an STI and is usually found together with other genital ulcer disease. Buboes are usually caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) and Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1- L3. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is an non ulcerative sexually transmitted disease of the genital area caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. It is important to elicit history of recent genital ulcer and examine the external genitalia in all patients presenting with bubos so that effective management can be given.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.6. Inguinal bubo (IBS) > Clinical features
text:
## **Clinical features**

- Inguinal buboes can occur as unilateral or bilateral, single or multiple painful swellings. Other STI's (such as gonorrhoea,
- Syphilis, herpes and HIV) may cause inguinal lymphadenopathy, which may typically be painful (herpes, gonorrhoea) or non-painful (syphilis, HIV).
- If during examination, genital ulcer(s) are seen along with inguinal buboes, the clinical management should follow the genital ulcer syndrome (GUS) protocol.

text:
# 45

# **Syndromic treatment of inguinal bubo**

- Ceftriaxone, 1 g IM STAT OR Azithromycin, 1g orally STAT and then 1 g orally per week for 2 weeks OR Erythromycin, 500mg orally QID for 14 days OR Ciprofloxacin, 500mg orally BID for 3 days.

**LGV:**

- Doxycycline, 100mg orally BID for 14 days OR Azithromycin, 1g orally STAT and then 1 g orally per week for 2 weeks OR Erythromycin, 500mg orally QID for 14 days.
- * In patients intolerant to Doxycycline, or pregnant and lactating women: Give 3 doses of Azithromycin, 1 g orally per week or Erythromycin, 500mg orally QID for 14 days

**NB:** For fluctuant Buboes, refer for aspiration.

text:
# 5.7. Neonatal conjunctivitis

47

## Description

Neonatal conjunctivitis is the condition where the baby develops purulent conjunctivitis in one or both eyes within four weeks of birth. It is a medical emergency and unless treatment is initiated within 24 hours there could be permanent damage to the eyes resulting in blindness. STI-related infections are passed from the mother to the neonate during vaginal delivery.

heading_path: 5.0 Management of STIs Associated Syndromes > 5.7. Neonatal conjunctivitis > Etiology
text:
## Etiology

N. Gonorrhoeae
C. Trachomatis

## Clinical features

New-born babies usually present with redness and swelling of eyelids or "sticky eyes" due to the discharge from the eyes. The symptoms and signs may occur within one week of the birth.

## Syndromic treatment of Neonatal conjunctivitis

## Prevention measures:

- Screen all pregnant women for Sexually Transmitted Infections during pregnancy and provide appropriate treatment;
- Routine application of tetracycline eye ointment (1%) to all new-born's at the time of delivery;
- Provide health promotion package to parents.

text:
# **Eswatini National Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and Viral Hepatitis (VH) Guidelines**

- All new-born babies with conjunctivitis should be treated for both N. gonorrhoea and C. trachomatis because of the possibility of mixed infections. Clean the eyes with distilled water or saline.
- Persons caring for infected infants should always wash their hands carefully. Parents (mother and father or partner) should be examined and treated.

* Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
* Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
* Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
* Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
* Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.

text:
## 7.1 **Management of reactive syphilis test cases**

In any health facility, there are instances when a client's blood sample is tested for syphilis either as a routine practice such as screening of pregnant women or screening for syphilis in most-at-risk groups (for example, sex workers or new detainees in prison) or vulnerable populations (for example, victims of sexual abuse). Often, syphilis tests are done to rule out clinical suspicion of secondary syphilis in patients presenting with generalized skin rashes or lymphadenopathy, or to rule out latent syphilis in **asymptomatic patients**.

text:
## **Non-treponemal tests**

The Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) and the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) tests detect the antibody to cardiolipin, a component of normal mammalian cell membrane. Therefore, these tests are sensitive but not specific for syphilis.

The advantage of these tests is that the results can be quantified and used for monitoring the treatment over time. Usually, these tests are positive 4-5 weeks after the occurrence of infection. A titre of 1:8 and above indicates probable active disease or recent infection (treated or untreated), although the RPR/VDRL can be negative in up to 30% of primary GUS cases.

text:
## **Treponemal tests**

Treponemal rapid diagnostic test (RDT/Tp), Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody test (FTA), the Treponema pallidum Haemagglutination Assay (TPHA) and the Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) assay are specific tests which, if positive, indicate true infection. Once they are positive, they remain positive for life even after successful treatment. Therefore, they cannot be used for monitoring the patient's response to treatment.

## **Treatment regimens for reactive syphilis test cases**

Benzethine Penicillin, 2.4millionIU IM weekly, after testing for sensitivity, for 3 weeks.

Alternative regimens for penicillin hyper- sensitive patients:
- Doxycycline, 100mg orally BID for 30 days (non-pregnant women).
- Erythromycin, 500mg orally QDS for 30 days (pregnant women).

**Note that Jarish Herxheimer reaction (mild fever, body aches and initiation of symptoms within 2 to 12 hours of injection) can occur with penicillin injection. This should be treated with Paracetamol, 500 mg to 1 g orally QDS on 1st day. The patient should be warned of the possibility of a reaction.**

text:
## **7.1.2 Syphilis in pregnancy**

The clinical symptoms of syphilis are not altered by pregnancy. Since asymptomatic adult syphilis infection is common, all pregnant women should be screened for syphilis. This can reduce the complications of congenital syphilis. A rapid plasma reagent (RPR) test should be routinely done on pregnant mothers at first contact with the health care provider and treatment should be instituted if the RPR result is reactive and the partner should be treated as well. If RPR test is negative repeat after 3 months

text:
## Description

Balanitis refers to the inflammation of the glans penis, whereas balanoposthitis is inflammation of the glans, foreskin and/ or shaft. The main complication of balanitis is phimosis, in which case the foreskin adheres to the inflamed and swollen glans penis and cannot be retracted.

## Etiology

Candida albicans or lactobacilli

text:
## Clinical features

- The common presentation is that of itch and swelling of the glans and foreskin.
  Sometimes pain may be reported.
- Patient may have a history of recent high-risk sexual practice, such as unprotected sex.
- A history of vaginal discharge from the partner may also be reported.

The physical examination may reveal signs of inflammation (such as red colour of skin (erythema), oedema, heat and tenderness).

The texture of the skin will also be altered, with white patches or streaks in typical cases of candidal infection. Presence of genital ulcerations and urethral discharge should be sought, and if present should be treated according to the appropriate syndromic algorithms.

Secondary bacterial infection may occur, causing superficial ulcers or erosions. Service providers should be aware that balanitis/balanoposthitis is commonly associated with

## **Recommended treatment regimens**

The treatment of balanitis or balanoposthitis consists of:
- Maintaining local hygiene by retracting the foreskin, if possible, when washing.
- Instruct patient to wash the affected area daily with weak saline solution (one teaspoon of salt dissolved in one litre of lukewarm water) and avoid soap while inflammatory. PLUS
- Application of an antifungal cream i.e Clotrimazole cream applied locally twice a day x 7
- Cloxacillin 500mg QID for 7 days and Metronidazole TDS for 7 days may be given if secondary bacterial infections present.

Patients with recurrent or severe balanitis or balanoposthitis should be screened for the presence of diabetes mellitus. If the test is positive, the patient should be referred for further management.

**Health promotion package**
* Educate, ensure compliance, and counsel on treatment.
* Promote abstinence or condom use during treatment.
* Promote correct and consistent condom use also provide condoms and lubricants.
* Issue one notification slip for each sexual partner and emphasize the importance of partner treatment.
* Offer HIV counselling and testing, as per Integrated HIV Guidelines.
* Offer voluntary medical male circumcision.
* Offer pre exposure prophylaxis as per guideline.

narrative: Assessment and management of oral and throat problems in an STI context (STI/VH guidelines draft 2026, page 80). Small ulcerated or vesicular painful lesions in clusters: herpes possible; clean with mouthwash, paracetamol, acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5-7 days (reduces symptom duration only if started within 5 days of a first episode, or within 24 hours of a recurrence). Mouth ulcers (early ulcers can still have a negative treponemal test in 30% of cases): treat syphilis with benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units IM single dose; if painful, with regional lymph nodes or not resolving, suspect soft chancre and add azithromycin 1 g single dose; treat partners of the last 3 months; give azithromycin 1 g to everyone; abstain or use condoms until resolved; follow up after 7 days. Painless warts or condyloma: complicated warts; surgical treatment or imiquimod, refer to hospital. Whitish coating: with pain on swallowing, dysphagia or extensive pharyngeal lesions, oropharyngeal candidiasis, fluconazole 400 mg/day for 14 days; otherwise oral candidiasis, miconazole muco-adhesive tablet daily for 7 days, or if severe or recurrent fluconazole 200 mg/day for 10 days; rule out HIV. Throat inflammation after fellatio: pharyngitis, mostly viral; if STI risk factors and oral sex, take an NG/CT pharyngeal swab for PCR and a syphilis RDT. Always offer an HIV test.

text:
## 63 ## Treatment options for upper vaginal infection

## 7.3 Genital Warts

#### **Etiology**

# **Eswatini National Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and Viral Hepatitis (VH) Guidelines**

Human Papilloma Virus (HPV type 6 and 145)
Syphilis (Treponema pallidum)
High risk types such as HPV-16 and HPV-18 are implicated in most cervical and other anogenital cancers.

## **Clinical features**

Most infections do not have clinical symptoms
HPV warts may appear as raised or soft pink cauliflower like growth in moist areas usually painless but may itch.

There are three varieties of exophytic warts, which are sexually transmitted:
**1. Condylomata Acuminata:** Moist or partially keratinized surfaces (e.g. introitus, anus, under foreskin). Typically, cauliflower appearance. HPV
**2. Keratotic warts:** finger-like projection, often cauliflower-like appearance and typically on dry skin (e.g. penile shaft, scrotum, labia majora).
**3. Papular warts:** Smooth surfaces, less finger-like projections than keratotic warts.

text:
### **Description**

Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a type of Pox virus. Transmission occurs most commonly through sexual or non-sexual contact, and is enhanced by friction or micro-trauma.

### **Etiology**

Poxy virus

### **Clinical features**

- The typical eruption appears as a pearly white dome-shaped papule with central umblication from which caseous material can be expressed.
- These lesions mostly appear at the point of contact (such as the genital area).
- Individual lesions usually regress without treatment in 9-12 months.

text:
# **Eswatini National Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and Viral Hepatitis (VH) Guidelines**

- Generalized lesions, especially <mark>multiple</mark> lesions on face, may indicate immunosuppression due to underlying infection.

## **Management**

- Excision curettage: Each lesion should be thoroughly opened with a fine sterile needle.
- The contents should be expressed and the inner wall touched with either Phenol/ Silver Nitrate. OR Trichloroacetic acid 30% solution or Iodine solution.
- OR Apply Podophyllotoxin 0.5% to the individual lesion BID for 3days.
- OR Imiquimod 5% cream.
- OR Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen.

## **Cases for referral**

Patients with generalized lesions should be encouraged to undergo HIV testing and counselling, if their sero-status is unknown. These patients should be referred to the dermatology unit for further management.

## 7.5 Management of Survivors Of Sexual Violence

### **Definition**

Sexual violence is defined as "any sexual act, attempt to obtain a sexual act, unwanted sexual comments or advances, or acts to traffic women's sexuality, using coercion, threats of harm or physical force, by any person regardless of relationship to the victim, in any setting, including but not limited to home and work".

Patients with generalized lesions should be encouraged to undergo HIV testing and counselling, if their sero-status is unknown. These patients should be referred to the dermatology unit for further management.

## 7.5 Management of Survivors Of Sexual Violence

### **Definition**

Sexual violence is defined as "any sexual act, attempt to obtain a sexual act, unwanted sexual comments or advances, or acts to traffic women's sexuality, using coercion, threats of harm or physical force, by any person regardless of relationship to the victim, in any setting, including but not limited to home and work".

## 70

## **Clinical features**

Survivors of sexual assault have experienced a traumatic event and should be rapidly evaluated to determine whether they need emergency medical, psychological or social intervention. It is important to remember that the trauma of the event may make examination difficult. Explain carefully the steps that will be taken and obtain written informed consent from the patient before proceeding with examination, treatment, notification or referral.

text:
## 7.6 Genital Scabies

**Definition**

Genital scabies is caused by the Scabies mite (Sarcoptes scabiei), and is transmitted by close contact with an infected case, either sexual or non-sexual.

**Etiology**

Sarcoptes scabiei

**Clinical features**

- The main complaint with genital scabies is itching especially at night-time.
- On physical examination, erythematous papules can be seen mainly on the flexure surfaces of the body, such as the axillae, elbow, and wrist, inter-digital spaces, around the umbilicus, inner thighs and back of the knee.
- Finding burrows tunneled by the female mites in the inter-digital spaces is diagnostic of scabies infection.

**Management**

Recommended treatment regimens in adults

- Benzyl Benzoate (BB) 25% lotion, to be applied all over the body below the neck, after a bath, for two consecutive nights. Patient should bathe 24 hours after the second application, and have a change of clothing. Bed linen is to be washed properly and dried under sunlight. A second course of drug application may be given after 7~10 days, if required.
OR
- Gamma Benzene Hex chloride (GBH) 1% lotion or cream applied as a very thin film all over the body below the neck at night without taking a bath, to be washed

off thoroughly next day morning, after 8~10 hours. The application of the drug should be repeated after 7days, if required. Clothes should be washed properly and dried under sunlight.

OR

- Permethrin 5% cream to be applied all over the body as a thin film and washed off after 8~10 hours. A second application is sometimes required.
OR
- Sulphur 6% in petrolatum applied to the entire body from the back down for 3 nights after a bath. Patients may bath before re-applying the drug and should bath 24 hours after the final application.
OR
- Crotamiton 10% cream to be applied to the entire body from the neck down at night for 2~5 nights and washed off thoroughly by taking a bath 24 hours after the last application.

Treatment in infants, children younger than 10 years, pregnant or lactating women
Gamma Benzene Hexachloride is contra-indicated in pregnant women, lactating mothers, infants and patients of scabies with secondary infection or with eczematisation, as it increases the risk of absorption, leading to systemic toxicity, resulting in seizures and aplastic anaemia. It should be applied with caution in the elderly. It should not be applied near the eyes.

The recommended regimen is:
- Crotamiton 10% cream/ sulphur 6% in petrolatum/ Permethrin 5%cream to be applied as above.

- The symptoms and clinical signs of the infection include severe itching around the pubic area, often resulting in scratching.
- The scratch markings on the skin may become secondarily infected with bacterial infections. Although the lice and nits remain mostly confined to pubic and peri-anal areas, they may spread to thighs, axillae, chest, eyelashes eyebrows and other areas.
- The diagnosis is established by clinical examination, as the parasite (adult or nits) is visible to the naked eye.
- The mature lice are brown or bluish grey in colour and approximately the size of pinheads.

text:
## Definition

Cervical cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer death in developing countries worldwide. The primary underlying cause is infection with one of more high-risk types of the human papilloma (HPV) virus, a sexually transmitted virus. HPV type 16 and 18 has been associated with 70% of all cervical cancers reported. The virus has also been implicated in other genital cancers: the attribute risk for 40% of penile cancer, 42% of anal cancer in men and 46% of vulvae and vaginal cancer is HPV type 16 and 18 infection. Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 are rarely associated with cancer, but commonly cause ano-genital warts.

heading_path: 7.0 Management of Other STI's And Related Clinical Conditions > 7.8 Human papilloma virus infection > Pre-disposing factors
text:
## Pre-disposing factors

The key determinants of HPV infection for both men and women are sexual behaviors, including young age at sexual debut, high number of sexual partner(s), and having a partner who has multiple partners.

Smoking is a potential risk factor for cervical cancer. Most HPV infections (low- or high-risk) resolve spontaneously. However, high-risk HPV infections that persist may lead to the development of precancerous and invasive cancer.

It usually takes 10-20 years for precursor lesions caused by HPV to develop into invasive cancers.

## Clinical features

Some types of HPV are warts, especially genital warts. Genital warts may appear as a small bump, cluster of lesions or sterm-like protrusions. They commonly affect the vulva, cervix, penis and scrotum. They may also appear around the anus and in the groin. They can range in size and appearance and be flat, small, large, or cauliflower shaped and may be white or flesh tone.

text:
## 79

## **Preventive measures**

Effective prevention interventions against ano-genital cancer include screening for and treatment of pre-cancer and invasive cancer. All women and men presenting at health facilities should be offered a complete ano-genital examination to determine whether they have this HPV-related cancer.

It is recommended that all sexually active women should have regular cervical cancer screening in accordance with the national guidelines. Male circumcision should be offered to all uncircumcised male patients and partners. Smoking cessation interventions should be implemented at the individual and community levels. Highly effective vaccines against high-risk types of HPV have recently become available.

text:
## **Hepatitis B and C viral infection**

Chronic viral hepatitis is a persistent liver infection, most often caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV), leading to ongoing inflammation and liver damage lasting longer than six months. Transmission occurs through exposure to infectious blood or body fluids, including unprotected sex, sharing of needles or unsterilised piercing/cutting instruments, blood transfusion, and from mother to child around the time of birth. HBV is 50-100 times more infectious than HIV. Both infections can be entirely asymptomatic, present as an acute illness (nausea, fatigue, dark urine, jaundice), or persist as a chronic infection that, over years, can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer; HCV is now a curable infection.

In 2016 WHO adopted a global strategy to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, targeting a 90% reduction in new infections, a 65% reduction in mortality, and treatment of 80% of those eligible. Eswatini is a high HBV-prevalence country, estimated at 8.7% in the general population; HCV prevalence is lower, estimated at 0.4%. Globally, only around 13% of people living with chronic HBV have been diagnosed and about 3% are on treatment, underlining the importance of the screening and linkage-to-care steps below.

text:
### **Target groups for screening**

All persons in Eswatini should be offered HBV and HCV testing at least once; the following groups should be prioritised:
- Patients with clinical or laboratory suspicion of acute or chronic hepatitis
- All pregnant women (HBV as part of the HIV/syphilis/HBsAg triple test in antenatal care; HCV where risk factors are present)
- People living with HIV, and people with known HCV infection
- Household contacts and sexual partners of a person with HBV or HCV
- Children born to HBsAg-positive mothers
- Health workers and students in health-related training, and other frontline personnel (police, armed forces)
- Blood, tissue and organ donors and recipients; haemodialysis patients
- Prisoners and other closed settings
- Key populations: people who inject or use drugs, sex workers, men who have sex with men
- Adolescents and young people, and persons with multiple sexual partners
- People born before 2004 (before hepatitis B vaccine was introduced into the national schedule)

text:
## **Diagnosis of hepatitis B**

Diagnosis is based on detection of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), using a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or ELISA on whole blood, capillary blood, dried blood spot, serum or plasma. A second positive HBsAg result after at least 6 months confirms chronic HBV infection. Where available, HBeAg and HBV DNA (viral load) further stage the infection and inform treatment eligibility but are not required to diagnose chronic infection.

text:
## **Diagnosis of hepatitis C**

Initial diagnosis is serological, using an RDT or ELISA for anti-HCV antibodies; a non-reactive result indicates no infection. A reactive antibody test indicates exposure only, and must be confirmed with a molecular test for HCV RNA (qualitative or quantitative) or HCV core antigen to distinguish current from past, spontaneously-cleared infection. If recent infection is suspected, a **81** confirmatory test should be repeated 12-24 weeks later before infection is excluded.

## **Prevention**

General prevention measures - infection prevention and control precautions, safe blood transfusion, injection and surgical safety, condom use, and hepatitis B vaccination of priority groups - are described in the STI and Viral Hepatitis prevention section (Section 3). There is currently no vaccine against hepatitis C. Sexual partners of a person with HBV should be tested and, if not immune, offered vaccine; sexual partners of a person with HCV should be tested with an anti-HCV test.

text:
## **Prevention of hepatitis B mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT)**

Most chronic HBV infection is acquired perinately or in early childhood, and infection acquired as a neonate becomes chronic in about 90% of cases, compared with under 5% when acquired as an adult. All pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis and HBsAg at least once, as early as possible in pregnancy, or at admission for delivery if not previously tested. Since 2020 WHO has recommended antiviral (tenofovir, TDF) prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA (≥200 000 IU/mL) or a positive HBeAg test, given from at least the second trimester until delivery. Where HBV DNA or HBeAg testing is not available, the 2024 WHO guideline recommends offering TDF prophylaxis to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women and adolescent girls. Regardless of maternal antiviral prophylaxis, every infant should receive a timely birth-dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by the remaining doses in the national EPI schedule; there is no evidence that caesarean delivery reduces HBV transmission risk, so standard obstetric practice should be followed.

*Figure 12: Algorithm on use of antiviral prophylaxis for prevention of mother-to-child transmission in pregnant women and adolescent girls with CHB, and assessment of treatment eligibility for their own health (WHO, 2024)*

### **Newborn care and follow-up of infants exposed to HBV**

All newborns should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth regardless of the mother's HBV status, with particular attention to infants of HBsAg-positive mothers; subsequent doses follow the national EPI schedule. If birth does not occur at a health facility, the birth dose should be given at first contact with a health facility. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in HBV infection. HBsAg testing of an exposed infant is unreliable before 6 months of age; exposed infants should be tested for HBsAg between 6 and 12 months, and referred for specialist evaluation if chronic infection (HBsAg positive for 6 months or more) is confirmed.

text:
## **Prevention of hepatitis C vertical transmission**

82

HCV vertical transmission occurs less often than with HBV (under 5-10% of pregnancies). There is currently no vaccine or antiviral prophylaxis to prevent HCV vertical transmission, and DAA treatment is not recommended during pregnancy. There is no evidence to recommend a particular mode of delivery for this purpose, though prolonged rupture of membranes (over 6 hours) and invasive procedures during delivery should be avoided where possible; breastfeeding is not contraindicated. Maternal anti-HCV antibody can persist in an infant up to 18 months of age without indicating true infection; testing of an HCV-exposed child should therefore use anti-HCV serology after 18 months, confirmed by HCV RNA if positive. A child with a positive antibody test and detectable HCV RNA after 18 months has confirmed chronic HCV infection and should be referred to a paediatrician.

text:
## **Treatment of chronic hepatitis B**

The goal of treatment is to prevent progression to cirrhosis, liver failure and hepatocellular carcinoma, and to improve survival; sustained suppression of HBV DNA is the primary marker of treatment success. Acute HBV infection does not usually require treatment, since most adults clear it spontaneously; antiviral treatment is occasionally needed for severe/fulminant acute hepatitis or in immunocompromised patients.

text:
## **Treatment regimen**

84

For all adults, adolescents and children aged 2 years or older who need antiviral therapy, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV) - nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high genetic barrier to resistance - are the preferred first-line regimens, used as monotherapy rather than combined. Where TDF monotherapy is not available, TDF plus lamivudine (3TC) or TDF plus emtricitabine (FTC) is an acceptable alternative first-line regimen. Entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is preferred for people with osteoporosis or impaired renal function. Older agents - telbivudine, lamivudine monotherapy and adefovir - are no longer recommended except on specialist advice, owing to a low barrier to resistance.

text:
*Figure 14: Algorithm for assessment, treatment and monitoring of people with chronic hepatitis B infection (WHO, 2024)*

## **Treatment monitoring**

People on treatment should be monitored at least annually with a non-invasive test (APRI or transient elastography) for fibrosis/cirrhosis progression, ALT (and AST for APRI), and HBV DNA and HBeAg/anti-HBe where available; adherence should be assessed at every visit. More frequent monitoring, every 3-6 months, is recommended during the first year of treatment, for people with compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, where adherence is a concern, for people with HIV coinfection, and for people with renal impairment. People with cirrhosis or a family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis should additionally be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma (ultrasound and AFP) every 6 months.

## **Treatment monitoring**

People on treatment should be monitored at least annually with a non-invasive test (APRI or transient elastography) for fibrosis/cirrhosis progression, ALT (and AST for APRI), and HBV DNA and HBeAg/anti-HBe where available; adherence should be assessed at every visit. More frequent monitoring, every 3-6 months, is recommended during the first year of treatment, for people with compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, where adherence is a concern, for people with HIV coinfection, and for people with renal impairment. People with cirrhosis or a family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis should additionally be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma (ultrasound and AFP) every 6 months.

text:
# 86

# Viral Hepatitis and HIV Co-infection

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HCV co-infection with HIV is commonly found in HBV-endemic countries in Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and South America. HIV and HBV/HCV share transmission routes; globally an estimated 2.73 million people are co-infected with HIV and HBV, and 2.3 million with HIV and HCV. As antiretroviral therapy (ART) has reduced HIV-associated opportunistic infections and mortality, HBV/HCV-related liver disease has become a leading cause of death among people living with HIV in some settings. Prevalence of HIV/HCV coinfection is generally higher where injection drug use is a primary route of HIV transmission. See Section 12.0 for guidance specific to HBV/HIV co-infected patients, including the choice of ART regimen.

## Description and etiology

Hepatitis C is a bloodborne viral infection of the liver. Most infections occur through injection drug use, unsterile equipment used for tribal markings/scarfification, unsafe injection or other healthcare practices, and use of unscreened blood for transfusion; sexual practices that expose a partner to blood can also transmit HCV.

text:
## Treatment of chronic hepatitis C

HCV infection is curable. WHO recommends pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens for all adults, adolescents and children aged 3 years and above with chronic HCV, regardless of disease stage, to prevent progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma and to stop onward transmission. Pangenotypic regimens remove the need for genotyping before starting treatment. Fibrosis assessment (APRI or transient elastography) can help determine whether cirrhosis is present and the follow-up needed after cure, but should not delay treatment initiation. DAAs have very few contraindications with other medicines and few side-effects, so routine toxicity monitoring can be limited to a specimen at the start and end of treatment. The goals of treatment are to achieve a sustained virologic response (cure), prevent progression to complications, prevent onward transmission, and improve quality of life.

text:
## **Management of treatment interruption**

Treatment interruption (missing at least 7 consecutive days of DAA therapy) is more common in patients who are difficult to follow up, such as people experiencing homelessness or people who use drugs; missing a couple of doses usually does not affect treatment success. Management depends on how much treatment had been completed before the interruption:
- **On treatment for under 4 weeks:** assess the reason for interruption, provide counselling and, if the patient wishes to continue, restart the regimen from the beginning.
- **On treatment for 4-8 weeks:** extend the treatment duration by the length of the interruption.
- **On treatment for over 8 weeks:** if the interruption was under 2 weeks, extend treatment by the interruption length. If 2 weeks or more: for non-cirrhotic patients in areas with low genotype-3 prevalence, stop treatment and check HCV RNA 12 weeks later; for cirrhotic patients or areas with high genotype-3 prevalence, extend treatment to complete the full planned course and check HCV RNA 12 weeks after completion. Document the interruption, management plan and follow-up result clearly in the notes.

text:
*Figure 17: Algorithm for screening, diagnosis, assessment, treatment and follow-up of people with chronic HCV infection (WHO)*

### **Special populations**

* **Renal impairment:** Daclatasvir, velpatasvir and voxilaprevir need no dose adjustment in renal failure; sofosbuvir, previously avoided when creatinine clearance was under 30 mL/min, is now considered safe even in end-stage renal failure. Ribavirin should be avoided when eGFR is under 30.
* **HIV/HCV co-infection:** liver disease progresses faster even when HIV is well controlled, so this group is prioritised for HCV treatment; whether to treat HCV before or alongside ART should be decided case-by-case, particularly because of drug-drug interactions.
* **HBV/HCV co-infection:** HCV is usually the main driver of liver inflammation, but HBV reactivation is possible during DAA treatment, particularly in patients with cirrhosis,

where it can precipitate liver failure. Patients who meet HBV treatment criteria should start lifelong HBV treatment alongside HCV treatment; where lifelong HBV treatment is not available, HBV treatment should continue at least until HCV treatment is complete.

- **People who use drugs:** people who use drugs are at risk of re-infection if needle sharing continues; adequate needle and syringe programmes (NSP) and opioid substitution therapy (OST) reduce HCV incidence, and OST alone has been shown to reduce transmission by 50-80%. Treatment should not be withheld because of concerns about adherence or re-infection - treating this group reduces HCV prevalence and transmission, especially combined with NSP/OST and peer support. People who remain at risk after cure should be tested with HCV antibody every 12 months if antibody-negative, or with HCV RNA (not antibody, which can remain positive lifelong) if previously cured.

text:
## **8.0 STI'S in Men Who Have Sex With Men**

STI's in men who have sex with men (MSM) are no different from STI's in the rest of the population, but the types of sexual practices determine the site where STI's occur. STI's in MSM can be transmitted by penile-anal contact, oro-anal contact, or fingering. Anogenital symptoms can result due to penile-anal contact. Symptoms due to peri-anal ulcers (for example, herpes, chancroid and syphilis) and warts can cause pain, tenesmus, bleeding, and discharge. Oro-anal intercourse can lead to the transmission of a wide variety of other organisms normally transmitted by the feaco-oral route.

These include hepatitis A virus, shigella, salmonella, and giardia, resulting in gastrointestinal symptoms. Anal intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive carcinoma may follow infection with high-risk subtypes of human papilloma virus. Oral and peri-oral symptoms can result because of oro-genital sexual activity. Oral STI's usually are asymptomatic. Neisseria gonorrhoea and Chlamydia infect the pharyngeal mucosa readily, but rarely cause pharyngeal infections. Syphilis, chancroid and herpes may cause ulcers on the tongue, oral mucosa, palate or lips. Warts may develop in and around the mouth.

text:
# Management of STI's in men<sup>91</sup> who have sex with men

In general, the clinical management of STI's in MSM is the same as outlined elsewhere in this document earlier. The service provider should conduct rectal and oro-pharyngeal examinations when providing care to MSM. Additional infections common in MSM that are not covered in the flow charts include oral or pharyngeal and ano-rectal STI's, and are described below. Service providers should be aware that oral and anal STI's can also occur in female patients practicing oral or anal sex. Therefore, as a standard of care every patient (irrespective of sex or gender) should be examined thoroughly to exclude STI's in these sites.

text:
## Management of sexually transmitted pharyngitis

Clinically, it is difficult to diagnose gonococcal or chlamydia l pharyngitis reliably. Additionally, service providers should be aware that pharyngeal gonorrhoea can be more difficult to clear than urethral infections. Other oro-pharyngeal STI's (such as herpes and warts) can often be detected by physical examination and can be managed according to the treatment guidelines. It is recommended that whenever a MSM patient is suffering from significant pharyngitis, and a history of unprotected oral sex makes pharyngeal gonococcal or chlamydia l infection a likely risk, the patient should be treated syndromically
